art/art-architecture.2cb0fc4e6ba4: This plaster cast is in Gallery three of the Fitzwilliam Museum in Cambridge, England. The original relief came from the fifth-century B C E Parthenon. Rotate the cast sideways and see how far the figures stand out.
art/art-architecture.428f47d7e10b: The curves of a pointed arch meet at a peak. Tall stained-glass windows color daylight and draw your eyes up. In “The Blue Virgin,” the light-blue central panels date to the twelfth century. The surrounding glass is from the thirteenth century.
art/art-architecture.a51703ef5907: Eight columns line each short end, and seventeen line each long side, counting the corner columns on both sides. The platform at the columns is about sixty-nine point five meters long and thirty point nine meters wide. The long side is about two point two five times the short side.

art/art-chinese.9df2bbd6c552: Four Treasures of the Study. Brush, ink, paper and inkstone — 笔, 墨, 纸, 砚. Brushes are made of animal hair, goat, weasel, rabbit, set in bamboo. Ink sticks of soot and glue are ground with water on a stone inkstone. Xuan paper, 宣纸, from Anhui soaks up ink instantly — no erasing! 笔墨纸砚: Brush, Ink, Paper, Stone.

art/art-color.9ab940d3478f: Tertiary colors. A primary and its neighbouring secondary: red-orange, blue-green… There are six: red-orange, yellow-orange, yellow-green, blue-green, blue-violet, red-violet. Primary name goes first in English: “blue-green”, not “green-blue”. Three plus three plus six equals the twelve colors of the wheel. Three primaries plus three secondaries plus six tertiaries equals twelve slices of the color pizza.
art/art-color.90d985233587: Secondary colors. Mix two primaries: orange, green, violet. Red plus yellow equals orange; yellow plus blue equals green; blue plus red equals violet. Each secondary sits halfway between its two parents on the wheel. Secondary equals second step: two primaries holding hands.
art/art-color.57e59efd6da1: Primary colors. Colors you can’t mix from others — you mix everything else from them. Paint, RYB: red, yellow, blue. Light, RGB: red, green, blue — screens, stage lights. Printing, CMY and K: cyan, magenta, yellow and black. Paint equals RYB, Really Yummy Berries. Light equals RGB, Really Glowing Bulbs.
art/art-color.0fca42909644: Value: tints and shades. How light or dark a color is. Tint equals color and white, pink is a tint of red. Shade equals color and black, navy is a shade of blue. Value contrast is what makes a design readable from far away. Tint equals Touch of white. Shade equals Shadow, black.

art/art-games.931ab98a83d7: From the aligned view, the centers of the two end cubes land on the same spot on screen. The ends look joined. Turn the three D model to see where they come apart.
art/art-games.790f435e6ca2: Tap or drag on the sixteen times sixteen grid and watch the enlarged preview. Can you redraw the sprout with just three colors and still make it easy to recognize?

art/art-history.1f49d966ca32: Street art and murals. Nineteen ninety, Berlin, Germany. Art leaves the museum. After the Berlin Wall fell, artists from around the world painted about one point three kilometers, zero point eight miles, of it — the East Side Gallery. Meanwhile in China: contemporary art was booming; Beijing’s seven nine eight Art District turned old factories into galleries in the early two thousands.
art/art-history.7f86474d4dce: Post-Impressionism. Eighteen eighty-nine, Saint-Rémy, France. Color and brushstroke show feeling, not just what the eye sees. Van Gogh’s sky swirls; Seurat built pictures from tiny dots, pointillism. Meanwhile in China: Ren Bonian and other Shanghai School painters mixed traditional ink painting with bright colors for city buyers.
art/art-history.36b3cf7ea471: Renaissance. about fifteen oh three to fifteen nineteen, Florence, Italy. Linear perspective and sfumato, “smoky”: no hard outlines, just soft glazes of oil paint so thin you can’t see brushstrokes. Meanwhile in China: the Ming dynasty — the Forbidden City was finished in fourteen twenty and Jingdezhen kilns were making blue-and-white porcelain.
art/art-history.3d9783c37813: Japanese woodblock prints. about eighteen thirty to eighteen thirty-two, Edo, Tokyo, Japan. Ukiyo-e prints: one carved wooden block per color, thousands of cheap copies. Hokusai used a new imported pigment — Prussian blue. Meanwhile in China: the Qing dynasty under the Daoguang Emperor; the Opium War would begin in eighteen forty.
art/art-history.6f75eeac9b8e: Song landscape painting. Eleven thirteen, Kaifeng, Northern Song China. Landscape becomes the hero. Eighteen-year-old Wang Ximeng painted mountains in brilliant mineral blue and green, azurite and malachite, on a scroll almost twelve meters, thirty-nine feet, long. Meanwhile in Europe: Romanesque churches with thick walls and round arches; the Bayeux Tapestry, about ten seventies, told a story in embroidery.
art/art-history.cd577fb9a73b: Impressionism. Eighteen seventy-two, Le Havre, France. Paint outdoors, fast, in broken dabs of color to catch changing light. Paint in metal tubes, invented eighteen forty-one, made it easy. A critic mocked this painting’s title — and the name “Impressionism” stuck. Meanwhile in China: the Self-Strengthening Movement, 洋务运动, was building China’s first modern factories and shipyards.
art/art-history.a4e73731e2bf: Cave art. about seventeen thousand years ago, Lascaux, France. Paint from the earth: red and yellow ochre, black charcoal — dabbed with moss or blown through hollow bones. Bumps in the rock became the bellies of animals. Meanwhile in China: people in Xianrendong Cave, Jiangxi, were making some of the world’s oldest known pottery, around twenty thousand years ago.
art/art-history.4addf86a97ef: Modern and abstract art. Nineteen thirty, Paris, Mondrian was Dutch. Art doesn’t have to show “things”: pure line, shape and color can be the whole subject, abstraction. Kandinsky had started painting abstracts around nineteen ten to nineteen thirteen. Meanwhile in China: Xu Beihong, 徐悲鸿, combined Western drawing with Chinese ink — famous for his galloping horses.
art/art-history.55549acb654b: Ancient Egypt. about thirteen fifty B C E, Thebes, Egypt. Rules beat realism: head and legs in profile, but eye and shoulders from the front. Important people are drawn bigger, hierarchical scale. Meanwhile in China: the Shang dynasty, about sixteen hundred to ten forty-six B C E, cast giant bronze vessels and carved writing on oracle bones.
art/art-history.02612d17eb87: Ancient Greece. Four hundred forty-seven to four hundred thirty-two B C E, Athens, Greece. Beauty equals harmony and math: ideal proportions, balanced columns, statues standing in a relaxed, natural pose. Meanwhile in China: the late Spring and Autumn or early Warring States period — Confucius, five hundred fifty-one to four hundred seventy-nine B C E, had died a few decades earlier.

art/art-sculpture.fa23504bf1ff: A turn through the torso and a forward knee give this standing figure movement. The three D view is a scan of a museum plaster cast of the marble. Compare the bare torso with the folds twisting below it.

art/art-theater.5765850f5f3d: Kunqu developed around Kunshan and influenced many other forms, earning the nickname “ancestor of a hundred operas.” UNESCO proclaimed it a Masterpiece in two thousand one and inscribed it on its Representative List in two thousand eight. In The Peony Pavilion, listen to how the voice and flute move together.
art/art-theater.104853f2715b: New York’s Chinatown has a tradition of staging opera in Cantonese. Yuèqǔ is Cantonese narrative singing, and some of its songs come from opera. UNESCO inscribed Cantonese opera on its Representative List in two thousand nine. Listen to the two performers sing to each other.

astronomy/big-bang.134cbe4dfaea: Protons and neutrons form. After about ten millionths of a second it is “cool” enough, a few trillion degrees, for quarks to clump in threes into protons and neutrons.
astronomy/big-bang.74d05261aa46: Life on Earth. At least three point five billion years ago, maybe earlier, simple single-celled microbes live in Earth’s oceans. Animals come much later: the first dinosaurs only two hundred thirty million years ago.
astronomy/big-bang.32f22c95fdef: Galaxy G N z one one. Found by Hubble, twenty sixteen, studied by Webb. We see it as it was about four hundred million years after the Big Bang. Its light set out almost nine billion years before the Sun and Earth formed.
astronomy/big-bang.209a63e73dc5: The first nuclei, three to twenty minutes. For about twenty minutes the whole universe is a nuclear fusion reactor. Protons and neutrons fuse into helium nuclei, plus a little deuterium and lithium. Result: about seventy-five percent hydrogen and twenty-five percent helium by mass, exactly what we measure in the oldest gas and stars.
astronomy/big-bang.4fb080f8a4a2: The Sun. One hundred fifty million kilometers away. Sunlight takes eight minutes twenty seconds to reach Earth. If the Sun suddenly vanished, we would keep seeing it, and orbiting it, for over eight minutes.
astronomy/big-bang.e3f5020975e6: Dark energy takes over. As galaxies spread apart, matter’s gravity weakens and dark energy wins. The expansion, which had been slowing down, starts to speed up. Astronomers discovered this in nineteen ninety-eight using Type one A supernovae.
astronomy/big-bang.34c3ffcd6bba: First atoms: the CMB is released, three hundred eighty thousand years. Until now light kept bouncing off free electrons, like headlights in fog. At about three thousand kelvins electrons join nuclei to make the first atoms, the fog clears, and light travels freely. That light is the cosmic microwave background we still detect today.
astronomy/big-bang.55bf96a9ff2d: Cosmic noon. About three billion years in, galaxies make new stars roughly ten times faster than today. Galaxies collide and merge, and giant black holes in their centers blaze as quasars.
astronomy/big-bang.ba7a1fb1cc04: The first galaxies. The James Webb Space Telescope has found galaxies seen just two hundred ninety million years after the Big Bang, such as JADES G S z one four dash zero, already surprisingly bright. Small galaxies merge to build bigger ones.
astronomy/big-bang.8b9e07670701: M eight seven in the Virgo Cluster. A giant elliptical galaxy, fifty-three million light-years away. Its light left about twelve million years after an asteroid wiped out the dinosaurs. Its central black hole was the first one ever photographed, twenty nineteen.
astronomy/big-bang.02d95fad96f1: The cosmic microwave background. The farthest light there is. Released three hundred eighty thousand years after the Big Bang, from every direction at once. Before this the universe was an opaque fog: no light from earlier can reach us.
astronomy/big-bang.2ee47d4ef27f: Galaxy JADES G S z one four dash zero. Found by JWST in twenty twenty-four; the distance record holder until twenty twenty-five. We see it only about two hundred ninety million years after the Big Bang. Its light was stretched so much that it arrives as infrared, which is why Webb was built to see infrared.
astronomy/big-bang.54da1d11ed13: Cosmic dawn: the first stars. Around one hundred to two hundred million years, gas in dark-matter clumps collapses into the first stars: huge, hot and blue, made only of hydrogen and helium. When they explode they make the first carbon, oxygen and iron, and their light starts to clear the hydrogen fog, reionization.
astronomy/big-bang.59744e804583: Today: thirteen point eight billion years. Space between the galaxies is just two point seven degrees above absolute zero, and the expansion is speeding up. If all of cosmic history were squeezed into one year, modern humans would appear in the last eleven minutes of December thirty-first.
astronomy/big-bang.25a9c2290cf2: Inflation. In far less than a trillionth of a trillionth of a second, a tiny patch of space balloons by an enormous factor, at least ten to the power of twenty-six times. Tiny quantum jitters get stretched into the seeds of every future galaxy. This is the least certain part of the story: strong clues, not yet proven.
astronomy/big-bang.6e09acab295f: Quasar three C two seven three. The first quasar identified, nineteen sixty-three. A galaxy whose central black hole is swallowing gas so fast that it outshines its whole galaxy hundreds of times over. When its light set out, life on Earth was still only single-celled.
astronomy/big-bang.f8bf3be71b4d: Center of the Milky Way. About twenty-six thousand light-years away. Its light left during the last ice age, when mammoths roamed North America. We can’t see it with our eyes, dust blocks it, but infrared and radio telescopes can.
astronomy/big-bang.6b84616c2fab: Proxima Centauri. The nearest star, four point two four light-years away. The light you would see tonight left it about four years ago. A message sent there by radio today would arrive around twenty thirty-one, and a reply would come back around twenty thirty-five.
astronomy/big-bang.300ca5245f26: The Moon. Three hundred eighty-four thousand kilometers away. Moonlight, really reflected sunlight, takes one point three seconds to reach you. So the Moon you see is the Moon of about one heartbeat ago.
astronomy/big-bang.fc44a5ec7dd8: The Sun and Earth form. Four point six billion years ago, a cloud of gas enriched by generations of earlier stars collapses into the Sun and a disk that becomes the planets. The iron in your blood and the calcium in your bones were made inside those earlier stars.
astronomy/big-bang.bdef9f019206: Andromeda Galaxy. The farthest thing you can see with your eyes alone. Two point five million light-years away: the light entering your eye left when the first members of our human genus, Homo, were appearing in Africa. On a dark autumn night you can see it as a faint smudge in the constellation Andromeda.

astronomy/black-holes.4492b1e31acb: The Sun. A normal star: a gentle dip. The Sun is one point four million kilometers, eight hundred seventy thousand miles, wide and holds ninety-nine point eight percent of the Solar System’s mass. Its gravity curves spacetime gently: the planets roll around the dip in orbits. To escape from its surface you need six hundred eighteen kilometers per second, only zero point two percent of the speed of light. The Sun will never become a black hole: it isn’t massive enough. It will end as a white dwarf. Same mass, bigger size, gentler dip.
astronomy/black-holes.7ebd2f98770f: White dwarf, Sirius B. A Sun’s mass squeezed to Earth’s size. Sirius B has about the Sun’s mass packed into a ball smaller than Earth. A teaspoon of white-dwarf matter would weigh several tons on Earth. Escape speed from its surface: about six thousand eight hundred kilometers per second, a little over two percent of light speed. This is how stars like our Sun end their lives. Smaller ball, same mass, deeper dip near it.
astronomy/black-holes.9894c4344cde: Black hole, Cygnus X one. About twenty-one Suns inside a sixty-two-kilometer horizon. Cygnus X one was the first object widely accepted as a black hole, nineteen seventies. It is about seven thousand light-years away. Its event horizon has a radius of about sixty-two kilometers, thirty-nine miles. At the event horizon the escape speed equals the speed of light, so nothing inside can get out, not even light. We “see” it because gas pulled from its companion star heats up to millions of degrees and glows in X-rays. Event horizon equals the point of no return.
astronomy/black-holes.01ae12602951: Neutron star. One point four Suns squeezed to the size of a city. A neutron star is about twenty-four kilometers, fifteen miles, across, roughly the size of a city like Atlanta. It is made almost entirely of neutrons packed as tightly as in an atomic nucleus. Escape speed from its surface is about sixty percent of the speed of light. Squeezed inside a radius of about four kilometers, the same mass would be a black hole. Neutron star: one step away from a black hole.

astronomy/eclipses.6f93f9611817: Common mix-up: It is the Moon’s five-degree orbit tilt, not Earth’s twenty-three point five-degree axis tilt, that prevents monthly eclipses.
astronomy/eclipses.844954575b03: The Sun. Four hundred times wider than the Moon, four hundred times farther away. The Sun is about four hundred times wider than the Moon, but also about four hundred times farther away, so both look almost the same size in our sky. That lucky match is why the Moon can just barely cover the Sun in a total solar eclipse. Never look straight at the Sun, even during a partial eclipse. Use certified eclipse glasses. Four hundred times bigger, four hundred times farther equals the same size in the sky.
astronomy/eclipses.0c42148f3672: Moon’s tilted orbit. Tilted about five degrees, drawn three times larger. The Moon’s orbit is tilted about five degrees compared with Earth’s orbit around the Sun. So in most months the new Moon passes a little above or below the Sun, and the full Moon passes above or below Earth’s shadow. That is why we don’t get a solar and a lunar eclipse every month. Tilt, the shadows miss most months.
astronomy/eclipses.f7977202084a: Moon’s umbra. Where people see a TOTAL solar eclipse. The Moon’s umbra is small: on Earth it makes a dark spot at most about two hundred seventy kilometers wide. As the Moon moves and Earth turns, the spot sweeps a narrow “path of totality”. Totality lasts at most about seven and a half minutes. When the Moon is far from Earth, the umbra ends before reaching Earth: people see an annular, ring, eclipse instead. Small umbra spot equals total eclipse for only a few people.
astronomy/eclipses.15abbdea6f64: Earth’s umbra. Darkest part of Earth’s shadow. Inside the umbra the Sun is completely hidden by Earth. If the whole Moon is inside it: total lunar eclipse. If only part: partial lunar eclipse. Earth’s umbra is wide enough to hold the whole Moon, so totality can last up to about one hour forty minutes. Umbra equals the dark, umbrella-like core.
astronomy/eclipses.52c4ae2dab5a: Nodes and eclipse seasons. Where the two orbits cross. The two points where the Moon’s orbit crosses the plane of Earth’s orbit are called nodes. An eclipse can only happen when a new or full Moon happens near a node. The nodes line up with the Sun about every six months, in “eclipse seasons”. Every year has at least two solar eclipses, most are partial. Eclipse equals new or full Moon and near a node.
astronomy/eclipses.7749967c0530: The Moon. Blocks the Sun, or moves into Earth’s shadow. A solar eclipse can only happen at new Moon; a lunar eclipse only at full Moon. In a total lunar eclipse the Moon turns coppery red, because Earth’s atmosphere bends reddish sunlight into the shadow, like all the world’s sunsets at once. The Moon is about four hundred times closer than the Sun. Solar equals new Moon. Lunar equals full Moon.

astronomy/exoplanets.666f0d57e75b: Earth crossing the Sun. A tiny dip once a year. Earth is one hundred nine times narrower than the Sun, so it blocks only one over one hundred nine, all squared, about zero point zero zero eight four percent of the light: eighty-four parts per million. The transit lasts about thirteen hours, once every three hundred sixty-five days. Only a telescope in space, like Kepler, is steady enough to measure such a tiny dip. Turn on “Add noise” to see why small planets are hard to find. Earth-size planet and Sun-size star equals a dip smaller than the noise.
astronomy/exoplanets.a27bdf381608: Kepler four five two b. A “cousin” of Earth found by Kepler, twenty fifteen. About one point six times as wide as Earth, with a three hundred eighty-five-day year around a Sun-like star. About one thousand eight hundred light-years away, much too far to visit. Its dip is only about zero point zero two percent deep, so it took four years of Kepler data to find. We still don’t know if it is rocky or more like a small Neptune. Long year and small planet equals years of watching.
astronomy/exoplanets.7c96bcba2f3c: Common mix-up: A transit is not an eclipse that makes the star go dark. Even Jupiter blocks only about one percent of the Sun.
astronomy/exoplanets.b9a5c9c6a33f: TRAPPIST one e. An Earth-size planet around a tiny red star. TRAPPIST one is a red dwarf only a little bigger than Jupiter, about forty light-years away. Because the star is so small, an Earth-size planet blocks about zero point five percent of its light: sixty times more than Earth blocks of the Sun. Its year lasts just six point one days. The star has seven known rocky planets. TRAPPIST one e sits in the star’s habitable zone, see below. Small star, deeper dip for the same planet.
astronomy/exoplanets.ae12599d47dc: Jupiter crossing the Sun. What aliens would see. Seen from far away, Jupiter would dim the Sun by about one percent. But it transits only once every eleven point nine years, and each transit lasts about thirty hours. To confirm it, an alien astronomer would need to watch for decades! That is why most planets found so far have short years: they are much easier to catch. Long year, rare transits, hard to find.
astronomy/exoplanets.42c24a0e5b74: Hot Jupiter: HD two zero nine four five eight b. The first planet ever seen to transit, nineteen ninety-nine. A gas giant one point four times as wide as Jupiter, circling its star in only three point five days. It blocks about one point five percent of its star’s light: one of the deepest, easiest dips to see. It is so hot, over one thousand degrees Celsius, that gas is escaping from its atmosphere into a comet-like tail. Hot Jupiters are rare, but they were found first because they give big, frequent signals. Big and close equals deep dips that come often.

astronomy/galaxies.e374461d2a30: Common mix-up: Elliptical does not mean flat like a plate. It is oval-shaped in three D.
astronomy/galaxies.9cb52bbf2fac: Spiral arms. Where new stars are born. Bright arms curl out from the ends of the bar. The two biggest are the Perseus Arm and the Scutum-Centaurus Arm. The arms are rich in gas and dust, so new stars form there. Hot young blue stars and pink glowing nebulae make the arms bright. The arms work like a traffic jam: stars move into and out of them as they orbit the center. The disk is about one hundred thousand light-years across but only about one thousand light-years thick. Blue and pink in the arms equals young stars and star nurseries.
astronomy/galaxies.6a857a05486e: Halo and globular clusters. A huge ball around the flat disk. A faint, round halo of very old stars surrounds the flat disk. About one hundred fifty globular clusters orbit in the halo. Each one is a tight ball of up to a million old stars. The halo also holds most of the galaxy’s dark matter: invisible matter we detect only by its gravity. Without the extra gravity of dark matter, the outer stars would move too fast to stay in the galaxy. Halo equals a giant ball around the flat pancake.
astronomy/galaxies.d155c491263a: Elliptical galaxy. A smooth ball or egg of old stars. Shaped like a ball, an egg or a rugby ball, with no disk and no arms. Mostly old red and yellow stars. There is very little gas and dust, so few new stars form. They range from small dwarfs to the biggest galaxies known. Giant ellipticals often form when galaxies merge. Example: M eight seven, a giant elliptical whose central black hole was the first ever photographed, twenty nineteen. Elliptical equals egg-shaped and old.
astronomy/galaxies.58b5223d4ae2: Central bulge and bar. A crowded hub of old stars. A thick, glowing bulge of mostly old yellow and red stars sits in the middle of the disk. A bar of stars about twenty-seven thousand light-years long crosses the center. That is why the Milky Way is called a barred spiral. Stars here are packed far more closely together than near the Sun. Thick dust hides the center from our eyes, so astronomers study it with infrared light and radio waves. Bulge equals the “yolk” of the galaxy’s fried egg.
astronomy/galaxies.7ddb11497e3a: Sagittarius A star. The supermassive black hole at the center. About four million times the mass of the Sun, packed into a space smaller than Mercury’s orbit. Astronomers found it by tracking stars racing around an invisible object. In twenty twenty-two the Event Horizon Telescope showed the first image of the glowing gas around it. It is about twenty-six thousand light-years from us, far too distant to pull Earth in. Most big galaxies have a supermassive black hole at the center.
astronomy/galaxies.1c1ef6e32cf5: Spiral galaxy. A flat, spinning disk with arms. A flat, rotating disk with a central bulge and arms that wind outward like a pinwheel. Plenty of gas and dust, so new stars keep forming in the arms. Some spirals have a bar across the middle, barred spirals, like the Milky Way. Andromeda, our nearest big neighbor, is a spiral about two point five million light-years away. Spiral equals pinwheel.
astronomy/galaxies.133958e688e4: The Sun, you are here. Our home in the Orion Spur. The Sun sits in a small arm called the Orion Spur, Orion Arm, between the Sagittarius and Perseus arms. It is about twenty-six thousand light-years from the center, a bit more than halfway out. The Sun and its planets orbit the center at about two hundred thirty kilometers per second, taking about two hundred thirty million years for one lap: one “galactic year”. The last time the Sun was at this spot in its orbit, the first dinosaurs were appearing on Earth. Address: Earth, Solar System, Orion Spur, Milky Way.

astronomy/gravity-orbits.ef0de166eac6: Inertia, green arrow. Keeps it moving straight ahead. Inertia is an object’s tendency to keep moving in a straight line at the same speed. The green arrow shows which way the satellite is moving right now; the dashed line shows where it would go if gravity switched off. In space there is almost no air to slow it down, so it does not need an engine to keep going. Inertia and gravity together make the curved path of an orbit. Orbit equals inertia, straight ahead, and gravity, toward the center.
astronomy/gravity-orbits.ec7530e620d1: Satellite, cannonball. Moving sideways while falling. Two things decide its path: its sideways motion, inertia, and gravity pulling it toward the planet. From this launch height, about one thousand one hundred kilometers up, about seven point three kilometers per second gives a circular orbit around an Earth-mass planet. The International Space Station orbits at about seven point seven kilometers per second and circles Earth every ninety minutes. Faster than about ten point three kilometers per second from here, gravity can no longer bring it back: it escapes. Too slow, falls. Just right, orbits. Too fast, escapes.
astronomy/gravity-orbits.8374bc41e08d: Newton’s mountain. A thought experiment from sixteen eighty-seven. Isaac Newton imagined a cannon on a mountain so tall it pokes above the air, so there is no air resistance. A slow cannonball curves down and hits the ground. Faster balls land farther away, because the planet’s surface curves away beneath them. Fast enough, the ball falls around the planet forever and never lands: it is in orbit! An orbit is falling while always missing the ground.

astronomy/kepler-laws.7691af8a379c: Kepler’s second law. Equal areas in equal times. The line from the Sun to a planet sweeps out equal areas in equal times, also published in sixteen oh nine. So a planet moves fastest at perihelion, closest, and slowest at aphelion, farthest. Earth moves about thirty point three kilometers per second in early January and twenty-nine point three kilometers per second in early July. Halley’s Comet races past the Sun at about fifty-five kilometers per second but crawls at under one kilometer per second far beyond Neptune. Newton explained why: gravity pulls straight toward the Sun, so it can speed a planet up or slow it down but never change its “spin” around the Sun, angular momentum stays the same. Close equals short, fat wedge, fast. Far equals long, thin wedge, slow. Same area. Equal areas does not mean equal distances. Near perihelion the planet covers a much longer stretch of its orbit in the same time.
astronomy/kepler-laws.82b459fe53a1: Kepler’s first law. Orbits are ellipses, with the Sun at one focus. Published in sixteen oh nine in Kepler’s book Astronomia Nova, “New Astronomy”. The clue was Mars: Tycho Brahe’s measurements disagreed with a circular orbit by eight arcminutes, about a quarter of the Moon’s width. Kepler trusted the data and gave up circles. Eccentricity e measures how stretched an ellipse is: zero is a circle; close to one is a long, thin oval. Earth’s e is only zero point zero one seven, so its distance from the Sun only changes from about one hundred forty-seven to one hundred fifty-two million kilometers. Ellipse equals two pins and a loop of string. The Sun is one pin. Seasons are NOT caused by Earth getting closer to the Sun: Earth is closest in early January, during northern winter. Seasons come from Earth’s tilt.
astronomy/kepler-laws.d48d47e7a9eb: Kepler’s third law. T squared equals a cubed, years and AU. Published in sixteen nineteen in Harmonices Mundi, “The Harmony of the World”. T is the orbital period in years; a is the semi-major axis, half the long axis, the “average” distance, in AU. For every planet, T squared is about a cubed. Example: Jupiter, a equals five point two AU: a cubed equals one hundred forty-one, so T equals the square root of one hundred forty-one, about eleven point nine years. Newton showed the full rule: T squared equals four pi squared a cubed divided by G M, where M is the mass of the central body. Measure a moon’s orbit and you can weigh its planet! Farther out, slower AND a longer path, a much longer year. The law uses a, the average distance, semi-major axis, not the starting distance. Launch from the same spot at different speeds and you get different a and different T.
astronomy/kepler-laws.315793af06d0: Hohmann transfer. The fuel-saving road between two orbits. Described by German engineer Walter Hohmann in nineteen twenty-five, decades before any spacecraft flew. The transfer orbit is an ellipse with perihelion at Earth’s orbit, one AU, and aphelion at Mars’s orbit, one point five two AU, so a equals one point two six AU. By Kepler’s third law its full period is one point two six to the power of one point five, about one point four two years; the probe flies half of it: about two hundred fifty-nine days, or eight point five months. Real missions often spend a bit more fuel to arrive sooner: Perseverance took about two hundred three days, launched July thirtieth, twenty twenty, landed February eighteenth, twenty twenty-one. Speed up at Earth, coast half an ellipse, speed up again at Mars. You don’t aim at where Mars is when you launch. You aim at where Mars WILL BE about eight point five months later.
astronomy/kepler-laws.074c46d78ab1: Newton’s cannon. Orbit equals falling around the planet. Just above Earth’s surface, a circular orbit needs about seven point nine kilometers per second, about seventeen thousand seven hundred miles per hour. Higher up, less speed is needed because gravity is weaker there. Escape speed is the square root of two — about one point four one — times the circular speed: about eleven point two kilometers per second from the surface. The International Space Station flies about four hundred twenty kilometers up at about seven point six six kilometers per second and goes around Earth in about ninety-three minutes. Newton drew this thought experiment in a book published in seventeen twenty-eight, just after his death; the law of gravity itself appeared in his Principia, sixteen eighty-seven. Slow, falls. Seven point nine kilometers per second, circle. Faster, ellipse. Eleven point two kilometers per second, gone for good. There is plenty of gravity at the space station’s height: about eighty-nine percent of what you feel on the ground. Astronauts float because they are falling together with the station.
astronomy/kepler-laws.e33e9c34dbf0: Launch windows. Every twenty-six months, Mars is in the right place. Earth laps Mars about once every seven hundred eighty days, about twenty-six months. This is called the synodic period. A Hohmann launch needs Mars about forty-four degrees ahead of Earth. That lines up for only a few weeks each synodic period. In July twenty twenty, three Mars missions launched within eleven days: the UAE’s Hope, China’s Tianwen one and NASA’s Perseverance. Miss the window and you wait about two more years, which is why mission teams work around the clock before a launch. Twenty-six months: two years and two months between chances. Mars is not closest to Earth on launch day. The probe launches months before the two planets are closest, and arrives months after.

astronomy/measuring-distance.ed84ea9a77c6: Proxima Centauri. The nearest star to the Sun. A small, cool red dwarf, far too faint to see without a telescope. Its parallax is zero point seven six eight arcseconds, so d equals one divided by zero point seven six eight equals one point three zero parsecs equals four point two four light-years. It belongs to the Alpha Centauri system, which you can see from the Southern Hemisphere. It has at least one planet, Proxima b, inside its habitable zone. Even the closest star shifts less than one arcsecond: smaller than a coin seen from five kilometers away.
astronomy/measuring-distance.d58146a2137c: Your star. Set any parallax angle with the slider. Parallax angle p is HALF of the total shift between January and July, one radius of Earth’s orbit as the baseline. With a one AU baseline: distance in parsecs equals one divided by p in arcseconds. Halve the angle, double the distance. Below about zero point zero zero one arcseconds even Gaia’s measurements get too uncertain for single stars. Parsec equals the distance where p equals one arcsecond, about three point two six light-years.

astronomy/moon-phases.f24fde3922db: First quarter. Right half lit, about day seven. The Moon has traveled a quarter of the way around Earth. From Earth we see half of the sunlit half: the right half of the disk. It rises around noon and is highest in the sky at sunset. “Quarter” is about the orbit, one quarter of the way around, not the shape.
astronomy/moon-phases.479f1fe7642e: Common mix-up: The orbit is tilted about five degrees, so we don’t get eclipses every month.
astronomy/moon-phases.48e50bf6439d: The Moon. Reflects sunlight, orbits Earth. The Moon orbits Earth once every twenty-seven point three days, but a full cycle of phases takes twenty-nine point five days, because Earth moves along its own orbit meanwhile. The Moon spins once per orbit, so the same side always faces Earth. The far side is not always dark: it gets sunlight during the new Moon! Half lit, always. We just see different amounts of that half.
astronomy/moon-phases.6667a2db3b36: The Sun. Lights the Moon. The Moon makes no light of its own. Moonlight is sunlight bouncing off the Moon. The Sun always lights the half of the Moon that faces it. The Sun is so far away, one hundred fifty million kilometers, that its rays arrive almost parallel. Moonlight is recycled sunlight.
astronomy/moon-phases.67b83e83226f: Full Moon. Earth is between the Sun and the Moon. The whole sunlit half faces Earth, so we see a complete bright disk, about day fifteen. It rises at sunset and sets at sunrise, so it shines all night. Earth’s shadow usually misses the Moon, because the Moon’s orbit is tilted about five degrees. Full Moon: Sun and Moon on opposite sides of the sky.
astronomy/moon-phases.c5442a1b66b9: Third quarter. Left half lit, about day twenty-two. The Moon has traveled three quarters of the way around Earth. We see the left half of the disk lit. It rises around midnight and is high in the sky at sunrise, so you can see it in the morning. Also called “last quarter”.
astronomy/moon-phases.37bee3a0457d: Moon’s orbit. One trip around Earth. The Moon is about three hundred eighty-four thousand kilometers away, roughly thirty Earth diameters. This model is not to scale. Seen from above the North Pole, the Moon moves counterclockwise, west to east. Because of this motion, the Moon rises about fifty minutes later each day. Counterclockwise from above, like Earth’s spin.
astronomy/moon-phases.1f5098e321e1: Waning crescent. A thin sliver, lit on the left. Only a thin sliver of the sunlit half still faces us. Look for it in the eastern sky just before sunrise. A few days later the cycle starts again with a new Moon, about twenty-nine point five days after the last one. Crescent equals a thin “C” or backwards “C” shape.
astronomy/moon-phases.1e3f6680c747: Common mix-up: It looks like a half Moon, but it is called a quarter because the Moon is one quarter of the way through its orbit.

astronomy/night-sky.059e5e9b9cc0: Polaris, North Star. Almost still, above Earth’s North Pole. Polaris sits less than one degree from the north celestial pole, the point in the sky that Earth’s axis points to. All night the other stars circle around it, while Polaris barely moves. Its height above the northern horizon equals your latitude: about thirty-four degrees in Georgia, forty degrees in Beijing. It is about four hundred thirty light-years away.
astronomy/night-sky.223628c15f2f: Canis Major, Sirius. Home of the brightest star at night. Contains Sirius, the brightest star in the night sky. Sirius looks so bright mainly because it is close: only eight point six light-years away. Canis Major is Orion’s big hunting dog, following him across the winter sky.
astronomy/night-sky.4648b2faa7c0: Canis Minor, Procyon. The Little Dog. Canis Minor is basically just two stars. Procyon is only eleven point five light-years away. Procyon, Sirius and Betelgeuse form the Winter Triangle.
astronomy/night-sky.f1c76f3bf389: Common mix-up: The Dipper’s stars are not all the same distance from us. Most are about eighty light-years away, but Dubhe is about one hundred twenty.
astronomy/night-sky.02bef2a6da11: Aquila, Altair. The Eagle. The Eagle also flies along the Milky Way. Altair is the Cowherd in the Chinese Qixi story; the Milky Way separates him from Vega. Altair is only about seventeen light-years away and spins very fast.
astronomy/night-sky.6d0117448a23: Common mix-up: Polaris is NOT the brightest star in the sky, it is only about forty-eighth. Sirius is the brightest. Polaris is famous because it does not move.
astronomy/night-sky.a166dc03998f: Common mix-up: Orion’s stars are not close together in space. Bellatrix is about two hundred fifty light-years away and Rigel about eight hundred sixty. They only look close from Earth.
astronomy/night-sky.949c4aa515f4: Pegasus. The Winged Horse of autumn. Pegasus is a sign of autumn evenings. Four stars make the Great Square of Pegasus, one corner, Alpheratz, officially belongs to Andromeda. The Square helps you find the Andromeda Galaxy, about two point five million light-years away: the most distant thing you can see with your eyes alone.
astronomy/night-sky.51fc8b49ad74: Cygnus, Northern Cross. The Swan flying along the Milky Way. The Swan flies along the Milky Way. Its brightest stars form the Northern Cross. Deneb, its tail, is extremely powerful and very far away: around two thousand six hundred light-years.

astronomy/planets-moons.045feb7a6492: Ganymede. Moon of Jupiter. The largest moon in the solar system: wider than the planet Mercury, but with only about half of Mercury’s mass. The only moon known to make its own magnetic field, which even gives it auroras. A salty ocean is probably buried deep under its ice. ESA’s JUICE spacecraft is due to orbit it in twenty thirty-four. Ganymede equals the giant moon. Bigger than Mercury does not make Ganymede a planet: it orbits Jupiter, so it is a moon.
astronomy/planets-moons.8815d11b6951: Jupiter. Gas giant. It has more than twice the mass of all the other planets combined; about one thousand three hundred Earths would fit inside. There is no solid surface: deep down, hydrogen is squeezed until it acts like a liquid metal, making a giant magnetic field. NASA’s Juno spacecraft has orbited Jupiter since twenty sixteen and found clusters of huge cyclones around both poles. Jupiter: biggest planet, shortest day, under ten hours. Jupiter is not a “failed star”: it would need about eighty times more mass to start nuclear fusion.
astronomy/planets-moons.e57ca87ac815: Enceladus. Moon of Saturn. Only five hundred four kilometers wide, about as wide as Arizona. Geysers from cracks at its south pole, “tiger stripes”, spray icy water into space, feeding one of Saturn’s rings. Cassini flew through the spray and found salt, organic molecules and hydrogen gas: signs of warm vents on the floor of a hidden ocean. Enceladus: tiny moon, giant geysers. Small does not mean frozen solid: tidal heating keeps Enceladus active inside.
astronomy/planets-moons.4f827ef708b8: Uranus. Ice giant. Tipped over ninety-eight degrees, so each pole gets about forty-two years of sunlight and then forty-two years of darkness. It has the coldest atmosphere of any planet: as low as minus two hundred twenty-four degrees Celsius. Only one spacecraft has ever visited: Voyager two, in January nineteen eighty-six. Uranus rolls around the Sun on its side. Neptune is farther away, but Uranus has the coldest air.
astronomy/planets-moons.a043d0edebbb: Saturn. Gas giant. It is less dense than water, zero point six nine grams per cubic centimeter. The main rings span about two hundred eighty thousand kilometers but are mostly only about ten meters thick, made of chunks of water ice. Cassini orbited Saturn from two thousand four to twenty seventeen and ended by diving into Saturn so it could never crash onto a moon that might hold life. Saturn: rings and the most known moons, two hundred ninety-three. The rings do not vanish: about every fifteen years we see them edge-on, and they are so thin they almost disappear.
astronomy/planets-moons.87e35133f749: Venus. Rocky planet. The air pressure at the surface is ninety-two times Earth’s, like being nine hundred meters, three thousand feet, under the ocean. It spins backward, so the Sun rises in the west. Sunrise to sunrise takes one hundred seventeen Earth days. Its carbon dioxide blanket traps heat, a runaway greenhouse effect: about four hundred sixty-five degrees Celsius, hot enough to melt lead. Venus: Earth-sized, but a greenhouse oven. Venus is not hot because it is close to the Sun; it is hot because its C O two air traps heat.
astronomy/planets-moons.9540baa7f83e: Io. Moon of Jupiter. The most volcanic world we know: more than four hundred active volcanoes. Jupiter’s tides squeeze and stretch Io as it orbits; the resonance with Europa and Ganymede keeps its orbit slightly oval, so the squeezing never stops and heats its insides. Sulfur and sulfur dioxide frost paint it yellow, orange, red and white. Io: innermost big moon, a world of volcanoes. Io’s heat does not come from the Sun; it comes from tidal squeezing by Jupiter.
astronomy/planets-moons.14f675e6f2fe: Neptune. Ice giant. The fastest winds in the solar system: about two thousand kilometers per hour, one thousand two hundred miles per hour. In eighteen forty-six it was found by math: astronomers predicted where it must be from the way it tugged on Uranus. Its largest moon, Triton, orbits backward and has geysers of nitrogen gas. Neptune: one year equals one hundred sixty-five Earth years. Neptune is blue because methane gas absorbs red light, not because it is covered in water.
astronomy/planets-moons.9079a710a759: Europa. Moon of Jupiter. Under an ice shell probably fifteen to twenty-five kilometers thick is a salty ocean holding about twice as much water as all of Earth’s oceans. Reddish-brown cracks and ridges criss-cross its smooth, young icy surface. NASA’s Europa Clipper launched in October twenty twenty-four and is due to reach Jupiter in twenty thirty to study whether Europa could support life. Europa: an ocean world wearing an ice shell. Europa is far too cold for liquid water on top; its ocean stays liquid because tidal heating warms it from inside.
astronomy/planets-moons.e8010d1945d3: Pluto. Dwarf planet. A dwarf planet in the Kuiper Belt, smaller than our Moon. In twenty fifteen New Horizons found a heart-shaped plain of frozen nitrogen and mountains made of water ice. Its moon Charon is half as wide as Pluto; the two orbit a point in the space between them. One Pluto year equals two hundred forty-eight Earth years. Pluto was not reclassified just for being small: it has not cleared its orbit of other objects.
astronomy/planets-moons.996846436fd1: Europa. Under an ice shell probably fifteen to twenty-five kilometers thick is a salty ocean holding about twice as much water as all of Earth’s oceans. Reddish-brown cracks and ridges criss-cross its smooth, young icy surface. NASA’s Europa Clipper launched in October twenty twenty-four and is due to reach Jupiter in twenty thirty to study whether Europa could support life. Europa: an ocean world wearing an ice shell.
astronomy/planets-moons.e07e65565897: GALILEAN MOONS. Four big moons. Galileo found them in January sixteen ten with a small telescope. Seeing moons circle another planet showed that not everything orbits Earth. Io, Europa and Ganymede tug on each other in a one to two to four rhythm, an orbital resonance. Those regular tugs keep their orbits slightly oval, so Jupiter’s tides flex them and heat their insides: volcanoes on Io, an ocean under Europa’s ice. You can see all four with ordinary binoculars as tiny dots next to Jupiter. MEMORY HINT. Order outward: “I Eat Green Cheese” equals Io, Europa, Ganymede, Callisto. Common mix-up: A resonance does not mean the moons line up all together: in fact Io, Europa and Ganymede can never all be on the same side of Jupiter at once.
astronomy/planets-moons.94b0bb1d5587: Jupiter. It has more than twice the mass of all the other planets combined; about one thousand three hundred Earths would fit inside. There is no solid surface: deep down, hydrogen is squeezed until it acts like a liquid metal, making a giant magnetic field. NASA’s Juno spacecraft has orbited Jupiter since twenty sixteen and found clusters of huge cyclones around both poles. Jupiter: biggest planet, shortest day, under ten hours.
astronomy/planets-moons.014266e969b3: Callisto. The most heavily cratered object in the solar system: its surface is about four billion years old. It orbits every sixteen point seven days and is NOT part of the one to two to four resonance, so tides barely heat it. It is far enough from Jupiter’s radiation that it may be a future base for astronauts. Callisto: the quiet, cratered outsider.
astronomy/planets-moons.10f0afaaee8f: The Moon. Moon of Earth. It probably formed when a Mars-sized body crashed into the young Earth about four point five billion years ago. Craters near its south pole that never see sunlight hold water ice, a target for NASA’s Artemis astronauts. It drifts about three point eight centimeters, one point five inches, farther from Earth every year. Moon gravity about one sixth of Earth’s. The Moon does spin: exactly once per orbit, which is why we always see the same face.
astronomy/planets-moons.c3469bfbe32b: Io. The most volcanic world we know: more than four hundred active volcanoes. Jupiter’s tides squeeze and stretch Io as it orbits; the resonance with Europa and Ganymede keeps its orbit slightly oval, so the squeezing never stops and heats its insides. Sulfur and sulfur dioxide frost paint it yellow, orange, red and white. Io: innermost big moon, a world of volcanoes.
astronomy/planets-moons.be378b2a75a1: Ganymede. The largest moon in the solar system: wider than the planet Mercury, but with only about half of Mercury’s mass. The only moon known to make its own magnetic field, which even gives it auroras. A salty ocean is probably buried deep under its ice. ESA’s JUICE spacecraft is due to orbit it in twenty thirty-four. Ganymede equals the giant moon.
astronomy/planets-moons.13da444e314c: Titan. Moon of Saturn. The only moon with a thick atmosphere; its orange haze hides the surface. Liquid methane and ethane fall as rain and fill rivers, lakes and seas; Ligeia Mare is bigger than Lake Superior. The Huygens probe landed there in two thousand five. NASA’s Dragonfly drone is planned to launch in twenty twenty-eight and fly between sites on Titan. Titan: a moon with weather, methane rain. Titan’s lakes are not water: at minus one hundred seventy-nine degrees Celsius water is as hard as rock. They are liquid methane and ethane.
astronomy/planets-moons.63e4c9f62841: Earth. Rocky planet. The densest planet in the solar system, five point five times the density of water. The only world known to have liquid water on its surface right now, and life. Its magnetic field and ozone layer shield life from the solar wind and ultraviolet light. Earth is the measuring stick: one gee, one day, one year, one AU. Earth is not a perfect ball: it bulges a little at the equator, twelve thousand seven hundred fifty-six kilometers across versus twelve thousand seven hundred fourteen kilometers pole to pole.
astronomy/planets-moons.530b43c8be7d: Mercury. Rocky planet. From one sunrise to the next takes one hundred seventy-six Earth days: that is two whole Mercury years. Even here, water ice hides in craters near the poles that never see sunlight. Its iron core fills about eighty-five percent of its radius, so for its size it is very dense. Mercury: smallest planet, shortest year, eighty-eight days. Closest to the Sun is not hottest on average: Venus is hotter.
astronomy/planets-moons.c3cdb451f903: Common mix-up: Heavy things do not fall faster. In nineteen seventy-one Apollo fifteen astronaut David Scott dropped a hammer and a feather on the airless Moon: they hit the ground together.
astronomy/planets-moons.95857155931b: Mars. Rocky planet. Olympus Mons is about twenty-two kilometers high, two point five times Mount Everest; the canyon Valles Marineris is about four thousand kilometers long, as wide as the USA. The air is so thin that liquid water quickly boils away or freezes, but ice fills its polar caps and lies under the ground. Since twenty twenty-one the Perseverance rover has been collecting rock samples in Jezero Crater, an ancient lake bed. A Mars day, a “sol”, is twenty-four hours forty minutes, almost like ours. Mars is red because of rust, iron oxide, in its dust, not because it is hot.

astronomy/rocketry.96446fe0ec1e: The gravity turn. Up first, then sideways. Rockets go straight up for the first few seconds to clear the tower and the thickest air. Then they tip a few degrees east, and gravity slowly bends the path over, so the rocket does not have to steer hard. Climbing straight up too long wastes fuel fighting gravity, “gravity loss”. Turning too early drags the rocket sideways through thick air, “drag loss”. Launching east from Florida adds about zero point four kilometers per second from Earth’s spin. Near the equator you get about zero point four six kilometers per second. A gentle nudge, then let gravity steer. Rockets do not go “up to space and then stop”. Without sideways speed they fall straight back down.
astronomy/rocketry.73a407e62f72: The rocket equation. Delta v equals exhaust velocity times the natural log of the quantity m zero divided by m sub f. Written down by Konstantin Tsiolkovsky in nineteen oh three. Delta v is the total change in speed a rocket can make. It depends only on exhaust speed and the mass ratio: full mass m zero divided by empty mass m sub f. Reaching low Earth orbit needs about nine point four kilometers per second of delta v, seven point eight kilometers per second of orbital speed plus about one point five kilometers per second lost to gravity and drag. With exhaust velocity equals three kilometers per second, getting nine point four kilometers per second from one stage would need m zero divided by m sub f about twenty-three: the rocket would have to be about ninety-six percent fuel. That is why real rockets use stages. More fuel helps less and less: the mass ratio sits inside a logarithm. Delta v is not the top speed you will see. Gravity and drag eat part of it on the way up.
astronomy/rocketry.8916954c6faa: Staging. Throw away what you no longer need. When a stage runs out of fuel, it drops off with its empty tanks and engines. The rest of the rocket no longer has to carry that dead weight. Saturn five had three stages; Falcon nine and Long March five have two, plus side boosters on Long March five. Engines on upper stages are designed for vacuum: hydrogen engines like the R L one zero reach exhaust speeds of about four point five kilometers per second. Falcon nine first stages now fly back and land so they can be reused; some boosters have flown more than twenty times. Staging equals a relay race: each runner hands on a lighter rocket. Stages are not dropped because they are “used up” like a battery. They are dropped because empty tanks are heavy and useless.
astronomy/rocketry.29d1461ceb2b: What “orbit” means. Fast enough sideways to keep missing Earth. Space officially starts at about one hundred kilometers, the Kármán line. Reaching it takes about one point four kilometers per second straight up, or just a few minutes of flight. Staying in space is the hard part: at two hundred kilometers you need about seven point eight kilometers per second sideways, roughly twenty-three times the speed of sound at sea level. A suborbital flight, like a quick hop to one hundred kilometers and back, needs only a small fraction of the energy of an orbital flight. In orbit the engines switch off. Nothing slows you down, so you keep falling around Earth. Space equals one hundred kilometers up. Orbit equals seven point eight kilometers per second sideways. Reaching space is not the same as reaching orbit. The first needs height; the second needs enormous sideways speed.
astronomy/rocketry.581f3341d535: Thrust equals mass flow rate times exhaust velocity. How much mass, how fast. Thrust, in newtons, equals mass thrown out per second, kilograms per second, times exhaust speed, meters per second. Double either one and the thrust doubles. Engineers like high exhaust speed best, because it gives more push from each kilogram of fuel. One F one engine of the Saturn five burned about two point six tonnes of propellant every second, with an exhaust speed of about two point six kilometers per second: about six point eight million newtons. To lift off, the thrust must be bigger than the rocket’s weight. Thrust divided by weight at liftoff is usually about one point two to one point five. Thrust equals how much times how fast. A bigger flame does not always mean a better engine. Exhaust speed, not flame size, decides how far each kilogram of fuel can take you.
astronomy/rocketry.6b2b5bf5cbd1: Action and reaction. Newton’s third law makes rockets go. When the rocket pushes gas backward, the gas pushes the rocket forward with a force of exactly the same size. A rocket does not push against the air or the ground. It works even better in the vacuum of space, where no air gets in the way of the exhaust. In nineteen twenty a New York Times editorial mocked Robert Goddard for claiming rockets could work in a vacuum. In nineteen sixty-nine, as Apollo eleven flew to the Moon, the paper printed a correction. A garden hose kicks back in your hands for the same reason: water pushed one way pushes you the other way. Push gas back, gas pushes you forward. Every action has an equal and opposite reaction. Rockets do not need air to push on. The flame is not pushing the ground; the rocket is pushing its own exhaust.

astronomy/scale-universe.48004ea2dd05: The inner planets. About twelve astronomical units across. The four rocky planets and the asteroid belt fit inside Jupiter’s orbit, five point two astronomical units. Planets are shown where they really are today: November twentieth, twenty twenty-six. One astronomical unit equals Earth-Sun distance about one hundred fifty million kilometers. Light takes eight minutes twenty seconds to cross one astronomical unit.
astronomy/scale-universe.f9c588b5dd5d: Light-days and light-weeks. About six thousand seven hundred astronomical units across. One light-day equals one hundred seventy-three astronomical units; one light-week equals about one thousand two hundred astronomical units. The whole planet zone, out to Neptune, is now a speck at the centre. One astronomical unit equals Earth-Sun distance about one hundred fifty million kilometers. Light takes eight minutes twenty seconds to cross one astronomical unit.
astronomy/scale-universe.0f9b04e08ea4: Near the Sun. About one astronomical unit across. Mercury orbits only zero point three nine astronomical units, fifty-eight million kilometers, from the Sun. NASA’s Parker Solar Probe dives to about six point one million kilometers from the Sun’s surface: the closest any spacecraft has ever been. One astronomical unit equals Earth-Sun distance about one hundred fifty million kilometers. Light takes eight minutes twenty seconds to cross one astronomical unit.
astronomy/scale-universe.30bbb6df0cad: Our star neighbourhood. About two thousand six hundred light-years across. Most stars you see at night are within a few thousand light-years. The Orion Nebula, a star nursery, is about one thousand three hundred forty-four light-years away. A light-year is a DISTANCE: how far light goes in a year, nine point four six trillion kilometers, five point eight eight trillion miles.
astronomy/scale-universe.e641f7e0bf1d: Earth. About eighteen thousand kilometers across. Earth is twelve thousand seven hundred fifty-six kilometers, seven thousand nine hundred twenty-six miles, wide at the equator. The International Space Station orbits only about four hundred twenty kilometers up: at this scale, just above the surface. Each step of one on the slider equals ten times wider. Six steps equals a million times!
astronomy/scale-universe.e0c3a19bf275: A city: Atlanta. About forty kilometers, twenty-five miles, across. The I two eight five “Perimeter” highway loops about sixty-four miles, one hundred three kilometers, around Atlanta. The football field is now smaller than one pixel. Each step of one on the slider equals ten times wider. Six steps equals a million times!
astronomy/scale-universe.0bdbd4663f47: The observable universe. The orange circle is about ninety-three billion light-years across. We can only see light that has had time to reach us since the Big Bang, thirteen point eight billion years ago. Because space has been expanding, the most distant light comes from matter that is now about forty-six billion light-years away. A light-year is a DISTANCE: how far light goes in a year, nine point four six trillion kilometers, five point eight eight trillion miles.
astronomy/scale-universe.b2c4d45c31ec: The Local Group. About seventeen million light-years across. The Andromeda Galaxy, two point five million light-years away, is the farthest thing you can see with your eyes alone. The Local Group has two big spirals, Andromeda and the Milky Way, Triangulum, and dozens of small galaxies. A light-year is a DISTANCE: how far light goes in a year, nine point four six trillion kilometers, five point eight eight trillion miles.
astronomy/scale-universe.8bc0617b54a1: The Oort cloud. About three point three light-years across. A giant shell of icy comets thought to reach about one hundred thousand astronomical units, one point six light-years, from the Sun. No one has seen it directly: this is an illustration. The Sun’s gravity still holds these comets, far beyond the planets. One astronomical unit equals Earth-Sun distance about one hundred fifty million kilometers. Light takes eight minutes twenty seconds to cross one astronomical unit.
astronomy/scale-universe.42478412e374: A football field. About one hundred sixty meters across. A US football field is one hundred twenty yards long with the end zones, one hundred ten meters, and fifty-three and a third yards, forty-nine meters, wide. You are the tiny dot in the middle. Each step of one on the slider equals ten times wider. Six steps equals a million times!
astronomy/scale-universe.904125517f86: Voyager one. About six hundred astronomical units across. Voyager one, launched in nineteen seventy-seven, is the farthest spacecraft: about one hundred seventy-two astronomical units away, roughly one light-day, approximate. In twenty twelve it crossed the heliopause, about one hundred twenty astronomical units, where the Sun’s wind gives way to interstellar space. One astronomical unit equals Earth-Sun distance about one hundred fifty million kilometers. Light takes eight minutes twenty seconds to cross one astronomical unit.
astronomy/scale-universe.e2469386af2e: A kid. About two point five meters across. A typical twelve-year-old is about one point five meters, five feet, tall; a basketball is twenty-four centimeters across. Light crosses this whole view in about eight billionths of a second. Each step of one on the slider equals ten times wider. Six steps equals a million times!
astronomy/scale-universe.dba9583fd1f9: The cosmic web. About seven hundred million light-years across. Galaxies gather in clusters strung along giant filaments, with huge empty voids between them. Our home supercluster, Laniakea, is about five hundred twenty million light-years across. Pattern is an illustration, not a real map. A light-year is a DISTANCE: how far light goes in a year, nine point four six trillion kilometers, five point eight eight trillion miles.
astronomy/scale-universe.7463cebea76b: Common mix-up: Constellations look flat, but their stars are at very different distances: here you see the real three D spacing.
astronomy/scale-universe.6dac1081d3da: The Milky Way. About one hundred thirty thousand light-years across. Our galaxy is a barred spiral about one hundred thousand light-years across with one hundred to four hundred billion stars. The Sun is about twenty-six thousand light-years from the centre and takes about two hundred thirty million years to go around once. A light-year is a DISTANCE: how far light goes in a year, nine point four six trillion kilometers, five point eight eight trillion miles.
astronomy/scale-universe.15ecf1c3ecf8: The nearest stars. About twenty-seven light-years across. The nearest star system, Alpha Centauri, is four point three seven light-years away, its small star Proxima is four point two four light-years. Most of our neighbours are small, dim red dwarfs you cannot see without a telescope. One astronomical unit equals Earth-Sun distance about one hundred fifty million kilometers. Light takes eight minutes twenty seconds to cross one astronomical unit.
astronomy/scale-universe.e720f6437aaf: The Sun. About four million kilometers across. The Sun is one million three hundred ninety-two thousand seven hundred kilometers wide: one hundred nine Earths side by side. The Moon’s whole orbit around Earth would fit inside the Sun with room to spare. Each step of one on the slider equals ten times wider. Six steps equals a million times!
astronomy/scale-universe.bbea9c819107: Earth and Moon. About nine hundred thousand kilometers across. The Moon is on average three hundred eighty-four thousand four hundred kilometers, two hundred thirty-eight thousand nine hundred miles, away: about thirty Earths lined up. Light takes one point three seconds to get from the Moon to us. Each step of one on the slider equals ten times wider. Six steps equals a million times!

astronomy/seasons.2685d23f8cbe: June solstice. About June twenty-first, longest day in the north. The north end of the axis leans toward the Sun. The noon Sun is directly over the Tropic of Cancer, twenty-three point five degrees north. Summer begins in the Northern Hemisphere; winter begins in the Southern Hemisphere. The Arctic has twenty-four-hour daylight. Solstice equals “Sun stands still”: the Sun reaches its highest noon point of the year in the north.
astronomy/seasons.bd7b1e3fafc7: September equinox. About September twenty-second, day equals night. Again, neither hemisphere leans toward the Sun. The noon Sun is directly over the equator. Autumn begins in the north, spring in the south. Two equinoxes a year: March and September.
astronomy/seasons.d372c7f2a9a5: Day-night line. Boundary between the lit half and the dark half. Sunlight always lights half of Earth. The edge between day and night is called the circle of illumination. As Earth rotates, places cross this line at sunrise and sunset. In June the whole Arctic stays inside the lit half all day: twenty-four hours of daylight, the “midnight Sun”. Antarctica has twenty-four hours of night. Half lit, always, just like the Moon.
astronomy/seasons.98f1378119ef: March equinox. About March twentieth, day equals night. Neither hemisphere leans toward the Sun. The noon Sun is directly over the equator. Day and night are about twelve hours everywhere. Spring begins in the north, autumn in the south. “Equinox” means “equal night”.
astronomy/seasons.d73ebd3bb85d: Equator and tropics. Where the Sun can be directly overhead. The equator, zero degrees, divides Earth into the Northern and Southern Hemispheres. On the June solstice the noon Sun is directly overhead at the Tropic of Cancer, twenty-three point five degrees north. On the December solstice it is directly overhead at the Tropic of Capricorn, twenty-three point five degrees south. Outside the tropics the Sun is never straight overhead. The tropics are twenty-three point five degrees from the equator, the same number as the tilt!
astronomy/seasons.94745a96e6c3: December solstice. About December twenty-first, shortest day in the north. The north end of the axis leans away from the Sun, it still points at Polaris! The noon Sun is directly over the Tropic of Capricorn, twenty-three point five degrees south. Winter begins in the north; summer begins in the south, so people in Australia often spend Christmas at the beach. Two weeks later, Earth is at its closest point to the Sun, in winter!
astronomy/seasons.608221d89e60: Earth. Spins once a day, orbits once a year. Rotation: Earth spins west to east on its axis once every twenty-four hours. This causes day and night. Revolution: Earth travels around the Sun once every three hundred sixty-five and a quarter days. That is one year. Because Earth spins toward the east, the Sun appears to rise in the east and set in the west. ROtation equals ROlling in place, spin. REVolution equals going aRound the Sun.
astronomy/seasons.d837afdc5b57: The Sun. Source of light and heat. The Sun always lights exactly half of Earth. That half has daytime. Sunlight takes about eight minutes to reach Earth. The real Sun is one hundred nine times wider than Earth and about one hundred fifty million kilometers away. This model is not to scale. The Sun stays put. Earth’s tilt and orbit make the seasons.
astronomy/seasons.c1c8ed8a40c1: Tilted axis, twenty-three point five degrees. The real cause of the seasons. Earth’s axis is tilted about twenty-three point five degrees from “straight up” compared with its orbit. The axis always points the same way in space, toward Polaris, the North Star, all year long. So in June the north end leans toward the Sun, and in December it leans away. Tilt and orbit equals seasons. Press “What if no tilt?” to test it.
astronomy/seasons.6eb25949b273: Earth’s orbit. Almost a perfect circle. Earth’s distance from the Sun changes by only about three percent: from one hundred forty-seven to one hundred fifty-two million kilometers. Earth is closest, perihelion, around January third, during northern winter, and farthest, aphelion, around July fourth, during northern summer. If distance caused seasons, both hemispheres would have summer at the same time. They don’t. Closest in January, yet it’s cold in Georgia: distance is NOT the reason.

astronomy/sky-tonight.d9a7a0e62d37: latitude thirty-four point zero degrees, November eighteenth, twenty twenty-six at six thirteen p.m.: twilight, getting dark, Sun negative nine degrees. The Moon is sixty-four percent lit and forty-five degrees up in the southeast. Planets up: Saturn, southeast thirty-five degrees. About five thousand real stars are on this map: every star down to magnitude six, roughly what your eyes can see from a dark countryside. The whole sky turns fifteen degrees every hour, once in twenty-three hours fifty-six minutes, because Earth spins from west to east. Planets always stay near the yellow dashed line, the ecliptic. It is the flat plane of the solar system seen edge-on. Each day the Moon moves about thirteen degrees east against the stars, so it rises about fifty minutes later each night. Stars twinkle; planets mostly shine steadily. If a bright “star” sits on the ecliptic and isn’t on a star chart, it’s a planet. Polaris is NOT the brightest star in the sky, it is about forty-eighth. It is famous because it barely moves: it sits almost exactly above Earth’s North Pole.
