astronomy/small-bodies.c4f223d04b54: Halley’s Comet. Edmond Halley predicted its return for seventeen fifty-eight using Newton’s laws, the first comet known to come back. In nineteen eighty-six the European spacecraft Giotto flew within six hundred kilometers of its nucleus: a dark, potato-shaped lump about fifteen kilometers long. Its orbit is tilted and goes around backward compared with the planets. Dust it left behind causes two meteor showers: the Eta Aquariids, May, and the Orionids, October. Comets live on long, stretched ellipses: fast near the Sun, slow far away.
astronomy/small-bodies.32f854ca25f4: Common mix-up: The Kuiper Belt is not the edge of the solar system: the Oort Cloud lies about fifty to two thousand times farther out.
astronomy/small-bodies.d2e8c44ca274: Oort Cloud, schematic. A giant, roughly spherical shell of icy bodies surrounding the whole solar system. We infer it from the orbits of comets that fall in from every direction. A passing star or the pull of the Milky Way can nudge an Oort Cloud object inward, and it becomes a long-period comet like Hale-Bopp. Its outer edge may reach a third of the way to the nearest star, Proxima Centauri, two hundred sixty-eight thousand astronomical units. Short trips, less than two hundred years, Kuiper Belt comets; very long trips, Oort Cloud comets.
astronomy/small-bodies.e6b1edbdb472: Common mix-up: Pluto is not the most massive dwarf planet: Eris has about twenty-seven percent more mass, though Pluto is slightly wider.
astronomy/small-bodies.91353631d262: Pluto and friends. Pluto’s stretched orbit sometimes brings it closer to the Sun than Neptune, last time nineteen seventy-nine to nineteen ninety-nine, but the two can never collide: Pluto goes around twice for every three Neptune orbits. New Horizons, twenty fifteen, found glaciers of nitrogen ice, mountains of water ice and a blue hazy sky. Eris, discovered in two thousand five, is almost exactly Pluto’s size; finding it led astronomers to create the “dwarf planet” category in two thousand six. Dwarf planet: round, orbits the Sun, but has not cleared its neighbourhood.
astronomy/small-bodies.abe37d7bc416: Kuiper Belt. A doughnut-shaped belt like the asteroid belt, but about twenty times wider and made mostly of ice. On January first, twenty nineteen, New Horizons flew past Arrokoth, a thirty-six kilometer “snowman” made of two lumps that gently stuck together: an untouched building block of planets. Many comets that return in less than two hundred years start out here or in the nearby scattered disk. Asteroid belt equals rock, close in. Kuiper Belt equals ice, far out.
astronomy/small-bodies.d88bce138070: Near-Earth asteroids. These asteroids were nudged out of the belt and now cross or come near Earth’s orbit. Osiris Rex collected a sample from Bennu and dropped it in the Utah desert in September twenty twenty-three. Asteroid Apophis, about three hundred forty meters, will pass Earth on April thirteenth, twenty twenty-nine, closer than some satellites, and will be visible without a telescope. It will not hit us. Planetary defense equals find them early, track them, and, if needed, push them.
astronomy/small-bodies.18b3d0be401d: Voyager one. The most distant human-made object. In August twenty twelve, at about one hundred twenty-one astronomical units, it crossed the heliopause into interstellar space. Around late twenty twenty-six it is about one light-day from Earth: a radio command takes about twenty-four hours to reach it. Even so, it would take about three hundred years to reach the inner edge of the Oort Cloud and perhaps thirty thousand years to pass through it. One light-day about one hundred seventy-three astronomical units.
astronomy/small-bodies.d6748601e57c: Main asteroid belt. Asteroids are rocky or metal leftovers from when the planets formed four point six billion years ago. Jupiter’s gravity kept them from ever building a planet. Vesta, five hundred twenty-five kilometers, has a giant crater at its south pole; pieces blasted out of it have landed on Earth as meteorites. NASA’s Psyche spacecraft is on its way to a metal-rich asteroid, arriving in twenty twenty-nine. The belt sits between Mars and Jupiter: “rocks between the red and the giant”.
astronomy/small-bodies.82bf160058af: Jupiter Trojans. Two swarms share Jupiter’s orbit, one leading and one trailing, held at balance points where the Sun’s and Jupiter’s gravity work together, Lagrange points L four and L five. They are dark, reddish and may be “fossils” left over from the outer solar system. NASA’s Lucy spacecraft, launched in twenty twenty-one, will fly past several Trojans starting in twenty twenty-seven. Trojans travel with Jupiter like two groups of runners sixty degrees ahead and behind.
astronomy/small-bodies.a2668ecc5d24: SMALL BODIES. The solar system’s leftovers. Besides eight planets, the Sun is circled by millions of asteroids, comets and dwarf planets. Where they live tells us what they are made of. Asteroids: rock and metal, mostly in the belt between Mars and Jupiter, warm enough that ice could not survive there. Comets: ice and dust, from the cold Kuiper Belt and Oort Cloud. Meteoroids: small pieces broken off asteroids and comets. MEMORY HINT. Rocks inside, ice outside: the “frost line”, about three astronomical units, split the young solar system. Common mix-up: A “shooting star” is not a star: it is a grain of dust burning up about one hundred kilometers above your head.

astronomy/solar-system.6899263902b6: The Sun. The star at the center. The Sun is a star: a giant ball of hot gas, mostly hydrogen and helium, that makes its own light by nuclear fusion. It holds ninety-nine point eight percent of all the mass in the solar system, so its gravity keeps everything in orbit. About one hundred nine Earths would fit across its face, and about one point three million Earths could fit inside it. Sunlight takes about eight minutes twenty seconds to reach Earth. The Sun is the only star in our solar system. Planets and moons shine only by reflecting its light.
astronomy/solar-system.6ce4155cf26f: Mars. The Red Planet. Its soil is rich in iron oxide, rust, which makes it look red. It has Olympus Mons, the tallest volcano in the solar system, about twenty-two kilometers high, about two point five times Mount Everest. Thin carbon dioxide atmosphere; ice at its poles and dry riverbeds show liquid water once flowed. A day on Mars is twenty-four hours thirty-seven minutes, almost the same as Earth’s. Rovers such as Perseverance explore it. Mars equals rust red, with two tiny moons, Phobos and Deimos.
astronomy/solar-system.57ed26c5064a: Mercury. Smallest and fastest planet. Closest planet to the Sun and the smallest of the eight planets. It has almost no atmosphere to trap heat: days reach four hundred thirty degrees Celsius, nights drop to minus one hundred eighty degrees Celsius. Its surface is covered in craters, a lot like our Moon. Fastest planet: it circles the Sun in only eighty-eight days. Mercury, named for the speedy messenger god, has the shortest year.
astronomy/solar-system.1ead82847350: Common mix-up: Summer is not caused by Earth being closer to the Sun; seasons come from Earth’s twenty-three point five degree tilt.
astronomy/solar-system.c7b8a9d3c1bb: Asteroid belt. Rocky leftovers between Mars and Jupiter. Millions of rocky and metal chunks orbit the Sun between Mars and Jupiter. They are leftover building material that never formed a planet, partly because of Jupiter’s strong gravity. The largest object, Ceres, about nine hundred forty kilometers wide, is a dwarf planet. It is mostly empty space: spacecraft fly through without hitting anything. Meteoroid, small rock in space. Meteor, streak of light in the air. Meteorite, rock that lands on the ground.
astronomy/solar-system.42942461a133: Common mix-up: Mars is red because of rust in its dust, not because it is hot. It is actually very cold, about minus sixty-five degrees Celsius.
astronomy/solar-system.4120a4ed57a8: Common mix-up: Pluto is no longer the “ninth planet”. Since two thousand six it has been a dwarf planet, so Neptune is the farthest planet.
astronomy/solar-system.e2cd5d90794e: Earth. Our home, the only known planet with life. The only planet known to have life and liquid water on its surface, water covers about seventy-one percent. Its atmosphere, mostly nitrogen and oxygen, protects us and keeps temperatures mild. It sits in the “habitable zone”: not too hot and not too cold for liquid water. The Earth-Sun distance is one astronomical unit, A U, about one hundred fifty million kilometers. One astronomical unit equals the Earth-Sun distance. Astronomers use it as a measuring stick.
astronomy/solar-system.134dd258dcea: Comet. A dirty snowball with a tail. A “dirty snowball” of ice, dust and rock, usually only a few kilometers wide. Near the Sun its ice turns to gas, forming a glowing coma, head, and long tails. The tail always points away from the Sun, pushed by sunlight and the solar wind, whichever way the comet is moving. Comets travel on long, stretched, elliptical, orbits and speed up near the Sun. This one is like Halley’s Comet, which returns about every seventy-six years. Comet equals ice and tail. Asteroid equals rock, no tail.
astronomy/solar-system.33e30449b01e: Kuiper belt and Pluto. Icy worlds beyond Neptune. A huge doughnut-shaped region of icy bodies beyond Neptune, about thirty to fifty astronomical units from the Sun. Pluto lives here. It is a dwarf planet: it orbits the Sun and is round, but it has not cleared its orbit of other objects. Pluto’s orbit is tilted and stretched; one Pluto year is two hundred forty-eight Earth years. In twenty fifteen New Horizons photographed its heart-shaped glacier. Many short-period comets come from here. Much farther out, the Oort Cloud may hold trillions of comets. A planet must, one, orbit the Sun, two, be round, three, clear its neighborhood. Pluto fails rule three.
astronomy/solar-system.d805f1fcffc9: Venus. The hottest planet. Similar in size to Earth, so it is sometimes called Earth’s “twin”. A thick carbon dioxide atmosphere causes a runaway greenhouse effect: about four hundred sixty-five degrees Celsius, hot enough to melt lead. It spins backward and very slowly: one spin takes two hundred forty-three Earth days, longer than its two hundred twenty-five-day year. It is the brightest planet in our night sky, often called the “morning star” or “evening star”. Venus equals very hot, very cloudy, very slow spin.
astronomy/solar-system.6e8644d30184: Jupiter. The largest planet. Largest planet: it has more than twice the mass of all the other planets combined. A gas giant made mostly of hydrogen and helium, with no solid surface to stand on. The Great Red Spot is a storm wider than Earth that has raged for hundreds of years. Shortest day of any planet, under ten hours. Its one hundred fifteen known moons include Ganymede, the largest moon in the solar system. Jupiter equals Jumbo: biggest planet, shortest day.
astronomy/solar-system.6d8e9c6a2088: The Moon. Earth’s natural satellite. Earth’s only natural satellite; it orbits Earth about every twenty-seven point three days. It is about one quarter as wide as Earth, and its gravity is about one sixth of Earth’s. It always shows the same face to Earth. This model draws the Moon far too close: in reality about thirty Earths would fit between Earth and the Moon. A moon orbits a planet; a planet orbits a star.
astronomy/solar-system.24fbdf4e4673: Saturn. The ringed planet. Famous for bright rings made of billions of pieces of ice and rock, some as small as dust and some as big as houses. The rings stretch about two hundred eighty thousand kilometers from the planet, yet the main rings are usually only about ten meters thick. It is the least dense planet: it would float in a, giant, bathtub of water. It has the most known moons. Titan has a thick atmosphere and lakes of liquid methane. Saturn equals Super rings.
astronomy/solar-system.23e8fe2b1a00: Uranus. The sideways planet. An ice giant: a deep atmosphere of hydrogen, helium and methane over an interior of water, ammonia and methane “ices”. Methane gas absorbs red light, giving it a blue-green color. It is tipped over about ninety-eight degrees, so it rolls around the Sun on its side, giving each pole about forty-two years of daylight followed by forty-two years of darkness. The first planet discovered with a telescope, William Herschel, seventeen eighty-one. Uranus rolls around the Sun like a ball on its side.
astronomy/solar-system.03cd83fb06c7: Neptune. The farthest, windiest planet. The farthest planet, about thirty astronomical units from the Sun; one Neptune year lasts almost one hundred sixty-five Earth years. The windiest planet: winds reach about two thousand kilometers per hour. A deep-blue ice giant. In eighteen forty-six it was predicted with math before anyone saw it through a telescope. Its largest moon, Triton, orbits backward and has icy geysers. Planet order: “My Very Educated Mother Just Served Us Noodles”, Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune.

astronomy/space-exploration.a1216890a26a: Reflecting telescope. Uses mirrors to gather light. A curved, concave, mirror at the bottom reflects light up to a focus. A small flat mirror sends the light out the side to the eyepiece, a Newtonian design, invented by Isaac Newton in sixteen sixty-eight. Mirrors can be made huge, so all the largest telescopes are reflectors. A bigger mirror collects more light and shows fainter objects.
astronomy/space-exploration.081859058706: Space telescope. Observes from above the atmosphere. Earth’s atmosphere blurs starlight and blocks most infrared, ultraviolet and X-ray light. Space telescopes orbit above the air: Hubble, nineteen ninety, sees visible and ultraviolet light; the James Webb Space Telescope, twenty twenty-one, sees infrared; Chandra sees X-rays. Hubble uses mirrors too: light bounces off a two point four meter primary mirror and a small secondary mirror before reaching its cameras.
astronomy/space-exploration.e5c22dcb6b29: Nineteen ninety. Hubble Space Telescope. Hubble is launched into an orbit more than five hundred kilometers up, above the blurring atmosphere. It helped measure the age of the universe.
astronomy/space-exploration.60d915398901: Twenty nineteen. Chang’e four on the Moon’s far side. Chang’e four makes the first soft landing on the far side of the Moon, and its rover Yutu two explores the surface.
astronomy/space-exploration.5bd505602442: Refracting telescope. Uses lenses to bend light. A big convex lens at the front, the objective, bends light so it comes together at a focus. A small eyepiece lens at the back magnifies the image. In sixteen ten Galileo used a small refractor to discover four moons of Jupiter. Big lenses sag and blur colours, so refractors cannot be made very large.
astronomy/space-exploration.d9a5e7536f86: Nineteen ninety-seven. First Mars rover. Sojourner, a rover the size of a microwave oven, rolls across Mars as part of the Mars Pathfinder mission.
astronomy/space-exploration.6524c1d7c28d: Twenty twenty-one. Perseverance and Ingenuity. The Perseverance rover lands on Mars to collect rock samples, and the small Ingenuity helicopter makes the first powered flight on another planet.
astronomy/space-exploration.eab9187a3753: Nineteen seventy-seven. Voyager one and two. The twin Voyager probes launch to visit the giant planets. In twenty twelve Voyager one became the first human-made object to reach interstellar space.
astronomy/space-exploration.3e97ff9b7bc4: Radio telescope. Catches radio waves from space. A giant metal dish reflects radio waves to a receiver at its focus. Radio waves pass through clouds and the atmosphere, so radio telescopes can work day and night and in cloudy weather. China’s FAST in Guizhou is five hundred meters across, one of the largest single-dish radio telescopes ever built.
astronomy/space-exploration.ba1a3c48d251: Second stage. Speeds up to orbital speed. Ignites after the first stage drops away, high above most of the air. Tips the rocket over so it builds up sideways speed: about twenty-eight thousand kilometers per hour, seven point eight kilometers per second, for a low orbit. Its engine is designed to work in the vacuum of space.
astronomy/space-exploration.599eea859ba2: Twenty twelve. Curiosity lands on Mars. The car-sized Curiosity rover lands in Gale Crater and finds evidence that Mars once had lakes of liquid water.

astronomy/star-life.7c9af8ba1163: Fomalhaut. Main-sequence star. Fusing hydrogen into helium in its core, like the Sun. About ninety percent of stars are here.
astronomy/star-life.3daf66ceeb25: Achernar. Main-sequence star. Fusing hydrogen into helium in its core, like the Sun. About ninety percent of stars are here. Spins so fast it is the flattest star known.
astronomy/star-life.8823d601038c: Rhenium. Merging neutron stars. Made when two neutron stars crash together: a flood of neutrons builds very heavy atoms in a flash, the “r-process”. Astronomers watched this happen in twenty seventeen.
astronomy/star-life.648dfb710c91: Europium. Merging neutron stars. Made when two neutron stars crash together: a flood of neutrons builds very heavy atoms in a flash, the “r-process”. Astronomers watched this happen in twenty seventeen.
astronomy/star-life.502a2b0c7cb5: Spica. Main-sequence star. Fusing hydrogen into helium in its core, like the Sun. About ninety percent of stars are here.
astronomy/star-life.114a853d1018: Common mix-up: Luminosity is how much light a star really gives off, not how bright it looks from Earth. Deneb looks fainter than Vega only because it is about one hundred times farther away; it really gives off thousands of times more light.
astronomy/star-life.ed01f71a166e: Castor A. Main-sequence star. Fusing hydrogen into helium in its core, like the Sun. About ninety percent of stars are here.
astronomy/star-life.5df746e7dbfa: Iron. Exploding white dwarfs. Made when a white dwarf in a two-star system gains too much mass and explodes, a “Type one A” supernova. Hemoglobin, which carries oxygen in your blood, about four grams in total
astronomy/star-life.8cc1dea6fee4: Betelgeuse. Supergiant. A massive star near the end of its short life; among the brightest stars there are. A red supergiant that will explode as a supernova, probably within the next one hundred thousand years.
astronomy/star-life.6dda7c6f367e: Iodine. Merging neutron stars. Made when two neutron stars crash together: a flood of neutrons builds very heavy atoms in a flash, the “r-process”. Astronomers watched this happen in twenty seventeen. Thyroid hormones that control growth
astronomy/star-life.0e0f4803fdbb: Regulus. Main-sequence star. Fusing hydrogen into helium in its core, like the Sun. About ninety percent of stars are here.
astronomy/star-life.49e3eb621a90: Proxima Centauri. Main-sequence star. Fusing hydrogen into helium in its core, like the Sun. About ninety percent of stars are here. The closest star to the Sun. It has at least one planet in its habitable zone.
astronomy/star-life.fdbabfc16cb9: Ruthenium. Merging neutron stars. Made when two neutron stars crash together: a flood of neutrons builds very heavy atoms in a flash, the “r-process”. Astronomers watched this happen in twenty seventeen.
astronomy/star-life.20ffcdab9a6e: Denebola. Main-sequence star. Fusing hydrogen into helium in its core, like the Sun. About ninety percent of stars are here.
astronomy/star-life.4e7f8b8915fe: Thorium. Merging neutron stars. Made when two neutron stars crash together: a flood of neutrons builds very heavy atoms in a flash, the “r-process”. Astronomers watched this happen in twenty seventeen.
astronomy/star-life.c00f3d3bcd5c: Cobalt. Exploding massive stars. Made by fusion inside massive stars and in their supernova explosions, which scatter them into space. Vitamin B twelve
astronomy/star-life.7c310cc89434: Gliese five eight one. Main-sequence star. Fusing hydrogen into helium in its core, like the Sun. About ninety percent of stars are here.
astronomy/star-life.59c419c7c42d: Silver. Merging neutron stars. Made when two neutron stars crash together: a flood of neutrons builds very heavy atoms in a flash, the “r-process”. Astronomers watched this happen in twenty seventeen.
astronomy/star-life.1c5aa171ef2c: Xenon. Merging neutron stars. Made when two neutron stars crash together: a flood of neutrons builds very heavy atoms in a flash, the “r-process”. Astronomers watched this happen in twenty seventeen.
astronomy/star-life.7933744d2f17: Lalande two one one eight five. Main-sequence star. Fusing hydrogen into helium in its core, like the Sun. About ninety percent of stars are here.
astronomy/star-life.f9b6e95fa259: Alpha Centauri A. Main-sequence star. Fusing hydrogen into helium in its core, like the Sun. About ninety percent of stars are here. Almost a twin of the Sun, in the nearest star system.
