astronomy/sun-stars.0fbe28a2be74: Radiative zone. Energy travels as light. Energy moves outward as light, photons, that is absorbed and given off again and again. Because of this zig-zag path, energy can take tens of thousands of years or more to cross this zone. The temperature drops from about seven million degrees Celsius to about two million degrees Celsius. It runs from about one quarter to seven tenths of the way to the surface. Radiative equals radiation: light bouncing like a pinball.
astronomy/sun-stars.22313f91de6d: Convection zone. Hot gas rises, cool gas sinks. Hot gas rises, cools near the top and sinks again, like a pot of boiling soup, convection currents. These currents carry the energy up to the surface. The tops of the convection cells show on the surface as granules, each roughly one thousand kilometers across. It is the outer thirty percent of the Sun: about two million degrees Celsius at the bottom and five thousand five hundred degrees Celsius at the top. Convection equals hot rises, cool sinks, like a lava lamp.
astronomy/sun-stars.ea9ed1045fc5: Sunspots. Cooler, darker patches. Darker, cooler areas on the photosphere, about three thousand five hundred to four thousand five hundred degrees Celsius. They form where strong magnetic fields block hot gas from rising. Their number rises and falls in an eleven-year cycle, solar minimum, solar maximum. Try the activity slider! Many sunspots are larger than the whole Earth. A sunspot is cooler, not cold. It only looks dark next to even brighter gas.
astronomy/sun-stars.d157892d1260: Protostar. A baby star heating up. A collapsing clump heats up as gravity squeezes it tighter. It glows from heat, but fusion has not started yet. When its core reaches about ten million degrees Celsius, hydrogen fusion begins and a true star is born. Proto equals first: a protostar is a star before fusion.
astronomy/sun-stars.7fd0563a9636: Main-sequence star. Fusing hydrogen: the longest stage. The star fuses hydrogen into helium in its core. Gravity pulling in is balanced by pressure pushing out, so the star stays steady. About ninety percent of stars, including the Sun, are main-sequence stars. More massive stars are hotter, bluer and brighter, and they use up their fuel much faster. Big stars live fast and die young.
astronomy/sun-stars.cc309ad7b35b: Core. The fusion power plant. The hottest part of the Sun: about fifteen million degrees Celsius. Hydrogen nuclei crash together and fuse into helium, nuclear fusion, releasing enormous energy. The Sun fuses about six hundred million tonnes of hydrogen every second. It reaches out to about one quarter of the Sun’s radius. Core equals fusion: hydrogen and hydrogen react to form helium and energy.
astronomy/sun-stars.f80af374cfe8: Chromosphere. A thin reddish layer. A thin layer of the Sun’s atmosphere just above the photosphere; “chromo” means color. Normally too faint to see next to the bright photosphere; it appears as a pinkish-red rim during a total solar eclipse. Strangely, it gets hotter with height, up to about twenty thousand degrees Celsius. Chromo equals color: the pink-red layer.
astronomy/sun-stars.e39941174b3d: Corona. The Sun’s outer atmosphere. The outermost layer, stretching millions of kilometers into space. It is over one million degrees Celsius, far hotter than the surface below it. During a total solar eclipse it appears as a pearly white crown. It streams outward as the solar wind; when the solar wind hits Earth’s magnetic field it can cause auroras. Corona equals crown, it looks like one during an eclipse.
astronomy/sun-stars.01e61d2d8895: Common mix-up: The energy is ancient by the time it escapes, but the final trip from the surface to Earth takes only about eight minutes.
astronomy/sun-stars.2c4e23d679d3: Red giant. Swollen, cooler outer layers. When the hydrogen in the core runs out, the core shrinks and heats up while the outer layers swell and cool. The star becomes hundreds of times wider and glows red. In about five billion years the Sun will become a red giant and may swallow Mercury and Venus. Red giant equals huge but cooler on the outside.
astronomy/sun-stars.b31d63907844: Photosphere. The visible “surface”. The layer we see: light escapes into space from here. About five thousand five hundred degrees Celsius. It is not solid. You could not stand on it; it is glowing gas a few hundred kilometers thick. It is covered with bubbling granules and, at times, dark sunspots. Photo equals light: the photosphere is the “light sphere”.

astronomy/telescopes-light.f2b601041bac: Radio waves. longer than thirty centimeters. Radio waves pass through clouds and even work in daytime, so radio telescopes can observe in any weather. Radio waves are so long that a dish must be enormous to see sharp detail. China’s FAST is five hundred meters, one thousand six hundred forty feet, across, the size of thirty soccer fields. Several dishes far apart can be linked to act like one giant telescope. In twenty nineteen, eight observatories linked across the whole Earth took the first picture of a black hole. Radio equals longest waves, lowest energy, biggest dishes.
astronomy/telescopes-light.9bb236c33fea: Gamma rays. shorter than zero point zero one nanometers. The most energetic light there is: one gamma-ray photon can carry millions of times the energy of a visible-light photon. Earth’s atmosphere absorbs them completely, which protects life on the ground. Space telescopes like NASA’s Fermi catch them directly. Ground telescopes can only see the faint blue flash a very high-energy gamma ray makes when it smashes into the upper air. Gamma equals the most energetic. Shortest wave, highest energy.
astronomy/telescopes-light.8a65d5b51687: X-rays. zero point zero one to ten nanometers. X-ray telescopes show the hottest places in the universe, from millions to hundreds of millions of degrees. X-rays would go straight into a normal mirror, so telescopes like Chandra use nested, barrel-shaped mirrors that X-rays skim off at a very low angle, like a stone skipping on water. Our atmosphere stops all of them, so X-ray astronomy only became possible with rockets and satellites. X-rays, extreme heat, millions of degrees.
astronomy/telescopes-light.4666198141cb: Infrared. seven hundred nanometers to one millimeter. Infrared, IR, passes through dust that blocks visible light, so it shows baby stars hidden inside dark clouds. Light from the most distant galaxies has been stretched by the expanding universe from visible into infrared. That is why JWST is an infrared telescope. Water vapour in our air absorbs most infrared. Only a few “windows” get through, best from high, dry mountains. JWST has to be kept colder than minus two hundred thirty degrees Celsius so its own warmth doesn’t drown out the faint signals. Infrared equals “below red”: you feel it as warmth from a campfire.
astronomy/telescopes-light.523ff1c6ad6b: Visible light. four hundred to seven hundred nanometers. The only light your eyes can detect: violet, about four hundred nanometers, through blue, green, yellow and orange to red, about seven hundred nanometers. It is a tiny sliver of the whole spectrum, much less than one millionth of the range on this slider, but it is where the Sun gives off the most light. It passes through clear air, which is why telescopes have been built on the ground for four hundred years. Roy G Biv: red has the longest visible wave, violet the shortest.
astronomy/telescopes-light.eaf4f9cde91a: Ultraviolet. ten to four hundred nanometers. Ultraviolet, UV, light comes from things hotter than the Sun’s surface, such as young blue stars. The ozone layer absorbs almost all UV shorter than about three hundred nanometers. A little of the longer UV gets through: that is what gives you a sunburn. Hubble can see in ultraviolet because it orbits above the atmosphere. UV equals “beyond violet”: just past the violet end of the rainbow.
astronomy/telescopes-light.3dacea045dfc: Microwaves. one millimeter to thirty centimeters. Every direction in the sky glows faintly in microwaves: it is the cosmic microwave background, light left over from about three hundred eighty thousand years after the Big Bang. ALMA, sixty-six dishes on a five thousand meter, sixteen thousand four hundred foot, high plateau in Chile, uses millimeter waves to see planets forming around young stars. Microwaves are often counted as short radio waves. Your microwave oven uses twelve centimeter waves; your Wi-Fi uses six or twelve centimeters. Microwaves: from the Big Bang’s afterglow to your kitchen.

astronomy/three-body.6d2f92860411: Each star feels the pull of the others. We choose model units for distance, mass and time so the gravity constant G has a value of one. The clock counts model seconds. Velocity Verlet updates the motion every zero point zero zero zero five model seconds. In B and C, a softening length, epsilon equals zero point zero zero eight, keeps acceleration finite during close passes. In A and the two-star preset, "epsilon equals zero" gives ordinary Newtonian gravity. The line in the sky view marks the distance r between stars one and two. Move the time slider to see how much acceleration star two alone gives star one. The mass of star two is m sub two.
astronomy/three-body.61407b981606: In an ideal, isolated pair, two bound stars that do not collide keep tracing ellipses around their shared center of mass. A circle is a special ellipse. Try the two-star control and see whether the stars retrace their paths. As the three stars move, all their pulls change. There’s no simple general formula for their motion from arbitrary starting conditions. Henri Poincaré’s work revealed how complicated the motion can get. In chaos, 混沌, tiny differences at the start can grow into big differences later, even under the same rules.
astronomy/three-body.28689b34d742: Three equal-mass stars chase each other around the same loop. Watch them take turns at the crossing. Chenciner and Montgomery published a proof of this orbit in two thousand.
astronomy/three-body.493d7d5b53ca: Alpha Centauri is the closest star system to ours. Stars A and B form a close pair, and Proxima Centauri orbits much farther out. Preset B shows this arrangement with a smaller difference in orbit sizes so you can see both at once. Picture two massive bodies circling each other. There are five special positions where a much lighter spacecraft can move along with them and keep the same position relative to both. In this circular-orbit model, those positions are called Lagrange points. Measurements of temperature and wind always have some uncertainty. Like the zero point zero zero one shift in the butterfly experiment, tiny starting differences can grow as the atmosphere moves. Research puts the limit for day-to-day forecasts in midlatitudes, where much of the United States lies, at about two weeks. Liu Cixin’s The Three-Body Problem is a science-fiction novel for older readers. It won the twenty fifteen Hugo Award for Best Novel. Its Trisolaran world has three suns. During Stable Eras, days and nights follow a pattern. During Chaotic Eras, sunrise and temperature become unpredictable.

astronomy/tides.55dd287af482: Your port. One spot on a coast. The red pin is a port on a coast, like Savannah, Georgia. As Earth spins, the port passes a high, a low, a high and a low in each lunar day, about twenty-four hours fifty minutes. Watch the “Port water level” bar under the model while Earth spins.
astronomy/tides.6fd715ca9546: Common mix-up: The Sun has far more mass, but the Moon is about three hundred ninety times closer. Its tide-raising effect is about twice as strong as the Sun’s.
astronomy/tides.2f83ff3a648e: Moon. The main cause of tides. The Moon’s gravity pulls on Earth and its oceans. It pulls hardest on the side closest to it. The Moon goes around Earth about once a month, so it is in a slightly different place each day. Earth has to turn about fifty extra minutes to face the Moon again, so high tide comes about fifty minutes later each day.
astronomy/tides.7d70225ae0ca: Sun. Makes tides bigger or smaller. The Sun also raises tides, but its effect is a bit less than half of the Moon’s, about forty-six percent. Sun, Earth and Moon in a line, the pulls add up, spring tides. Sun and Moon at a right angle, the pulls partly cancel, neap tides.
astronomy/tides.22882513be74: Low tide. Water drawn away from the sides. Halfway between the two bulges, ninety degrees from the Moon, the water is lower: low tide. The water that builds the bulges comes from these regions. A coast usually has a low tide about six hours twelve minutes after each high tide.
astronomy/tides.a28c26401c79: The Moon’s pull. Weaker with distance. Gravity gets weaker with distance. The near side of Earth is about twelve thousand seven hundred kilometers, one Earth diameter, closer to the Moon than the far side, so it feels a stronger pull. The DIFFERENCE in pull across Earth stretches the oceans into two bulges. Scientists call it the tidal force.
astronomy/tides.55b755c1cd7a: Earth. Spins once a day under the bulges. Earth rotates once about every twenty-four hours, carrying every coast through both bulges. That is why most coasts get two high tides and two low tides each day. The bulges stay lined up with the Moon while Earth turns underneath them.

biology/animals.c81778b4aabe: Common mix-up: Spiders are not insects. Insects have six legs and three body parts; spiders have eight legs and two body parts.
biology/animals.e70b17b04fd8: Arthropods. for example, ants, spiders, crabs, centipedes. A hard exoskeleton covers the body; it must be shed, molted, for the animal to grow. Jointed legs and a segmented body. The biggest animal group: more than three out of four known animal species are arthropods.
biology/animals.bb20af4785fc: Backbone, spine. a feature, not a group. A chain of small bones called vertebrae that protects the spinal cord. Animals with a backbone are vertebrates. Only about five percent of animal species have one! A backbone is part of an internal skeleton, which grows along with the body.
biology/animals.09287583cb46: Worms. For example, earthworm, segmented. Planarian, flat. Roundworm. Bilateral symmetry with a head end. That’s where nerves and senses gather. An earthworm’s body is made of about one hundred to one hundred fifty ring-shaped segments. Earthworms breathe through their moist skin and mix air into soil.

biology/body-systems.71f8e499cc82: Muscular system. Moves the body, holds posture and makes heat. The body has more than six hundred skeletal muscles. Muscles can only pull, so they work in pairs, like the biceps and triceps. Three types: skeletal, you control. Smooth, in organs. And cardiac, heart.
biology/body-systems.81816f958bc8: Bladder. Stores urine. A stretchy muscular bag. It can hold about four hundred to six hundred milliliters.
biology/body-systems.04019bbbfd27: Nervous system. Senses, controls and coordinates the body. The brain, spinal cord and nerves carry electrical signals. Signals can travel about one hundred twenty meters per second, faster than a race car. Reflexes, like pulling your hand off a hot pan, go through the spinal cord before the brain even knows.
biology/body-systems.530b3c8db64c: Large intestine. Absorbs water and forms feces. About one point five meters long but wider than the small intestine. Helpful bacteria here make some vitamins.
biology/body-systems.2e4216be212f: Esophagus. Food tube to the stomach. About twenty-five centimeters long. Waves of muscle, peristalsis, push food down, even if you are upside down!
biology/body-systems.a3fda74a8347: Bones. Skull, spine, ribs and limb bones. The femur, thigh bone, is the longest and strongest bone. The spine is made of thirty-three vertebrae.
biology/body-systems.93ca2e26e3df: Brain. The control center. About eighty-six billion neurons. Uses about twenty percent of the body’s energy. Cerebrum: thinking, cerebellum: balance, brainstem: heartbeat and breathing.
biology/body-systems.d891f59033cd: Excretory system. Removes cell wastes and balances water. Kidneys filter about one hundred eighty liters of blood plasma every day and make one to two liters of urine. Urine flows down the ureters to the bladder. Skin, sweat, and lungs, C O two, also help excrete wastes.
biology/body-systems.df97a17d1dd2: Respiratory system. Takes in oxygen and removes carbon dioxide. Air path: nose or mouth, trachea, bronchi, millions of tiny air sacs, alveoli. In the alveoli, O two moves into the blood and C O two moves out. Breathing is driven by the diaphragm muscle.
biology/body-systems.fb7c85701b8e: Digestive system. Breaks food into nutrients and absorbs them. Mechanical digestion, chewing, churning, and chemical digestion, enzymes, acid, work together. The small intestine is about six meters long; its villi absorb nutrients into the blood. The large intestine absorbs water from what is left.
biology/body-systems.5f2c3caed437: Skeletal system. Supports, protects and helps the body move. An adult has two hundred six bones. Babies have about three hundred, and some fuse together. The skull protects the brain; the ribs protect the heart and lungs. Red marrow inside bones makes new blood cells.
biology/body-systems.b03d50d3e579: Stomach. Churns food with acid and enzymes. Strong acid kills most germs in food. After two to four hours food becomes a soupy mix called chyme. A layer of mucus stops the stomach from digesting itself.
biology/body-systems.13d80f1e07f3: Small intestine. Finishes digestion and absorbs nutrients. About six meters long, folded up in your belly. Millions of finger-like villi pass nutrients into the blood.
biology/body-systems.2de8b69c6ad0: Circulatory system. Transports oxygen, nutrients and wastes. The heart beats about one hundred thousand times a day. Arteries carry blood away from the heart; veins carry it back. Tiny capillaries are where oxygen and nutrients pass into cells.
biology/body-systems.f749abec24ff: Common mix-up: Excretion is not the same as getting rid of feces! Excretion removes cell wastes, urine, sweat, C O two. Feces are leftover undigested food, which the digestive system eliminates.
biology/body-systems.1ec4b4537707: Heart. A muscular pump with four chambers. Two atria receive blood; two ventricles pump it out. The right side pumps blood to the lungs; the left side pumps it to the whole body. About the size of your fist; the left ventricle has the thickest wall.

biology/cell-city.7527c5d75855: Mitochondrion. Power plant: releases energy from food, sugar and oxygen, in cellular respiration.
biology/cell-city.d356fdd6d5a4: Plant versus animal check: tap the three parts of this plant cell that an animal cell does NOT have.

biology/cell-division.9ccc930de4c6: Chromosome, sister chromatids. Packaged DNA that is easy to move. Before dividing, DNA coils tightly into chromosomes that you can see with a microscope. A copied chromosome has two identical halves called sister chromatids, joined at the centromere. Human body cells have forty-six chromosomes, twenty-three pairs. This model shows only four, two pairs, to keep it simple.

biology/cell-theory.1a1c63adb794: Tissue: heart muscle. Similar cells with one job. A tissue is a group of similar cells that work together to do the same job. Animals have four main tissue types: muscle, nervous, epithelial and connective tissue. Heart muscle cells are branched and linked end to end, so they contract together as one team.
biology/cell-theory.5ac4109c39d0: Organ: the heart. Several tissues working together. An organ is a structure made of two or more kinds of tissue that work together for a specific job. The heart contains muscle tissue, to pump, nervous tissue, to control the beat, connective tissue and epithelial tissue, lining. Your heart beats about one hundred thousand times every day.
biology/cell-theory.89646d087ce3: Organ system. Organs working together. An organ system is a group of organs that work together to do one big job. The circulatory system equals heart, blood vessels and blood. It carries oxygen and nutrients to every cell. Systems also team up: the respiratory system brings in oxygen, and the circulatory system delivers it.
biology/cell-theory.6c6ca0aa6740: Eyepiece, ocular lens. The lens you look through. The eyepiece usually magnifies ten times. Total magnification equals eyepiece power times objective power. Ten times, times forty times, equals four hundred times.
biology/cell-theory.6a68faa77728: Fine adjustment knob. Small focus moves. The small knob moves the stage just a tiny bit to make the image sharp. At high power, forty times, use ONLY the fine knob.
biology/cell-theory.7f3294e467f5: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek. Ground amazing single lenses, up to about two hundred seventy times, and became the first person to see LIVING cells: tiny swimming “animalcules” in pond water, and later bacteria and blood cells.
biology/cell-theory.d85adab0eddc: Organism. A whole living thing. An organism is a complete living thing that can carry out all life processes on its own. A human body is made of about thirty-seven trillion cells, more than two hundred kinds of them. A unicellular organism, like a bacterium or paramecium, is just ONE cell, so for it the cell level and the organism level are the same.
biology/cell-theory.c5943c0e5fe7: Light source. Shines light up through the slide. A compound microscope needs light to pass THROUGH the specimen. Older microscopes use a mirror, 反光镜, to reflect light instead of a lamp.
biology/cell-theory.13f4bdb272ab: Objective lenses. Main magnifying lenses. Most school microscopes have four times, low, ten times, medium, and forty times, high, objectives. Higher-power objectives are LONGER, so they come very close to the slide. Always start with the lowest-power objective: it shows the largest area and is easiest to focus.

biology/cell-transport.2cd5fdd8da5d: Salt particles, solute. Dissolved particles that cannot cross. A solute is the stuff dissolved in a liquid; the liquid, water, is the solvent. Body cells contain about zero point nine percent salt, so zero point nine percent salt water is “balanced”, isotonic, for them. Saltier outside, hypertonic, water leaves the cell. Fresher outside, hypotonic, water enters.

biology/cells-review.adca72266b93: Elodea and egg labs. Elodea in salt water: water leaves, chloroplasts clump away from the wall, plasmolysis; tap water brings them back. Vinegar dissolves the eggshell, C O two bubbles. Corn syrup, hypertonic, shrinks the egg; distilled water, hypotonic, swells it. percent change equals, final minus initial, divided by initial, times one hundred. IV equals type of solution; DV equals mass.
biology/cells-review.855db786c3bc: In sixteen sixty-five Robert Hooke saw tiny boxes in cork and called them cells. A few years later Antonie van Leeuwenhoek saw the first living cells swimming in pond water.
biology/cells-review.c949849dc5f4: Cell theory and its timeline. One. All living things are made of one or more cells. Two. The cell is the basic unit of structure and function. Three. All cells come from pre-existing cells. Hooke sixteen sixty-five, cork, named “cells”; Leeuwenhoek sixteen seventies, first living cells; Schleiden eighteen thirty-eight, plants; Schwann eighteen thirty-nine, animals; Virchow eighteen fifty-five, cells from cells. Better microscopes made each discovery possible.
biology/cells-review.6fce66eaa69d: The sodium-potassium blank uses ATP to move ions against their gradients.
biology/cells-review.58eb286e1957: Microscopes. Total magnification equals eyepiece times objective, ten times, times forty times, equals four hundred times. Start on low power; use the coarse knob only at low power and the fine knob at high power. Wet mount: specimen, drop of water and coverslip lowered at an angle, no air bubbles.
biology/cells-review.867bba4be51b: He looked at cork in sixteen sixty-five and named the little boxes “cells”.
biology/cells-review.14a4546b3449: Challenge: At four hundred times, the field of view is about four hundred micrometers wide. A cell stretches across one quarter of it. About how long is the cell? One hundred micrometers. Four hundred micrometers. One thousand six hundred micrometers. Twenty-five micrometers
biology/cells-review.e857108832d3: Cell analogies, Cell City. Nucleus equals city hall, mitochondria equals power plant, ribosomes equals factories, ER equals roads. Golgi equals post office, lysosomes equals recycling or clean-up crew, vacuole equals water tower or warehouse. Membrane equals border checkpoint, cell wall equals city wall, chloroplasts equals solar power plant.
biology/cells-review.13c0f14be394: To see cells we use a microscope. Multiply the eyepiece by the objective: ten times forty is four hundred times. Use only the fine focus knob at high power.
biology/cells-review.3e63bd974c8f: Challenge: An egg goes from sixty-five point zero grams to fifty-two point zero grams in salt water. What is the percent change in mass? Plus twenty percent. minus thirteen percent. minus twenty-five percent. minus twenty percent
biology/cells-review.6668372430cf: Hyper, hypo, and isotonic. Always compare the solution OUTSIDE with the inside of the cell. Water follows solute. Hypertonic, water out, animal: shrivels; plant: plasmolysis. Hypotonic, water in, animal: swells or bursts; plant: turgid. Isotonic, no net movement, zero point nine percent saline for blood cells.
biology/cells-review.e6a6ffcc6d9f: Passive transport. No energy needed: particles move from HIGH to LOW concentration, down the gradient. Diffusion, for example, oxygen in, C O two out. Osmosis equals diffusion of WATER across a membrane. Facilitated diffusion: still high, low, but through a protein channel, for example, glucose.
biology/cells-review.c0ee6b1383ea: An egg goes from sixty grams to seventy-five grams. Its percent change in mass.

biology/characteristics-of-life.e7929a9c47ae: A dry bean seed in a packet. It has been in a kitchen drawer for five years. It doesn’t move, eat or grow.
biology/characteristics-of-life.45476a45b5fa: A honeycomb of tiny empty boxes: cells! Robert Hooke saw exactly this in sixteen sixty-five.
biology/characteristics-of-life.d93fb2e27ff2: A dried-out tardigrade, water bear. This half-millimeter animal has been bone dry for ten years, curled into a tiny barrel.
biology/characteristics-of-life.d294b5ce1d94: One of your red blood cells. It carries oxygen for about one hundred twenty days. It has no nucleus and can’t divide.

biology/classification.c9e74fe76819: Common mix-up: Not all protists are microscopic: giant kelp can grow more than thirty meters long.
biology/classification.057e207eff6e: All life. Every living thing starts here: about two million named species, and millions more not yet named. Each ring below holds fewer organisms that share more traits.
biology/classification.56e521515496: Animalia. Consumers that eat other organisms. Animals must eat, ingest, other organisms to get energy. Most can move on their own for at least part of their life. About ninety-five percent of animal species are invertebrates, no backbone. Animals: no cell walls, and they eat their food.
biology/classification.c9c18a9953e4: Archaebacteria. Single cells that love extreme places. Many live where little else can: boiling hot springs, very salty lakes, places with no oxygen. Methanogens live in swamps and even in cows’ stomachs and give off methane gas. Carl Woese showed in nineteen seventy-seven that their DNA is very different from bacteria, so they got their own domain. Archaea equals “ancient” extremists: heat, salt, no oxygen.
biology/classification.a20f5f417043: Domain. Eukarya. The broadest level. There are three domains: Bacteria, Archaea and Eukarya. Eukarya equals every organism whose cells have a nucleus.
biology/classification.809710756c52: Species. Homo sapiens. A species is a group of organisms that can breed together and produce fertile offspring. Its scientific name has two words: Genus and species, like Canis lupus.
biology/classification.599e749cac64: Species. Canis lupus. A species is a group of organisms that can breed together and produce fertile offspring. Its scientific name has two words: Genus and species, like Canis lupus.

biology/diffusion.488c56f81810: Fresh blood keeps bringing O two and glucose and carries C O two and wastes away. Try making the cell sprint! The cell keeps making C O two, so there is more inside the cell than in the blood: it diffuses out into the blood.
biology/diffusion.c9c3738e9d73: Lungs: oxygen in, C O two out. Gas exchange in the alveoli. Your lungs end in hundreds of millions of tiny air sacs called alveoli. Each one is wrapped in capillaries, tiny blood vessels. The wall between the air and the blood is less than one hundredth as thick as a hair, so molecules cross it easily. Fresh air in the alveolus has MORE oxygen than the blood arriving from the body, so oxygen diffuses into the blood. Red blood cells carry it, and the heart pumps it to every cell. The blood has MORE carbon dioxide than the air, so C O two diffuses into the alveolus, and you breathe it out.
biology/diffusion.dc567e142e05: Spreading from high, left, to low, right… zero seconds. Hot water: warmer molecules move faster, so they spread out faster. Test it with the temperature slider!
biology/diffusion.37da8f306932: O two is diffusing from the HIGH side to the LOW side. Watch the bars and the net-flow numbers. There is more oxygen in the air sac than in the blood, so the net flow is air, blood.
biology/diffusion.50e987c7f508: O two is diffusing from the HIGH side to the LOW side. Watch the bars and the net-flow numbers. The cell keeps making C O two, so there is more inside the cell than in the blood: it diffuses out into the blood.
biology/diffusion.c4fb265af14c: Wastes go the other way. The cell makes carbon dioxide, so there is more inside. C O two diffuses into the blood, which carries it to the lungs, and you breathe it out.
biology/diffusion.5ce9edb5e94f: Body cell: supplies in, wastes out. Diffusion between blood and cells. Your cells use oxygen and glucose all the time, cellular respiration, in the mitochondria, to release energy. Because they use them up, cells have a LOWER concentration of oxygen and nutrients than the blood around them, so these diffuse IN. The featured video shows this process. Respiration makes carbon dioxide and other wastes. They build up to a HIGHER concentration inside the cell than in the blood, so they diffuse OUT. Blood carries C O two to the lungs, you breathe it out, and other wastes such as urea to the kidneys, they leave in urine.

biology/dna.e3beaa82ad33: Guanine, G. Always pairs with C. Guanine pairs only with cytosine. G and C are held together by three hydrogen bonds, so a G with C pair is a little stronger than A with T.
biology/dna.ac872abd45c7: Sugar, deoxyribose. Holds a base. DNA’s sugar is called deoxyribose. That is the “D” in DNA, DeoxyriboNucleic Acid. Each sugar has one base attached to it. One sugar, one phosphate and one base equals a nucleotide, the building block of DNA.
biology/dna.cb3577a87f9f: Adenine, A. Always pairs with T. One of the four bases, the “letters” of the genetic code. Adenine pairs only with thymine. A and T are held together by two hydrogen bonds.

biology/ecosystems.835336d3e2ff: Common mix-up: The tundra is very dry, almost like a desert: it gets less than twenty-five centimeters of precipitation a year.
biology/ecosystems.8f86250c8864: Dark zone. Below about one thousand meters there is no sunlight at all. It is near freezing, with crushing pressure. Abiotic factor: a non-living part of the ecosystem that affects the living things.
biology/ecosystems.0aa883012312: Sunlit zone. The top about two hundred meters gets enough light for photosynthesis, so most ocean life lives here. Abiotic factor: a non-living part of the ecosystem that affects the living things.
biology/ecosystems.24fe1f8de869: Marine, ocean. The ocean covers about seventy-one percent of Earth. Life depends on sunlight near the surface; the deep ocean is dark, cold and under great pressure. phytoplankton, seaweed, kelp, algae in coral. fish, whales, sharks, coral, anglerfish
biology/ecosystems.8e32d1060bb2: Desert. The driest biome: less than twenty-five centimeters of rain a year. Hot deserts have scorching days but cold nights. cacti, succulents, shrubs with deep roots. lizards, kangaroo rats, rattlesnakes, camels

biology/endocytosis.5f21dc63194c: Take a sip. Tap near the membrane: it folds inward and takes a sip of the fluid outside. One. Fold inward: The membrane folds inward and makes a small pocket filled with outside fluid and the things dissolved in it, blue. Two. Pinch off: The pocket closes and pinches off into a tiny vesicle. Three. Move inside: The vesicle travels into the cytoplasm. Four. Release: The vesicle opens and releases its contents into the cytoplasm.
biology/endocytosis.42bbe596ea55: Amoeba hunt. Steer the amoeba: drag or tap toward the green paramecium. One. Reach out: The membrane flows out into pseudopods, “false feet”. Moving them uses energy, ATP. Two. Wrap around: The pseudopods wrap around the paramecium like a cupped hand. Three. Pinch off: The tips meet and fuse. A piece of membrane pinches off around the food: now it is inside a vesicle called a food vacuole. Four. Move inside: The vesicle carries the food deeper into the cytoplasm. Five. Lysosome joins: A lysosome fuses with the vesicle and adds digestive enzymes. Six. Digest: The food is broken down. Small nutrient molecules, yellow, pass into the cytoplasm for the cell to use.
biology/endocytosis.720c854566f3: Catch only cholesterol. Receptors, Y shapes, grab only LDL particles: orange “cholesterol packages” from the blood. Tap outside the cell to add more LDL. One. Bind: LDL particles stick to their matching receptors, like a key in a lock. Two. Coated pit: When enough receptors are full, a protein coat, clathrin, gray spikes, bends the membrane inward into a pit. Three. Pinch off: The pit pinches off into a coated vesicle carrying only LDL. Four. Uncoat and move in: The coat falls off and the vesicle moves inside. The receptors are recycled back to the membrane. Five. Release: The LDL is broken down and the cholesterol, yellow, is released for the cell to use.
biology/endocytosis.80738bc0bedc: White blood cell versus bacteria. You are a neutrophil, a white blood cell, in the blood. Eat the bacteria before they multiply! One. Chase: The white blood cell crawls toward the bacteria, pushing out pseudopods. This uses energy, ATP. Two. Wrap around: The membrane wraps around the bacterium. Three. Pinch off: The membrane pinches off: the bacterium is trapped inside a vesicle. Four. Move inside: The vesicle carries the bacterium into the cytoplasm. Five. Lysosome joins: Lysosomes fuse with the vesicle and pour in enzymes that kill the germ. Six. Destroy: The bacterium is broken down into harmless small molecules.

biology/evolution.80de26a7636e: Tree bark, environment. Decides which colors are hidden. Moths rest on tree trunks during the day, where birds hunt them. Before factories, English tree trunks were pale. Coal smoke in the eighteen hundreds darkened them with soot. Use the Bark color slider: the environment changes, so the “best” moth color changes too.
biology/evolution.1918cf11ef7d: Dark peppered moth. Camouflaged on sooty bark. The dark form comes from a mutation in one gene, and it is inherited. The first dark moth was recorded near Manchester, England in eighteen forty-eight. By eighteen ninety-five about ninety-eight percent of moths there were dark. It did not appear BECAUSE of the soot; it already existed and was favored by selection.
biology/evolution.7b592944e1d3: Lichen and soot. A change in the environment. Pale lichens grow on trees where the air is clean. Air pollution killed the lichens and coated bark in black soot, so dark moths became better hidden. After clean-air laws, nineteen fifty-six in Britain, lichens returned and light moths became common again.

biology/exocytosis.39b057a591d8: Pancreas beta cell. Someone just ate a cookie and blood sugar is rising! Ship three packages of insulin OUT into the blood. One. Ribosome builds it: A ribosome on the rough ER builds the protein, following the DNA recipe from the nucleus. Two. Inside the ER: The new protein slides into the endoplasmic reticulum, ER, and travels through its tubes. Three. Vesicle: ER, Golgi: A vesicle buds off the ER and carries the protein to the Golgi body. Four. Golgi packs and labels: The Golgi body finishes the protein, packs it and labels where it must go. Five. Vesicle, membrane: A new vesicle carries the package along tracks to the cell membrane. Moving it uses ATP. Six. Fuse and release: The vesicle fuses with the membrane and the contents spill outside. Exocytosis!

biology/food-webs.fcb62e5da388: Producers. Make their own food, level one. Plants, algae and some bacteria are producers. Photosynthesis: carbon dioxide and water and light energy react to form sugar, glucose, and oxygen. Producers form the base of every energy pyramid and hold the MOST energy. In this model: grass, trees and wildflowers.
biology/food-webs.81639769d66d: Energy lost as heat. Where about ninety percent goes at each step. Organisms use most of their energy to move, grow, breathe and keep warm, cellular respiration. That energy finally leaves as heat, which no organism can use as food. Some energy also stays in parts that are not eaten, bones, fur, roots, or leaves in wastes. Only about ten percent is stored in the body and passed up: the ten percent rule.
biology/food-webs.237d6ca67d4c: Primary consumers. Herbivores that eat producers, level two. Herbivores such as rabbits, grasshoppers and deer eat only plants. They get only about ten percent of the energy stored in the plants they eat. If producers hold ten thousand kilojoules, primary consumers get about one thousand kilojoules.
biology/food-webs.baefc33dcd9d: Tertiary consumers. Top predators, level four. They eat secondary consumers. Examples: hawks, owls and eagles. Only about zero point one percent of the producers’ energy reaches them. That is why an ecosystem can support only a few top predators, and food chains rarely have more than four to five links.
biology/food-webs.df6d469c3f47: Common mix-up: Plants do not “eat” soil. Soil gives water and minerals, but the food, sugar, is built from C O two and water using light energy.
biology/food-webs.58e81c729581: The Sun. Source of energy for almost every food web. Sunlight is the original energy source for nearly every ecosystem on Earth. Only producers can capture light energy directly, by photosynthesis. Plants capture only a small part, about one percent, of the sunlight that reaches them. That small part powers the whole pyramid.
biology/food-webs.24afac7efc83: Secondary consumers. Eat primary consumers, level three. They can be carnivores, frog, snake, or omnivores, a fox eats rabbits AND berries. They receive about one percent of the energy that the producers stored. In this model: frog, snake and fox.

biology/habitat-niche.8c139b847a79: Ecological factors, 生态因素, affect how and where organisms live. Sunlight, water, and temperature are abiotic factors. The grass rabbits eat, the foxes that hunt them, and the microbes that make them sick are biotic factors for rabbits. An ecosystem includes living and nonliving parts. Grasses are producers, rabbits and foxes are consumers, and some bacteria and fungi are decomposers. They interact with water, air, and nonliving parts of the soil.

biology/heredity.2ed91758a0aa: Punnett square. A grid that predicts offspring. One parent’s alleles go across the top, the other parent’s down the side. Each box is one possible offspring genotype. In a two times two square each box is a twenty-five percent chance. Named after the British geneticist Reginald Punnett, early nineteen hundreds. Letter on top and letter on the side react to form box.
biology/heredity.f5be2d97e94b: Dominant allele. Shows up even with only one copy. Written with a CAPITAL letter, like T. Capital T capital T and capital T lowercase t plants look the same: both are tall. Gregor Mendel found that one “factor” could hide another in his pea experiments, eighteen fifty-six to eighteen sixty-three. CAPITAL letter equals the “loud” allele that covers up the quiet one.
biology/heredity.81369264ec7a: Common mix-up: A three to one prediction does not mean exactly three of every four offspring will be tall. Each offspring is a new “coin toss”.
biology/heredity.aa5193976485: Careful: A Punnett square gives probabilities, not promises. Four offspring will not always be exactly three tall and one short.
biology/heredity.269e441a0c86: Offspring. Gets one allele from each parent. Half of an offspring’s chromosomes come from each parent. Capital T lowercase t times capital T lowercase t can produce a short, lowercase t lowercase t, plant, even though both parents are tall! Because each offspring gets a new mix of alleles, sexual reproduction creates variation. One allele from parent one plus one allele from parent two equals two alleles.
biology/heredity.3bfad8653b2d: Chromosome. A tightly coiled package of DNA. Made of one long DNA molecule wound around proteins. Genes sit at fixed spots along it, like beads on a string. Pea plants have seven pairs, fourteen chromosomes; humans have twenty-three pairs, forty-six. Simplified model: here all three genes are drawn on one pair. In real peas they lie on different chromosomes. Chromosome equals cookbook, gene equals recipe, allele equals one version of the recipe.

biology/microorganisms.797b220513e6: Common mix-up: Bacteria are cells, but much simpler and about ten times smaller than your body cells.
biology/microorganisms.2033984d8c6d: Capsid, protein coat. A protein shell that protects the genes. The head is a twenty-sided protein shell called a capsid. A virus has no cytoplasm, no ribosomes and no cell membrane: it is not a cell. Viruses are about ten to one hundred times smaller than bacteria. Virus equals genes in a protein box.

biology/osmosis.5bc9890310dd: Why IV drips are zero point nine percent saline. Fluid that goes straight into a vein must match your blood: about zero point nine percent salt, “normal saline”. Pure water would make red blood cells swell and burst; very salty water would shrivel them.
biology/osmosis.5a8a806a9473: Why seawater makes you thirstier. Seawater is about three point five percent salt, almost four times saltier than your body fluids. Salty blood pulls water out of your cells by osmosis, and your kidneys must use even more water to get rid of the extra salt. You lose more water than you drank!
biology/osmosis.e5493ef7507c: Kidneys, guts and rehydration. Your kidneys save water: as urine is made, most of the water moves back into the blood, much of it by osmosis. Your large intestine absorbs water the same way. After sweating or being sick, a rehydration drink, water, a little salt and sugar, helps: the salt and sugar are absorbed, and water follows them by osmosis.
biology/osmosis.53fb933134c5: That is why drinking seawater makes you thirstier. At three point five percent salt it pulls water out of your cells, and your kidneys need even more water to get rid of the salt.
biology/osmosis.e2e423988254: Isotonic, just right: same salt inside and out. Water crosses both ways equally, so the cell keeps its dimpled disc shape. This is why IV drips use zero point nine percent saline!
biology/osmosis.3e650faf22e5: Your red blood cells have no wall. In fresh water they swell and can burst. In zero point nine percent saline they stay normal. In salty water they shrivel.

biology/photosynthesis.eccff03ca778: Memory hint: Plants make O two in the light; everyone, plants too, uses O two all the time.
biology/photosynthesis.0cae71f17ebe: Mitochondrion. Where cellular respiration happens. Found in almost all plant AND animal cells. Its inner membrane is folded into cristae, giving lots of surface area for making ATP. Busy cells, such as muscle cells, contain thousands of mitochondria. Cellular respiration is not breathing. Breathing moves air in and out of lungs; respiration is a chemical reaction inside every cell. Breathing supplies its O two.
biology/photosynthesis.fcd3f97dcf20: Glucose, C six H twelve O six. Sugar that stores chemical energy. Glucose is built in the chloroplast and has six carbon atoms. Plants burn it for energy, use it to build cellulose for cell walls, or store it as starch, potatoes, rice, seeds. When an animal eats a plant, it takes in this stored energy. Glucose is not energy itself. It is matter that stores energy in its chemical bonds.
biology/photosynthesis.641c3c181998: Carbon dioxide, C O two. Input of photosynthesis, output of respiration. C O two from the air enters the leaf through tiny pores called stomata. Its carbon atoms become the backbone of glucose. Making one glucose takes six C O two. Mitochondria give C O two back out when they break glucose down. A tree does not grow by “eating soil”. Most of its mass comes from C O two in the air!
biology/photosynthesis.ff43a0ba3a66: In seventeen seventy-nine, Jan Ingenhousz showed that green parts of plants need light to release oxygen. Melvin Calvin and his team worked out how plants use carbon dioxide to start making sugars, a process called the Calvin cycle. He won the nineteen sixty-one Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Yuan Longping and his team developed higher-yielding hybrid rice that helped feed hundreds of millions of people.
biology/photosynthesis.46a79d6c9e63: Water, H two O. Input of photosynthesis, output of respiration. Roots absorb water; it travels up xylem tubes into the leaves. In the chloroplast, water molecules are split. Their oxygen atoms are released as O two gas. Making one glucose uses six H two O. Respiration gives six H two O back.
biology/photosynthesis.6abce2512c10: Oxygen, O two. Output of photosynthesis, input of respiration. Oxygen leaves the leaf through the stomata. Almost all the oxygen in the air was made by photosynthesis. Ocean algae and phytoplankton make about half of it. Mitochondria need O two to break glucose down completely.

biology/plants.f73484c22ed3: Filament. Holds up the anther. A thin stalk that lifts the anther up high. Raised anthers brush pollen onto visiting insects, or release it into the wind. Stamen equals anther and filament.
biology/plants.0aa6d060e0e5: Style. Connects stigma to ovary. A stalk that holds the stigma up. After pollination, a pollen tube grows down through the style to reach the ovules. Pistil equals stigma, style and ovary.
biology/plants.ab0fa22df38d: Stomata. Tiny pores for gases and water vapor. Stomata are tiny openings, mostly on the underside of leaves. Each is guarded by two guard cells. C O two goes in; O two and water vapor go out. Water vapor escaping through stomata is called transpiration. It pulls water up the xylem like a straw.

biology/protein-synthesis.a2b72a91a95a: Messenger RNA, mRNA. The working copy. mRNA is a single strand that carries the gene’s message from the nucleus to a ribosome. RNA uses the base U, uracil, instead of T, and the sugar ribose instead of deoxyribose. Every three bases form a codon. A U G is the START codon; U A A, U A G and U G A are STOP codons.
biology/protein-synthesis.61af73855951: Ribosome. The protein factory. A ribosome has a small and a large subunit that clamp around the mRNA. It slides along the mRNA one codon, three bases, at a time. It links amino acids together with peptide bonds.
biology/protein-synthesis.5238060df20a: Transfer RNA, tRNA. The delivery truck. Each tRNA carries one specific amino acid. Its anticodon, three bases, pairs with a matching codon on the mRNA, like a key in a lock. Example: the codon A U G pairs with the anticodon U A C, which carries methionine.
biology/protein-synthesis.a252283325d2: DNA and the gene. The master recipe. A gene is a section of DNA that holds the instructions for one protein. Only ONE of the two DNA strands, the template strand, is read to make the mRNA. The highlighted gene here is eighteen base pairs long. Real genes are often thousands.
biology/protein-synthesis.f6a535c77fad: Protein. The finished, working product. When the ribosome reaches a STOP codon, the chain is released. The chain folds into a three D shape. Its shape lets it do its job: enzymes, muscle, hair, keratin, hemoglobin…. Proteins build and run your body, and they are how genes produce traits.
biology/protein-synthesis.4f10e32a5382: Amino acids. The building blocks of proteins. There are twenty kinds of amino acids in living things. The ORDER of amino acids decides the shape and job of the protein. Here the chain spells M A G I C: M E T, A L A, G L Y, I L E, C Y S.

biology/reproduction.61557b6722ce: Hydra, parent. A tiny freshwater animal. Hydra is a small animal related to jellyfish, about one centimeter long. It catches tiny prey with stinging tentacles. When food is plentiful it reproduces asexually by budding. It can also reproduce sexually. Hydra can even regrow lost parts, regeneration, like the monster in the myth.
biology/reproduction.acf39db79320: Stamen, male part. Makes pollen. Stamen equals anther, makes pollen, and filament, the stalk. Pollen grains carry the plant’s male sex cells, sperm. A flower usually has several stamens around the pistil. STAMEN has “MEN” in it: the male part.
biology/reproduction.d9abdd7efa2a: Binary fission. One cell splits into two. Bacteria reproduce this way. It is a type of asexual reproduction. The cell copies its DNA, grows longer, then pinches in two across the middle. In good conditions, some bacteria such as E. coli can divide about every twenty minutes. Fission equals splitting: one, two, four, eight …
biology/reproduction.45a35163135b: Pistil, female part. Stigma, style and ovary. The sticky stigma at the top catches pollen. The style is the stalk that connects the stigma to the ovary. The ovary holds the ovules. After fertilization the ovary becomes the fruit. Ovary, fruit, ovule, seed.

biology/tonicity-labs.b267930301c1: Day one: a raw egg goes into vinegar. Bubbles cover it: the acid reacts with the calcium carbonate shell and gives off carbon dioxide gas.
biology/tonicity-labs.8735569a0667: Day zero: start by measuring the egg in its shell. Tare the scale first!
biology/tonicity-labs.70771cef85bc: The string is wrapped around the widest part. Read the ruler to the nearest zero point one centimeter.
biology/tonicity-labs.c078bac941b8: Weigh each egg every day. Percent change equals final minus initial, divided by initial, times one hundred. Then graph mass against time.
biology/tonicity-labs.9b9a7ed533a0: Tared: with the empty weigh boat, the scale now reads zero point zero grams. Now only the egg will be weighed.
biology/tonicity-labs.937e2da89934: Claim: The naked egg in corn syrup lost mass. Evidence: Its mass went from seventy point zero grams on Day two to thirty-eight point five grams on Day five, a change of minus forty-five point zero percent. In comparison, the simulated trials in distilled water changed by plus seventeen point seven percent on average. Reasoning: The egg’s membrane is selectively permeable, so water can cross it but the sugar or salt mostly cannot. Corn syrup is hypertonic to the egg: it has more solute and less water than the inside of the egg. By osmosis, water moved from the high water concentration inside the egg to the low water concentration outside, so the egg lost mass.

chemistry/acids-bases.7c40d94f71f1: Baking soda solution. pH eight point three. Basic. Baking soda, sodium bicarbonate, is a mild base. It neutralizes acids — and fizzes with vinegar, giving off carbon dioxide.
chemistry/acids-bases.4f6d10b54274: Antacid, milk of magnesia. pH ten point five. Basic. Antacids are bases that neutralize extra stomach acid to relieve heartburn. Stomach acid, hydrochloric acid, has a pH of about one point five to three point five.
chemistry/acids-bases.064778f8cb5f: Seawater. pH eight point one. Basic. Seawater is slightly basic, about pH eight point one. As the ocean absorbs C O two from the air its pH slowly drops, ocean acidification, which harms shells and coral.
chemistry/acids-bases.8d562653caf9: The pH scale. Measures acidity from zero to fourteen. pH runs from zero, most acidic, through seven, neutral, to fourteen, most basic. pH tells how many hydrogen ions are in a solution: the more hydrogen ions, the lower the pH. Each step is a times ten change: pH three is ten times more acidic than pH four and one hundred times more acidic than pH five.
chemistry/acids-bases.e184573b3a70: Household ammonia. pH eleven point six. Very basic. A base used in glass cleaners. Never mix ammonia with bleach — it makes a toxic gas!
chemistry/acids-bases.c336a86b3864: Battery acid. pH zero point eight. Very acidic. Car batteries contain sulfuric acid, H two S O four. It is corrosive: it can burn skin and eat holes in clothing.
chemistry/acids-bases.e0ff77f9b800: Neutralization. Acid and base react to form salt and water. When an acid and a base react, hydrogen ions and hydroxide ions join to make water: hydrogen ions and hydroxide ions react to form H two O. The other ions form a salt. Example: H C l and N a O H react to form N a C l and H two O. If equal amounts react, the solution ends up neutral, pH about seven. Everyday uses: antacids for heartburn, soapy water on itchy insect bites, formic acid, and slaked lime to fix acidic soil.
chemistry/acids-bases.bbf80f09ec63: Base. pH above seven. Bases release hydroxide ions in water. They taste bitter and feel slippery, like soap. Bases turn red litmus blue and turn phenolphthalein pink.
chemistry/acids-bases.9cc1cbcbd5e9: Milk. pH six point six. Acidic. Milk is almost neutral, just slightly acidic. When milk goes sour, bacteria make lactic acid and the pH drops.
chemistry/acids-bases.7240d67993f4: Tomato. pH four point three. Acidic. Tomatoes are mildly acidic — that’s why tomato sauce tastes tangy.
chemistry/acids-bases.336f94954620: Lemon juice. pH two point two. Very acidic. Citric acid gives lemons their sour taste. A sour taste is a property of acids.
chemistry/acids-bases.f916e5576f44: Neutral. pH equals seven. A neutral solution is neither acidic nor basic: pH seven. Pure water is neutral because it has equal amounts of hydrogen ions and hydroxide ions. Salt water and sugar water are neutral too.
chemistry/acids-bases.42c0e979639a: Black coffee. pH five. Acidic. Coffee is only weakly acidic. Normal rain is also slightly acidic, about pH five point six, because carbon dioxide from the air dissolves in it.
chemistry/acids-bases.5c8859da73e1: Drain cleaner. pH thirteen point eight. Very basic. Contains sodium hydroxide, lye, one of the strongest common bases. It dissolves hair and grease in pipes — and can badly burn skin and eyes.
chemistry/acids-bases.f982345e658d: Pure water. pH seven. Neutral. Pure, distilled, water is neutral: pH seven at twenty-five degrees Celsius. It has equal amounts of hydrogen and hydroxide ions. Tap water is usually between pH six point five and eight point five.
chemistry/acids-bases.44b77ef48edc: Acid. pH below seven. Acids release hydrogen ions in water. They taste sour, lemons, vinegar — but never taste lab chemicals! Acids turn blue litmus paper red and purple litmus solution red. Many acids react with metals such as zinc to make hydrogen gas.
chemistry/acids-bases.c7640a907e4f: Vinegar. pH two point nine. Very acidic. Vinegar is about five percent acetic acid in water. It is used for cooking, pickling and removing hard-water scale.
chemistry/acids-bases.bce4997f28f6: Orange juice. pH three point five. Acidic. Contains citric acid and ascorbic acid, vitamin C. Lemon juice, pH two point two, is about twenty times more acidic.
chemistry/acids-bases.be71458c666b: Bleach. pH twelve point six. Very basic. Bleach, sodium hypochlorite solution, is strongly basic and a powerful disinfectant. Bases feel slippery because they react with the oils on your skin.

chemistry/atoms.262fcdf767dc: Neutron. Neutral, zero, particle in the nucleus. Charge: zero. Mass: about one atomic mass unit, a tiny bit heavier than a proton. Neutrons help hold the nucleus together. Without them, the positive protons would push each other apart. Atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons are called isotopes.
chemistry/atoms.3fb186243859: Nucleus. The tiny, heavy center of the atom. Made of protons and neutrons packed tightly together. Holds more than ninety-nine point nine percent of the atom’s mass, but only a tiny part of its volume. If an atom were the size of a football stadium, the nucleus would be about the size of a pea at the center. The nucleus has a positive charge because of its protons.
chemistry/atoms.43dd1909ec37: Electron. Negative, minus one, particle around the nucleus. Charge: minus one. Mass: about one over one thousand eight hundred thirty-six of a proton, so it barely counts toward the mass. Electrons are arranged in shells, energy levels, around the nucleus. In a neutral atom, the number of electrons equals the number of protons. Electrons in the outermost shell, valence electrons, take part in chemical reactions.
chemistry/atoms.da8361adfee6: Atomic number. equals number of protons. Every element has its own atomic number: H is one, C is six, O is eight. The periodic table is arranged in order of atomic number. In a neutral atom, it also equals the number of electrons.
chemistry/atoms.de81465ff36c: Mass number. equals protons plus neutrons. Electrons are so light that we don’t count them. Neutrons equals mass number minus atomic number. Example: carbon fourteen has fourteen minus six equals eight neutrons. The number after an element’s name, carbon twelve, is its mass number.
chemistry/atoms.3e30816245c1: Common mix-up: The third shell can actually hold eighteen electrons, but for the first twenty elements it holds eight before the fourth shell starts.
chemistry/atoms.7396bc35da59: Schrödinger and others. Electron-cloud, quantum, model. Electrons do not follow exact paths. We can only say where they are likely to be: a fuzzy electron cloud. In nineteen thirty-two Chadwick discovered the neutron, completing today’s picture. Experiments showed that electrons behave like waves as well as particles.
chemistry/atoms.428f222e73d5: Electron shell. Energy levels where electrons are found. For elements one to twenty: shell one holds up to two electrons, shell two up to eight, shell three up to eight, the two-eight-eight rule. Electrons fill the inner shells first, then move outward. Atoms with a full outer shell, like helium, neon and argon, are very stable and unreactive.
chemistry/atoms.e232784686e1: Proton. Positive, plus one, particle in the nucleus. Charge: plus one. Mass: about one atomic mass unit, A M U. The number of protons is the atomic number, and it decides WHICH element the atom is. Add or remove one proton and the atom becomes a different element. Try it!
chemistry/atoms.7e493199129c: Electron cloud. Today’s model: where electrons are LIKELY to be. Scientists cannot know exactly where an electron is at any moment, only where it is likely to be. Where the cloud is thicker, the electron is more likely to be found. This quantum, cloud, model came from scientists such as Schrödinger in the nineteen twenties.
chemistry/atoms.02b72df6be1b: Ion. An atom with unequal protons and electrons. Lose electrons, more protons than electrons, positive ion, cation, for example, sodium ion. Gain electrons, more electrons than protons, negative ion, anion, for example, chloride ion. Table salt is made of sodium and chloride ions held together.
chemistry/atoms.5c7b59fd782b: Isotope. Same protons, different neutrons. Carbon twelve, carbon thirteen and carbon fourteen are all carbon: each has six protons. Some isotopes are radioactive, unstable. Carbon fourteen is used to find the age of things that were once alive, up to about fifty thousand years old. Hydrogen has three isotopes: protium, zero neutrons, deuterium, one neutron, and tritium, two neutrons.

chemistry/carbon.c433617a9b50: Burning fossil fuels transfers carbon from long-term underground stores to the air as C O two.
chemistry/carbon.56c95b392c8e: C O poisoning happens when C O binds to hemoglobin, the protein in blood that carries oxygen. This interferes with oxygen delivery and can cause headaches, dizziness and even death. If a C O alarm sounds or you suspect poisoning, get to fresh air outside immediately and call emergency services from there, nine one one in the US.
chemistry/carbon.878db50a741c: The surface absorbs sunlight and emits infrared radiation. Greenhouse gases such as C O two absorb and re-emit some infrared radiation. The natural greenhouse effect keeps Earth warm. Added C O two strengthens it. Arrows show direction and relative change.
chemistry/carbon.8b650e92fdc9: C O two can also leave surface water and return to the air. Ocean-air exchange goes both ways.
chemistry/carbon.42f933d9287d: Why is the C O two heavier than the methane used? The oxygen in C O two comes from O two in the air. Count the water as well when comparing total masses.
chemistry/carbon.895a9a0d65b4: Organisms release C O two during cellular respiration. Decomposers also return carbon to the air as they break down dead plants and animals.
chemistry/carbon.afdff4744e0a: Some C O two from the air dissolves in surface seawater. Some of that dissolved C O two reacts with water to form carbonic acid. The carbon can also enter other dissolved forms or become part of living things.
chemistry/carbon.46f265f4182b: Limestone or marble reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid without heating. At the same temperature and pressure, C O two is denser than air. Feed it near the bottom of an upright jar so it displaces air upward. Some C O two dissolves in water, so collection over water loses some gas.
chemistry/carbon.e74425d063f4: A C sixty molecule is a hollow cage with a carbon atom at each corner. Its twelve pentagons and twenty hexagons form a pattern like the panels of a soccer ball. Sixty atoms in one molecule. Each carbon has three bonded neighbors.
chemistry/carbon.6124381cfa59: Plants take C O two from the air during photosynthesis and use its carbon to make sugars.
chemistry/carbon.266a035afd3e: The same two carbon atoms get enough oxygen to form two C O two molecules. The equation shows the simplest ratio.

chemistry/changes.7cf6a6ca848f: Baking soda and vinegar. Is it a physical or a chemical change? Make a prediction, then run the experiment.

chemistry/chemical-equations.161fa10ac27c: Common mix-up: the coefficient two in front of H two counts two copies of H two. To find hydrogen’s term in the mass ratio, multiply: two times two equals four.
chemistry/chemical-equations.403c86bff3be: Write correct formulas first. Balance one element at a time, adjusting only coefficients, and recount after each change. Reduce to the smallest whole-number ratio and omit any coefficient of one in the finished equation.

chemistry/density.8e31f1330d02: Aluminum cube. Two point seven grams per cubic centimeter. It is denser than every liquid, so it sinks all the way to the bottom.
chemistry/density.f7bac8a71dea: Ping-pong ball. Zero point zero eight grams per cubic centimeter. It floats on top of the Rubbing alcohol, with about ten percent of it under the surface.
chemistry/density.3dc3309c4bf1: Your object. Two point seven grams per cubic centimeter. It is denser than every liquid, so it sinks all the way to the bottom.
chemistry/density.91d3582c100b: Your object. One point two grams per cubic centimeter. It sinks through Rubbing alcohol, Vegetable oil, Water, Dish soap, all less dense than one point two, and floats on top of the Corn syrup, one point three three.
chemistry/density.0982f2485dd5: Vegetable oil. Zero point nine two grams per cubic centimeter. Vegetable oil is about zero point nine two grams per cubic centimeter. Oil and water do not mix, and the less dense oil floats on top. That’s why an oil spill spreads out over the surface of the sea.
chemistry/density.687b9a20ab81: Corn syrup, dyed purple. One point three three grams per cubic centimeter. Corn syrup is sugar, glucose, dissolved in water. One hundred milliliters has a mass of about one hundred thirty-three grams. It is a little less dense than honey, so it floats on top of the honey.
chemistry/density.912783d7c291: Dish soap. One point zero six grams per cubic centimeter. Dish soap is about one point zero six grams per cubic centimeter — just a little denser than water. One hundred milliliters has a mass of about one hundred six grams. It must be poured slowly, or it mixes with the water layer.
chemistry/density.86b5c2200a8c: Cork. Zero point two four grams per cubic centimeter. It floats on top of the Rubbing alcohol, with about thirty percent of it under the surface.
chemistry/density.34edf3f9a9f3: Water, dyed blue. One gram per cubic centimeter. Water has a density of one point zero zero grams per cubic centimeter, zero point nine nine eight at room temperature. So one milliliter of water has a mass of one gram — an easy number to remember! Objects less dense than one gram per cubic centimeter float in water; denser objects sink.
chemistry/density.d569a0a25870: Honey. One point four two grams per cubic centimeter. Honey is mostly sugar with a little water — lots of mass packed into each cubic centimeter. One hundred milliliters of honey has a mass of about one hundred forty-two grams. It is also very viscous, thick, so objects sink through it slowly.
chemistry/density.1be604382f30: Density. Mass per unit volume. Density equals mass divided by volume, D equals m divided by V. Units: grams per cubic centimeter, the same as grams per milliliter. It tells how tightly matter is packed — how much mass is squeezed into each cubic centimeter. Density is a physical property: each pure substance has its own density, which helps identify it. Cutting an object in half halves both the mass and the volume, so its density stays the same.
chemistry/density.dfce6c098e7d: Pine wood block. Zero point five grams per cubic centimeter. It floats on top of the Rubbing alcohol, with about sixty-three percent of it under the surface.
chemistry/density.2e26f61c8eb8: Steel nut. Seven point eight seven grams per cubic centimeter. It is denser than every liquid, so it sinks all the way to the bottom.
chemistry/density.3cf7405f288e: Rubbing alcohol, dyed red. Zero point seven nine grams per cubic centimeter. Rubbing, isopropyl, alcohol is about zero point seven nine grams per cubic centimeter — the least dense liquid here. It would mix with water, but the oil layer keeps them apart. One hundred milliliters has a mass of only about seventy-nine grams.

chemistry/elements-compounds.18613adceb15: Common mix-up: N H three is not flat. Nitrogen also has a pair of unshared electrons on top, which pushes the three H atoms down into a pyramid.
chemistry/elements-compounds.ebfa33402985: Table salt, sodium chloride. Compound, pure substance. Ions stacked in a crystal. Sodium ions and chloride ions attract each other and stack in a repeating cube pattern called a crystal lattice. There are no separate N a C l molecules. The formula gives the ratio: one N a for every one C l. Sodium is a soft metal that reacts violently with water, and chlorine is a poisonous gas. Bonded together, they make the salt you eat! Salt grains are little cubes because the ions stack like cubes.
chemistry/elements-compounds.b7c9cb9ad6a3: Carbon dioxide. Compound, pure substance. A straight-line molecule. One carbon atom sits between two oxygen atoms in a straight line, one hundred eighty degrees. Each C equals O double bondlink is a double bond. You breathe out C O two; plants take it in for photosynthesis. “di” means two: carbon DIoxide has two oxygens.
chemistry/elements-compounds.408b75c54594: Common mix-up: Sand is mostly the compound S i O two and iron is an element, but mixing them does not make a new compound.
chemistry/elements-compounds.99da708bd1c7: Common mix-up: The four belongs only to H, not to C. C H four does not have four carbons.
chemistry/elements-compounds.c4a6b020cbc6: Sand and iron filings. Heterogeneous mixture. You can see the parts. You can see the different parts: tan sand grains and gray iron bits. One spoonful might have more iron than another. The mixture is not the same everywhere. A magnet pulls out the iron because iron is magnetic and sand is not. Mixtures can be separated by physical means. Heterogeneous equals “different” parts you can see or pick out.
chemistry/elements-compounds.729aa574553f: Oxygen gas. Element, pure substance. Only one kind of atom. Made only of oxygen atoms, so it is an element, a pure substance. Two oxygen atoms share electrons in a double bond to form one O two molecule. About twenty-one percent of the air is O two. You need it to breathe, and fires need it to burn. Element equals only ONE kind of atom, even if the atoms are joined in pairs.
chemistry/elements-compounds.2f3562e6a19c: Iron. Element, pure substance. A metal made of single atoms. Iron is an element: every atom in it has twenty-six protons. Metal atoms are not grouped into molecules. They pack together in a repeating crystal. Iron is magnetic, which helps us pull it out of mixtures. Symbols: first letter CAPITAL, second letter lowercase. F e comes from the Latin word “ferrum”.
chemistry/elements-compounds.31b77b4067a8: Common mix-up: O two is a molecule, but it is NOT a compound. A compound needs two or more DIFFERENT elements.
chemistry/elements-compounds.36be04f9576e: Ammonia. Compound, pure substance. A pyramid-shaped molecule. One nitrogen atom bonds to three hydrogen atoms. The molecule is a short pyramid with N at the top, H N H about one hundred seven degrees. Ammonia is used to make fertilizers and is found in some cleaners. It has a strong smell. N H three: one Nitrogen, three Hydrogens.
chemistry/elements-compounds.6eb9c3f09f7a: Air. Homogeneous mixture. A mixture of gases. Air is about seventy-eight percent nitrogen, N two, twenty-one percent oxygen, O two, almost one percent argon, A r, plus a tiny bit of C O two, about zero point zero four percent, and water vapor. The gases are mixed evenly but are NOT bonded to each other. Each keeps its own properties. The amounts can change: a crowded room has more C O two, and air near the ocean has more water vapor. Mixture equals substances mixed but not bonded; the “recipe” can change.
chemistry/elements-compounds.d72334c81049: Methane. Compound, pure substance. A tetrahedron-shaped molecule. Methane is the main part of natural gas, used for cooking and heating. The four hydrogen atoms point to the corners of a tetrahedron, one hundred nine point five degrees apart, as far from each other as possible. Carbon usually forms four bonds. That is why it can build so many different molecules. No subscript means one: C H four equals one C plus four H equals five atoms.
chemistry/elements-compounds.cdb4b5844075: Common mix-up: Air contains O two and N two molecules, but air is not a compound. There is no single formula for air.
chemistry/elements-compounds.1f609ad9f51d: Common mix-up: C O, carbon monoxide, “mono” equals one, is a different, poisonous gas. One oxygen atom makes a big difference.
chemistry/elements-compounds.aa558d7439db: Water. Compound, pure substance. Two hydrogen and one oxygen, bonded. Two elements, hydrogen and oxygen, are chemically bonded, so water is a compound. The molecule is bent: the H O H angle is about one hundred four point five degrees. Every water molecule has the same two to one ratio of H to O. A compound always has a fixed ratio. Water is totally different from its elements: H two burns and O two helps fires, but water puts fires out! A subscript counts the atom just before it: H two O equals H double bond, H, O.
chemistry/elements-compounds.b4db0a0fee68: Common mix-up: H two O two, hydrogen peroxide, is a different compound. Change a subscript and you change the substance.

chemistry/formulas-valence.a2ba6bb4b1e0: Each molecule has one oxygen atom. With one molecule, the total is one.
chemistry/formulas-valence.11c0d416bdee: Each molecule has two hydrogen atoms. With three molecules, the total is six.
chemistry/formulas-valence.0bc5b7c56a8f: Chinese textbooks use huàhéjià, 化合价, to describe how elements combine. For the examples here, the signed values match what English chemistry calls oxidation numbers for atoms, or charges for whole groups. Write each value above its symbol or group, sign first. In a neutral compound, multiply each value by its count and add to get zero.
chemistry/formulas-valence.a023f5b43ee1: Each molecule has two oxygen atoms. With one molecule, the total is two.
chemistry/formulas-valence.7078adde3a13: Changing the coefficient only changes the number of molecules. Changing H two O to H two O two gives a different substance, hydrogen peroxide.
chemistry/formulas-valence.fdeca7b1c6ff: Each molecule has one oxygen atom. With two molecules, the total is two.
chemistry/formulas-valence.d5c3dc90c852: Each molecule has one carbon atom. With two molecules, the total is two.
chemistry/formulas-valence.8c37ca162998: Each molecule has two hydrogen atoms. With two molecules, the total is four.
chemistry/formulas-valence.6ebe29dac00c: Each molecule has one nitrogen atom. With two molecules, the total is two.
chemistry/formulas-valence.563d031dd029: Each molecule has two hydrogen atoms. With one molecule, the total is two.
chemistry/formulas-valence.cf05ee7bf0bb: Each molecule has two hydrogen atoms. With four molecules, the total is eight.
chemistry/formulas-valence.a5860cd85545: Each molecule has two oxygen atoms. With two molecules, the total is four.

chemistry/metals.0650fc81d762: Many metals react with oxygen to form metal oxides. The metal and the reaction conditions determine what you observe. Fine iron wire burns with sparks in oxygen and can form black F e three O four. In damp air, iron rusts slowly.
chemistry/metals.5a2e981df288: Most metals are shiny and conduct heat and electricity well. They can usually be pressed into sheets, malleability, or drawn into wires, ductility. Hardness, density, and melting point vary. Mercury is liquid at room temperature. An alloy, héjīn, 合金, is a metallic material made by combining a metal with other elements. Many alloys are harder than their main pure metal. Many also start melting at a lower temperature than that metal. Copper is common in wires because it conducts electricity well and is easy to draw into wire. Brass is a copper-zinc alloy. Its combination of workability and corrosion resistance makes it useful for fittings such as taps.
chemistry/metals.aa3cde02fbfa: Most metals are shiny and conduct heat and electricity well. They can usually be pressed into sheets, malleability, or drawn into wires, ductility. Hardness, density, and melting point vary. Mercury is liquid at room temperature. An alloy, héjīn, 合金, is a metallic material made by combining a metal with other elements. Many alloys are harder than their main pure metal. Many also start melting at a lower temperature than that metal. Copper is common in wires because it conducts electricity well and is easy to draw into wire. Tin bronze is a copper-tin alloy. It can be cast into shapes and is used for objects such as bells.
chemistry/metals.0a2feadea190: Most metals are shiny and conduct heat and electricity well. They can usually be pressed into sheets, malleability, or drawn into wires, ductility. Hardness, density, and melting point vary. Mercury is liquid at room temperature. An alloy, héjīn, 合金, is a metallic material made by combining a metal with other elements. Many alloys are harder than their main pure metal. Many also start melting at a lower temperature than that metal. Copper is common in wires because it conducts electricity well and is easy to draw into wire. Steel is primarily iron and carbon. Its strength makes many grades useful in structures such as bridges.
