china/spring-warring.62552b43ee71: About two hundred fifty-six B C E Li Bing, governor of Shu for the state of Qin, led the building of Dujiangyan on the Min River. The Chengdu Plain became “the Land of Abundance” — a rich rear base for Qin.

china/strategy-battles.bb137e0ba4d0: Pins, 键. Bronze pins the parts turn on. Two pins go right through the housing and the stock.
china/strategy-battles.c5014d062819: Crossbow square, kneeling and standing. The front corner of Pit two. Kneeling crossbowmen in the middle, standing archers around them. One idea: one group shoots while the other reloads, so the arrows never stop. An L-shaped pit with four mixed units; roughly one thousand three hundred figures and eighty-plus chariots, approximate.
china/strategy-battles.f9124c109431: Armoured infantry. Filling the long corridors of Pit one. The main body of the army: thousands of soldiers in armour, in columns four wide. They carried long bronze weapons such as spears and halberds, 戈, 矛, 戟. About two hundred thirty meters times sixty-two meters, seven hundred fifty-five times two hundred three feet — longer than two US football fields. Estimated about six thousand clay soldiers and horses.
china/strategy-battles.6802e689e05d: Teeth, 牙. Two bronze hooks that catch and hold the string. When you cock the crossbow, the string is pulled back and locks behind the teeth. The teeth and the sight are one piece that turns on a bronze pin.
china/strategy-battles.d2696a30c28a: Battle of Guiling. Three hundred fifty-three B C. Guiling, one view: today’s Changyuan, Henan Province. Qi, Tian Ji, Sun Bin, versus Wei, Pang Juan 庞涓. Qi wins; Wei’s attempt to swallow Zhao fails. The plan lives on as the idiom “besiege Wei to rescue Zhao”, 围魏救赵. 避实而击虚. Avoid the enemy’s strong points; strike the weak ones.
china/strategy-battles.4bec9f1ea3d9: Don't mix up: A crossbow, 弩, is not just a bow, 弓: the trigger lets you hold the string drawn and aim calmly, so less strength and training are needed.
china/strategy-battles.53a8056678a7: Sunzi says: 兵者, 诡道也. — War is a game of deception: when strong, look weak; when near, look far away.
china/strategy-battles.f8ec801e351c: Sunzi says: 避实而击虚. — Avoid the enemy’s strong points; strike the weak ones.
china/strategy-battles.6785b47802e8: Vanguard: archers and crossbowmen. The three front rows at the east end of Pit one. About two hundred figures in three rows face the enemy first. Most wear battle robes but no armour — light and quick. Their job: shoot first, from long range. About two hundred thirty meters times sixty-two meters, seven hundred fifty-five times two hundred three feet — longer than two US football fields. Estimated about six thousand clay soldiers and horses.
china/strategy-battles.024cd9d0053b: Sunzi says: 上下同欲者胜. — The side whose leaders and soldiers want the same thing will win.
china/strategy-battles.9983fe7e25c9: Battle of Chibi, Red Cliffs. Two hundred eight A D. Chibi on the Yangtze River, one view: today’s Chibi City, Hubei Province. Sun Quan and Liu Bei, 刘备, versus Cao Cao. The allies win with far fewer men. Cao Cao retreats north; the three-way split of China, 三国鼎立, begins to take shape. 兵者, 诡道也. War is a game of deception: when strong, look weak; when near, look far away.
china/strategy-battles.7610f202bf4c: String, 弦. Pushes the bolt forward when released. A complete Qin crossbow found in the pits still had traces of a string thought to be made of animal tendon.
china/strategy-battles.4ba7fd813d91: Stock, 臂. The wooden body with a groove for the bolt. The wood has rotted away in the pits; the bronze parts survived.
china/strategy-battles.6fc6de6e596c: Don't mix up: The Terracotta Army pits are not the First Emperor’s tomb. They lie about one point five kilometers, one mile, east of the tomb mound, which has never been opened.
china/strategy-battles.a4cb4dc910ae: Trigger, 悬刀. The hanging “knife” you pull to shoot. A small pull on a long lever releases a huge force: that is leverage.
china/strategy-battles.05bb184204f2: Linzi. Today: Zibo, Shandong. One of the biggest cities in the world two thousand three hundred years ago — so crowded that “raising your sleeves makes shade”.
china/strategy-battles.63fa6e434521: Sear, 牛, also 钩心. The hidden middle link that holds the teeth in place. It sits between the teeth and the trigger, inside the housing. Pull the trigger and the sear drops — the teeth are free to swing down.
china/strategy-battles.8b7ac12c9cc4: Bolt, 矢. A short arrow with a bronze three-sided head. Tens of thousands of bronze arrowheads have been found with the Terracotta Army.
china/strategy-battles.2874328b452c: Command post. Pit three, the smallest pit. Only sixty-eight figures: guards lining the walls, facing each other, and one chariot. It is thought to be the headquarters that commanded the army in Pits one and two. A small U-shaped pit with sixty-eight figures and one chariot: the command post.
china/strategy-battles.df7a09f6cefc: Sight, 望山. The aiming blade — like the sight on a rifle. It sticks up when the crossbow is cocked. Line it up with the target. Some Han-dynasty sights even had a scale of marks for different distances.
china/strategy-battles.7346fb3fa9cb: Sunzi says: 不战而屈人之兵, 善之善者也. — The very best victory makes the enemy give up without a fight.
china/strategy-battles.e4d9bee8d30c: Bow, 弓. Stores energy when it bends. The harder the bow is to bend, the more energy it stores — and the faster the bolt flies.
china/strategy-battles.0e3865f717da: Housing, 郭. The bronze box that holds all the parts together. Archaeologists found Qin trigger parts made to very similar sizes — almost like standard spare parts.
china/strategy-battles.a516defe63d1: Sunzi says: 军无辎重则亡, 无粮食则亡. — An army without supply wagons is lost; an army without food is lost.
china/strategy-battles.342fdcfb0769: Rear guard. The last rows at the west end, facing backwards. They guard the army’s back. About two hundred thirty meters times sixty-two meters, seven hundred fifty-five times two hundred three feet — longer than two US football fields. Estimated about six thousand clay soldiers and horses.
china/strategy-battles.2de254e60ba9: Battle of the Fei River. Three hundred eighty-three A D. The Fei River near Shouyang, today’s Shou County, Anhui Province. Eastern Jin, Xie Shi, Xie Xuan, versus Former Qin, Fu Jian 苻坚. Eastern Jin wins with far fewer men. Former Qin falls apart and the north splits again; the south stays safe and keeps developing. 上下同欲者胜. The side whose leaders and soldiers want the same thing will win.
china/strategy-battles.31add7b99dc2: Flank guards. The outer rows along the north and south sides. The outermost soldiers face outwards, so the army can’t be attacked from the side. About two hundred thirty meters times sixty-two meters, seven hundred fifty-five times two hundred three feet — longer than two US football fields. Estimated about six thousand clay soldiers and horses.
china/strategy-battles.e738582464ed: Memory hint: Pit one equals the main army, Pit two equals the mixed strike force, Pit three equals the headquarters.
china/strategy-battles.084eddb368cb: Battle of Muye. Circa ten forty-six B C. Muye, near today’s Xinxiang, Henan Province. Zhou and allied tribes, King Wu, versus Shang, King Zhou 纣王. Zhou wins. The Shang dynasty falls and the Western Zhou begins, with its capital at Haojing. 不战而屈人之兵, 善之善者也. The very best victory makes the enemy give up without a fight.
china/strategy-battles.938b1c39e2b7: Battle of Guandu. Two hundred A D. Guandu, northeast of today’s Zhongmou, Henan Province. Cao Cao versus Yuan Shao, 袁绍. Cao Cao wins with far fewer men — a famous “small beats big” battle. It lays the foundation for Cao Cao to unite the north. 军无辎重则亡, 无粮食则亡. An army without supply wagons is lost; an army without food is lost.

china/sui-tang.602f50c97013: Deck and stone railings. The road across, with carved railings. The bridge is about fifty metres long and about nine metres wide. Its stone railings are carved with dragons and other beasts — the bridge is a work of art as well as engineering. After about one thousand four hundred years of floods and earthquakes it still stands.
china/sui-tang.afbe67c90e0a: In six forty-one Princess Wencheng married Songtsen Gampo, ruler of Tubo, bringing Central Plains techniques and books with her and strengthening Han-Tibetan friendship. This was a link between peoples within China.
china/sui-tang.413261a0f221: Memory hook: twenty-eight rings side by side — easy to repair.
china/sui-tang.229202c7af57: Chang’an became an international metropolis and Tang poetry reached its peak: Li Bai is called the “Poet Immortal” and Du Fu the “Poet Sage”. The An-Shi Rebellion of seven fifty-five turned the Tang from prosperity to decline; the dynasty ended in nine oh seven.
china/sui-tang.b8a832f39be4: Twenty-eight parallel arch rings. How the main arch is built. Look under the arch: the main arch is made of twenty-eight separate arch rings laid side by side. If one ring is damaged it can be repaired on its own, without rebuilding the whole bridge.
china/sui-tang.248b865bdfa5: Memory hook: Grand Canal “one, two, three, four, five”: one canal, two aims, north-south transport, firmer rule, three points, Zhuojun, today: Beijing, Luoyang, Yuhang, today: Hangzhou, four sections, Yongji, Tongji, Hangou, Jiangnan, five rivers, Hai, Yellow, Huai, Yangtze, Qiantang.
china/sui-tang.116de640b6b9: Main arch. One great, flat stone arch over the river. The Zhaozhou Bridge, Anji Bridge, in today’s Zhao County, Hebei, was designed and built under the direction of the Sui craftsman Li Chun. Its single main arch spans more than thirty-seven metres. The arch is a low, flat segment of a circle, so the deck slopes gently and carts can cross easily. It is the oldest surviving open-spandrel stone arch bridge in the world.
china/sui-tang.db492cc89bb4: Sui tyranny led to uprisings and the Sui fell in six eighteen. That year Li Yuan founded the Tang with its capital at Chang’an. Emperor Taizong’s reign brought the “Reign of Zhenguan”; the early reign of Emperor Xuanzong brought the “Heyday of Kaiyuan”, the height of the Tang.
china/sui-tang.1840d71386b1: In five eighty-one Yang Jian founded the Sui with its capital at Chang’an; he is Emperor Wen of Sui. In five eighty-nine Sui armies conquered the Chen in the south, ending a long period of division and reuniting north and south.
china/sui-tang.36f2dc975ea0: To improve north-south transport and strengthen control of the whole country, Emperor Yang of Sui began the Grand Canal in six oh five. Centred on Luoyang, it reached Zhuojun in the north and Yuhang in the south — over two thousand kilometers long.

china/taiwan-hkm.e659caca781b: Sun Moon Lake. Taiwan’s largest natural lake. Sun Moon Lake, 日月潭, lies in the central mountains, about seven hundred fifty meters, two thousand four hundred fifty feet, above sea level. Its northern part is round like the sun and its southern part curved like a crescent moon, hence the name. It is also a reservoir for hydropower, and home to the Thao, 邵族, people. Round like the sun, curved like the moon.
china/taiwan-hkm.dac28155351c: Taiwan Strait. about one hundred thirty kilometers, eighty-one miles, wide at its narrowest. The Taiwan Strait, 台湾海峡, separates Fujian from Taiwan Island. At its narrowest, from Pingtan Island to near Hsinchu, it is only about one hundred thirty kilometers, eighty-one miles, wide, roughly New York City to Philadelphia. It is shallow, mostly less than one hundred meters deep. In the last Ice Age, when sea level was much lower, it was dry land. It is a busy shipping lane between the East China Sea and the South China Sea. Narrowest about one hundred thirty kilometers: NYC to Philadelphia.
china/taiwan-hkm.1e5d6c6671d9: Rainfall. Most of the island: over two thousand millimeters a year. Moist winds from the sea plus high mountains equals lots of rain, especially on the slopes the wind blows against, windward slopes. The northeast is wettest: Huoshaoliao averages over six thousand millimeters, two hundred thirty-six inches, a year. The Penghu Islands, low and flat in the strait, are much drier. Sea air and mountains equals rain on the windward side.
china/taiwan-hkm.43d6a8b6bae9: Keelung. Northern port, the “rainy port”. Keelung, 基隆, is the main port of northern Taiwan, serving Taipei. In winter the northeast monsoon blows straight off the sea, so it rains here very often: it is nicknamed the “rainy port”. Huoshaoliao, in the hills nearby, is one of the wettest places in China. Taiwan’s two big ports: Kaohsiung, south, and Keelung, north.
china/taiwan-hkm.2a3ad1dbddc6: Taiwan Province. China’s largest island, about thirty-six thousand square kilometers, about twenty-three million people. Taiwan Province is Taiwan Island plus the Penghu Islands, Diaoyu Dao, Chiwei Yu and other islands. Its capital city is Taipei. It lies off China’s southeast coast, across the Taiwan Strait from Fujian, with the Pacific Ocean to the east. Size check: a little smaller than Maryland and Delaware put together, about fourteen thousand square miles. Taiwan has been an inseparable part of China’s territory since ancient times.
china/taiwan-hkm.e91dc070249e: Typhoons. Mostly July to September. Typhoons form over the warm Pacific and often hit Taiwan, Hong Kong and Macao in summer and autumn. They bring fierce winds and torrential rain: floods, landslides and damage to crops. But typhoon rain also fills reservoirs. The east coast and the mountain slopes facing the wind get the most. Typhoon: wind and rain; windward slopes get soaked.
china/taiwan-hkm.86148d9d61d3: Western plains. Rice, sugar cane, fruit, and most of the cities. Taiwan’s plains lie mostly along the west coast; the Jianan Plain, 嘉南平原, is the largest. Warm and wet: rice gives two or three crops a year; sugar cane, tea and tropical fruit, bananas, pineapples, mangoes, thrive. Taiwan is called a “home of fruit”. Most people, cities, highways and railways crowd onto this flat western strip. West: plains, rice, fruit, cities.
china/taiwan-hkm.d6cbf11ef3ba: Taipei. Largest city, in the Taipei Basin. Taipei sits in a basin in the north, ringed by hills. It is Taiwan’s biggest city and its centre of business and culture. Its five hundred eight-meter, one thousand six hundred sixty-seven-foot, Taipei one oh one tower was the world’s tallest building from two thousand four to twenty ten. Taipei: a city in a bowl of hills.
china/taiwan-hkm.5a1613bd8f46: Alishan. Sunrise over a sea of clouds. Alishan, 阿里山, is a mountain area famous for five sights: sunrise, the sea of clouds, sunset glow, forest and its mountain railway. The narrow-gauge Alishan Forest Railway was built in the early nineteen hundreds to haul timber, climbing from the plain at Chiayi to over two thousand meters, six thousand six hundred feet. Giant ancient cypress trees grow here; some are thousands of years old. Alishan’s five wonders: sunrise, clouds, sunset, forest, railway.
china/taiwan-hkm.e37426c06fb8: Kaohsiung. Largest port, export processing zone. Kaohsiung, 高雄, in the southwest is Taiwan’s largest port and a centre of heavy industry: steel, shipbuilding and petrochemicals. It opened an export processing zone in nineteen sixty-six: factories import materials, process them and export the products. This “process and export” model is how Taiwan, with few raw materials, built its economy. Kaohsiung: biggest port, steel and ships.
china/taiwan-hkm.bbf9daaf1e76: Fujian Province. Same roots, same language. Most people in Taiwan have family roots in Fujian and Guangdong. Both sides speak Mandarin, Minnan, Hokkien, and Hakka, eat similar food and keep the same festivals. Fujian and Taiwan trade heavily; since two thousand eight there have been direct mail, trade and flights across the strait, the “Three Links”. Same roots, same language, same festivals.
china/taiwan-hkm.4ed3d4b7cc24: Yushan, Jade Mountain. Three thousand nine hundred fifty-two meters, twelve thousand nine hundred sixty-six feet: highest peak in eastern China. Yushan, 玉山, “Jade Mountain”, is Taiwan’s highest peak and the highest in eastern China. It sits almost exactly on the Tropic of Cancer, yet its summit gets snow in winter: height beats latitude. It is almost twice as high as Mount Mitchell, six thousand six hundred eighty-four feet, the tallest peak in the eastern US. Yushan three thousand nine hundred fifty-two meters: number one in the east.
china/taiwan-hkm.b365a7aef96e: Tropic of Cancer, about twenty-three point four degrees north. Splits the island into two climates. The Tropic of Cancer crosses central Taiwan, near Chiayi in the west and Hualien in the east. North of it: subtropical monsoon climate. South of it: tropical monsoon climate. At noon on the June solstice the Sun is straight overhead here. Taiwan’s south is closer to the equator than Key West, Florida, twenty-four point five degrees north. North: subtropical. South: tropical.
china/taiwan-hkm.089b97311cfb: Common mix-up: one hundred thirty kilometers is the NARROWEST point; most of the strait is wider, up to about four hundred kilometers.
china/taiwan-hkm.5a52845db2f1: Penghu Islands. About ninety islands in the strait. The Penghu Islands, 澎湖, lie in the Taiwan Strait, between Fujian and Taiwan Island. They are low, flat and very windy in winter, with little rain: much drier than Taiwan Island. Fishing is the traditional way of life. Penghu: flat, windy, dry islands in the strait.
china/taiwan-hkm.47a34cd9d909: Common mix-up: The Tropic does not make the north cold: northern Taiwan still has warm winters, Taipei about sixteen degrees Celsius in January.
china/taiwan-hkm.7b98480827e3: Hsinchu Science Park. Electronics and computer chips. Opened in nineteen eighty, the Hsinchu Science Park, 新竹, is the heart of Taiwan’s high-tech electronics industry. Factories here make semiconductor chips that end up in phones, cars and computers worldwide. Chips need very clean water and power, skilled engineers and good ports and airports nearby. Hsinchu equals chips.

china/terrain.269a8265e247: Tarim Basin. About one thousand meters, three thousand three hundred feet. China’s largest basin, between the Tianshan and Kunlun Mountains. The Taklimakan, China’s largest desert, fills its centre. The Tarim River is China’s longest inland river; rich in oil and gas, start of the West-East Gas Pipeline. Tarim equals biggest basin and biggest desert.
china/terrain.3ed0e8dc7278: Junggar Basin. About five hundred meters, one thousand six hundred feet. China’s second-largest basin, between the Altai and Tianshan Mountains. Contains the Gurbantünggüt Desert. The Karamay oil field is here. Three ranges hold two basins: Altai — Junggar — Tianshan — Tarim — Kunlun.
china/terrain.1a0cfdf858f7: Tibetan, Qinghai-Tibet, Plateau. Average over four thousand meters, thirteen thousand feet. The highest plateau in the world: the “Roof of the World”. Snow-capped ranges and glaciers everywhere; “mountains from afar, flat valleys up close”. It forms the first step. Source of the Yangtze and the Yellow River. Four plateaus in one word each: Tibetan HIGH, Inner Mongolian FLAT, Loess BROKEN, Yunnan-Guizhou RUGGED.
china/terrain.9d8897c10c9e: Inner Mongolian Plateau. About one thousand meters, three thousand three hundred feet. China’s second-largest plateau, on the second step. Wide, flat and open: “you can see to the horizon”. Huge grasslands such as Hulunbuir and Xilin Gol. FLAT: “The sky is vast, the land boundless; the wind bends the grass and you see the cattle and sheep.”
china/terrain.76fa83ae41e5: Third step. Mostly below five hundred meters, one thousand six hundred feet. Plains: Northeast, North China, Middle-Lower Yangtze. Hills: Liaodong, Shandong, Southeast Hills. East of it, the land continues under the sea as a shallow continental shelf. Step three equals three plains and three hills.
china/terrain.572461b08a4f: Common mix-up: The Turpan Basin, Aydingkol Lake, minus one hundred fifty-four meters, is China’s lowest point — it is a different, small basin.
china/terrain.449b5aea6c80: Yunnan-Guizhou Plateau. One thousand to two thousand meters, three thousand three hundred to six thousand six hundred feet. Rugged land with many small flat basins called “bazi”, 坝子. Karst, limestone, landforms are widespread, for example the Stone Forest. On the second step; its eastern edge is the Xuefeng Mountains. RUGGED: “No three li of flat land.”
china/terrain.d5bf99025d10: Common mix-up: Four basins total, but only three are on step two — Qaidam is on step one.
china/terrain.37b30fb465ac: Common mix-up: It is a plateau even though it looks flat — its height is about one thousand meters.
china/terrain.d7d6f8fd4c88: Second step. One thousand to two thousand meters, three thousand three hundred to six thousand six hundred feet. Plateaus: Inner Mongolian, Loess, Yunnan-Guizhou. Basins: Tarim, Junggar, Sichuan. Boundary with step three: Greater Khingan — Taihang — Wushan — Xuefeng. Step two equals three plateaus and three basins.
china/terrain.8b5ead8b799f: Middle-Lower Yangtze Plain. Mostly below fifty meters, one hundred sixty feet. Low and flat, with many rivers and lakes and a dense water network. Called the “land of fish and rice”, 鱼米之乡. Includes the Lianghu, Poyang Lake and Yangtze Delta plains. Yangtze Plain equals rivers, lakes, fish and rice.
china/terrain.534b08f29ea9: Loess Plateau. One thousand to two thousand meters, three thousand three hundred to six thousand six hundred feet. The world’s largest area of loess, thick yellow soil. Cut into countless gullies: “a thousand ravines and ten thousand gullies”. Serious soil erosion feeds mud into the Yellow River. BROKEN: thousands of gullies. Bounded by Taihang, east, Wushaoling, west, the Great Wall, north, Qinling, south.
china/terrain.d472052b9606: Qaidam Basin. Two thousand six hundred to three thousand meters, eight thousand five hundred to nine thousand eight hundred feet. The highest basin in China, inside the Tibetan Plateau. Called the “treasure bowl”, 聚宝盆: salt, oil and non-ferrous metals. Qarhan Salt Lake is China’s largest salt lake. Qaidam equals HIGHEST basin equals “treasure bowl”.

china/territory.c7db322a5dd1: Location. Eastern and Northern Hemispheres, East Asia, west coast of the Pacific. Hemispheres: China is in both the Eastern and the Northern Hemisphere. Land-sea position: in eastern Asia, on the west coast of the Pacific Ocean. The east faces the ocean, the west reaches deep into Eurasia. Latitude: it spans nearly fifty degrees of latitude. Most of China is in the north temperate zone, a small southern part is in the tropics, and none is in a frigid zone. The Tropic of Cancer, twenty-three point five degrees north, crosses Taiwan, Guangdong, Guangxi and Yunnan. Advantages: land and sea both help transport and links with the world; mostly temperate, so the climate suits farming and living. Tropic of Cancer, east, west: Taiwan, Guangdong, Guangxi, Yunnan, 台粤桂滇.
china/territory.366816642214: Shanxi. Short name 晋. Capital: Taiyuan. On the Loess Plateau; very rich in coal.
china/territory.fe1b47ebd215: Qinghai. Short name 青. Capital: Xining. Source of the Yangtze and Yellow rivers; Qinghai Lake is China’s largest saltwater lake.
china/territory.53693ff71028: Shandong. Short name 鲁. Capital: Jinan. The Shandong Peninsula reaches out between the Bohai and Yellow Seas; the Yellow River enters the sea here.
china/territory.56050d5a8e70: Seas and sea neighbours. Mainland coastline over eighteen thousand kilometers. From north to south China borders the Bohai, Yellow, East China and South China Seas. The Bohai Sea and the Qiongzhou Strait are China’s inland seas. The South China Sea is the largest and deepest. More than five thousand four hundred islands: Taiwan Island is the largest, Hainan Island is second. The South China Sea Islands, Dongsha, Xisha, Zhongsha and Nansha, belong to Hainan Province. Six countries face China across the sea: South Korea, Japan, the Philippines, Malaysia, Brunei and Indonesia. Seas north, south: 渤, 黄, 东, 南. Sea neighbours: 韩日菲, 马文印, 尼.
china/territory.dcd01884cb08: Inner Mongolia. Short name 内蒙古. Capital: Hohhot. Spans the most longitude of any division and borders eight others.
china/territory.ae63cb83158f: Hebei. Short name 冀. Capital: Shijiazhuang. Wraps around Beijing and Tianjin.
china/territory.9319146c4017: Shaanxi. Short name 陕 or 秦. Capital: Xi’an. The Qinling Mountains cross it; Xi’an was the capital of many dynasties.
china/territory.c3f5e8139c7d: Jiangsu. Short name 苏. Capital: Nanjing. Low and flat with many rivers and lakes; crossed by the Yangtze and Huai rivers.
china/territory.240513a1c300: Gansu. Short name 甘 or 陇. Capital: Lanzhou. Long and narrow; the Hexi Corridor was part of the Silk Road.
china/territory.0c6c9f0b1621: Tibet, Xizang. Short name 藏. Capital: Lhasa. On the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, average over four thousand meters; Mount Qomolangma is on its border.
china/territory.0c6a87338e36: Sichuan. Short name 川 or 蜀. Capital: Chengdu. The Sichuan Basin and Chengdu Plain: the “Land of Abundance”, 天府之国.

china/three-gorges.4fc6ac2da224: Nanjing. Nanjing, 南京, an ancient capital, sits on the lower river. Ocean-going ships can sail upstream as far as here.
china/three-gorges.92d4d62726d0: Hukou: end of the middle reaches. Hukou, 湖口, “lake mouth”, in Jiangxi, where Poyang Lake — China’s largest freshwater lake — joins, divides the middle and lower reaches.
china/three-gorges.4f203bbec4a6: Yichang: end of the upper reaches. Yichang, 宜昌, marks the end of the upper reaches, about four thousand five hundred kilometers. Here the river leaves the mountains for the flat Jianghan Plain.
china/three-gorges.79e3366d7d6e: The Jing River bends and Dongting Lake. Below Yichang the river slows and wanders in tight loops — the Jing River stretch, 荆江, nicknamed “nine twists of the intestine”, 九曲回肠. Water drains slowly, so this is where floods are most dangerous.
china/three-gorges.efbcbddf18e9: First Bend and Tiger Leaping Gorge. At Shigu in Yunnan the river makes a sudden U-turn — the “First Bend of the Yangtze”. Just below, it races through Tiger Leaping Gorge, 虎跳峡, one of the deepest gorges in the world.
china/three-gorges.a53f65f9b414: Shanghai: into the East China Sea. After about six thousand three hundred kilometers, three thousand nine hundred miles, the Yangtze reaches the East China Sea at Shanghai. It is the longest river in Asia and the third longest in the world.
china/three-gorges.56bd5c7b7747: Yibin: “the first city on the Yangtze”. The Min River joins at Yibin, 宜宾, in Sichuan. From here on the river is called the Chang Jiang, 长江, “long river”, and bigger boats can sail.
china/three-gorges.d0ecddcc114f: Chongqing: the mountain city. Chongqing, 重庆, where the Jialing River joins, is the biggest port on the upper Yangtze. The Three Gorges reservoir stretches all the way back here — about six hundred sixty kilometers, four hundred ten miles, from the dam, roughly Washington, DC to Boston.
china/three-gorges.4901d3b97bc6: Source: Geladaindong glacier. The Yangtze begins as melt-water from glaciers on Geladaindong, 各拉丹冬, six thousand six hundred twenty-one meters, the highest peak of the Tanggula Mountains on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau. The source stream is the Tuotuo River.
china/three-gorges.7765af0a88a5: Qutang Gorge — the first gorge. The Three Gorges, 长江三峡, run about one hundred ninety-three kilometers from Baidicheng, 白帝城, to Nanjinguan near Yichang. First comes Qutang Gorge, 瞿塘峡: only about eight kilometers long, but the narrowest and most dramatic.

china/unity-diplomacy.15802cd46541: Don’t mix up: nineteen fifty-one equals peaceful liberation of Tibet; nineteen sixty-five equals Tibet Autonomous Region founded.
china/unity-diplomacy.8598a1511d8f: Don’t mix up: The nineteen seventy-two communiqué began normalisation; it did not establish diplomatic relations.
china/unity-diplomacy.0e252d64d70c: Beijing. Capital of China. February nineteen seventy-two: Chairman Mao Zedong met President Nixon here. Twenty fourteen: Beijing hosted the APEC leaders’ meeting. Twenty seventeen: the first Belt and Road Forum for International Cooperation.
china/unity-diplomacy.9e22d14b1bcb: Taiwan Province. Cross-Strait relations since nineteen seventy-nine. The textbook teaches that Taiwan has been part of China since ancient times; the two sides of the Strait have been separated since nineteen forty-nine. Nineteen seventy-nine: policy of peaceful reunification. Nineteen eighty-seven: family visits begin. Nineteen ninety-two: the “nineteen ninety-two Consensus” on the one-China principle. Two thousand five: Anti-Secession Law. Two thousand eight: direct mail, flights and shipping. Twenty fifteen: the two sides’ leaders meet.
china/unity-diplomacy.27430332a20a: Don’t mix up: Guangxi, March nineteen fifty-eight, came before Ningxia, October nineteen fifty-eight.
china/unity-diplomacy.4cbd2bda046e: Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region. Founded March nineteen fifty-eight. The Zhuang are China’s largest ethnic minority. The only autonomous region on the sea coast, next to Vietnam. Famous for the limestone peaks of Guilin.
china/unity-diplomacy.deda15098e0c: Hong Kong SAR. Returned July first, nineteen ninety-seven. Britain took Hong Kong in stages after the Opium War, eighteen forty-two, eighteen sixty, eighteen ninety-eight. July first, nineteen ninety-seven: China resumed exercising sovereignty. Hong Kong keeps its capitalist system — “Hong Kong people administering Hong Kong” with a high degree of autonomy. First Chief Executive: Tung Chee-hwa, 董建华. The regional flag shows a bauhinia flower.
china/unity-diplomacy.e7bb071372af: Don’t mix up: Hong Kong: Britain, nineteen ninety-seven. Macao: Portugal, nineteen ninety-nine.
china/unity-diplomacy.d1e80b638f86: Tibet Autonomous Region. Founded September nineteen sixty-five. The last of the five to be founded. Tibet had been peacefully liberated in nineteen fifty-one. Average height above four thousand meters, thirteen thousand feet — nearly as high as the tallest peaks of the Rocky Mountains. Two thousand six: the Qinghai-Tibet Railway reached Lhasa.
china/unity-diplomacy.bf7e1b5e6ef2: Macao SAR. Returned December twentieth, nineteen ninety-nine. Portugal gradually occupied Macao from the mid-fifteen hundreds. December twentieth, nineteen ninety-nine: China resumed exercising sovereignty; “Macao people administering Macao”. First Chief Executive: Edmund Ho, 何厚铧. The regional flag shows a lotus flower.
china/unity-diplomacy.41bb36e8786f: Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region. Founded October nineteen fifty-eight. The smallest autonomous region — about the size of West Virginia. The Yellow River waters its plain, a green strip in dry country. The Hui are a largely Muslim ethnic group who speak Chinese.
china/unity-diplomacy.9b9732eef798: Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region. Founded May first, nineteen forty-seven. China’s first provincial-level autonomous region — set up two years before the People’s Republic. A long arc of grassland across the north: about one point one eight million square kilometers, bigger than Texas and California together. “Autonomous” means the local ethnic group helps run local affairs, inside one united country.
china/unity-diplomacy.677de4aa30c7: Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region. Founded October first, nineteen fifty-five. China’s largest provincial-level region: about one point six six million square kilometers — nearly the size of Alaska. On the old Silk Road, bordering eight countries. Home to Uygur, Han, Kazakh, Hui and dozens of other ethnic groups.
china/unity-diplomacy.480d6c3ab48a: Don’t mix up: Nixon’s visit, nineteen seventy-two, is not the same as establishing relations, nineteen seventy-nine.
china/unity-diplomacy.ac172bbb5756: Don’t mix up: It was founded in nineteen forty-seven — before nineteen forty-nine, not after.
china/unity-diplomacy.650d5933474b: Shanghai. China’s largest city. February nineteen seventy-two: China and the US issued their Joint Communiqué here — often called the Shanghai Communiqué. Two thousand one: Shanghai hosted the APEC leaders’ meeting. Two thousand one: the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation was founded here.

china/xia-shang-zhou.2ebcf8fe72bb: About ten forty-six B C E King Wu of Zhou defeated King Zhou of Shang at the Battle of Muye. The Shang fell and the Western Zhou began, with its capital at Haojing, near Xi’an.
china/xia-shang-zhou.46bd0a7066e5: Four rams. The rams’ bodies form the belly; their heads stick out. A ram stands at each of the four corners; its curled horns and head project from the shoulder. Late Shang dynasty; unearthed at Ningxiang, Hunan; fifty-eight point three centimeters tall. Its unusual shape and exquisite craft make it a masterpiece of Shang bronze casting.
china/xia-shang-zhou.830155c0364a: Inscription “后母戊”. Three characters cast inside the wall. The inner wall carries three characters: 后母戊, Hou Mu Wu. A Shang king had it cast to offer sacrifices to his mother, named “Wu”. Characters cast on bronzes are called bronze script, jinwen.
china/xia-shang-zhou.75e6bfde7d7e: About twenty seventy B C E Yu founded the Xia, China’s first dynasty. After Yu died his son Qi took the throne: hereditary rule replaced abdication — “shared by all” became “owned by one family”.
china/xia-shang-zhou.41b474d71d1f: Watch the pictures slowly turn into today’s square characters: sun 日, moon 月, mountain 山, person 人, tree 木. Chinese characters have developed continuously for over three thousand years.
china/xia-shang-zhou.12b70dfaef28: Yin Ruins, Yinxu. Today: Anyang, Henan. Over one hundred fifty thousand oracle bones with the earliest Chinese writing were dug up here, and the eight hundred thirty-two kilogram Houmuwu Ding.
china/xia-shang-zhou.9f04fec67217: Luoyang. Thirteen dynasties made Luoyang their capital. Near the city, the Longmen Grottoes hold about one hundred thousand Buddhist statues carved into the cliffs.
china/xia-shang-zhou.0ddd4b285cc6: Late Western Zhou rule decayed: in eight hundred forty-one B C E the people of the capital rose up. In seven hundred seventy-one B C E the Western Zhou fell. The next year, seven hundred seventy B C E, King Ping moved the capital east to Luoyi — the Eastern Zhou began.
china/xia-shang-zhou.ac3a9b23bef9: Ding body and taotie pattern. A rectangular ritual cauldron of the late Shang. Cast in the late Shang dynasty; unearthed in nineteen thirty-nine at Anyang, Henan. It weighs eight hundred thirty-two point eight four kilograms and stands one hundred thirty-three centimeters tall: the heaviest ancient Chinese bronze yet found. The walls are covered with beast-face, taotie, patterns on a background of thunder-cloud spirals.
china/xia-shang-zhou.bed1a25ac507: Four column legs. Hold up eight hundred thirty-two kilograms — and leave room for a fire. Four thick hollow column legs support the vessel. A ding was first a cooking pot; later bronze ding became ritual vessels and symbols of power. Each leg is decorated with a beast face near the top.
china/xia-shang-zhou.d930ff96003c: Memory hint: Four rams, square vessel: 四羊方尊.
china/xia-shang-zhou.05bb184204f2: Linzi. Today: Zibo, Shandong. One of the biggest cities in the world two thousand three hundred years ago — so crowded that “raising your sleeves makes shade”.
china/xia-shang-zhou.1f5abce30b8d: Memory hint: eight, three, two: “Houmuwu, eight hundred thirty-two kilograms”.
china/xia-shang-zhou.0090c9db2cdc: A one point six meter student, scale. Compare the sizes. The Houmuwu Ding, one hundred thirty-three centimeters, is almost as tall as a middle-school student. The Four-Ram Zun, fifty-eight point three centimeters, reaches about up to the student’s thigh.
china/xia-shang-zhou.caef772e2598: Three dynasties in a row: Xia, about twenty seventy to sixteen hundred B C E, Shang, about sixteen hundred to ten forty-six B C E, and Western Zhou, about ten forty-six to seven hundred seventy-one B C E.
china/xia-shang-zhou.a01766ecb82b: Erlitou. Today: Yanshi, Luoyang, Henan. Archaeologists found palace foundations, bronze workshops and a dragon made of over two thousand pieces of turquoise.
china/xia-shang-zhou.dcf5dac90b98: Memory hint: Round ding have three legs, square ding have four.
china/xia-shang-zhou.bf42d12f1952: Here on a schematic map: the Erlitou site near Yanshi, Henan may have been a Xia capital. About sixteen hundred B C E Tang overthrew Xia and founded the Shang. About thirteen hundred B C E King Pangeng moved the capital to Yin, Anyang — after that Shang rule was stable.

cs/cs-algorithms.75501029ec22: Bubble sort. Walk along the list comparing neighbours; swap them if they are in the wrong order. Big values “bubble” to the end. Compare items one and two, swap if needed; then two and three; … to the end. After one pass the biggest item is in its place. Repeat passes until a pass makes no swaps. Worst case for n items: n times the quantity n minus one, over two comparisons — ten items equals forty-five, one thousand items about five hundred thousand.
cs/cs-algorithms.5fe927277f1c: Binary search. In a sorted list, look at the middle item. Too big? Throw away the right half. Too small? Throw away the left half. Repeat. Each guess halves what is left: one hundred, fifty, twenty-five, thirteen, seven, four, two, one. At most seven guesses for one hundred, ten for one thousand, twenty for one million. Doubling the list adds only ONE more guess.
cs/cs-algorithms.676109808b4b: Breadth-first search. Explore a maze like a spreading wave: first every square one step away, then two steps, then three… The first time the wave reaches the exit, that is the shortest path. Needs a map of the whole maze, the robot’s rules don’t. GPS route planners use relatives of this idea, like Dijkstra’s algorithm.
cs/cs-algorithms.0d2647585beb: Merge sort. Split the list into tiny pieces, then merge pieces back together in order — two sorted piles merge quickly. A list of one item is already sorted. Merge pairs of one into sorted twos, then twos into fours, fours into eights…. To merge, compare the fronts of two piles and take the smaller. About n times log base two of n comparisons: one thousand items about ten thousand instead of five hundred thousand.
cs/cs-algorithms.c1032811e8f4: Quick sort. Pick a “pivot”, here: the last item. Move everything smaller to its left, everything bigger to its right. Then quick-sort each side. One pass around the pivot puts the pivot in its final place. Each side is a smaller problem: divide and conquer, like merge sort, but in place. Average: about one point four times n times log base two of n comparisons — O of n log n. Bad luck: if the pivot is always the biggest or smallest — try “Already sorted” — it needs n times the quantity n minus one, over two — O of n squared.
cs/cs-algorithms.f78f4c96f8cf: Don’t mix up: Selection sort makes few swaps, at most n minus one, but it never gets to skip comparisons.
cs/cs-algorithms.01e6fe439f4b: Linear search. Check items one by one from the start until you find what you want. Works on any list, sorted or not. Worst case: n looks, the item is last or missing. Control plus F in a document is a kind of linear search.
cs/cs-algorithms.3babc464665a: Selection sort. Find the smallest item and put it first; then find the smallest of the rest and put it second; and so on. Scan the whole unsorted part to find the smallest. Swap it to the front of the unsorted part. The sorted part grows by one each round. Always about n times the quantity n minus one, over two comparisons, even if the list was already sorted.
cs/cs-algorithms.5311a5fbb676: Insertion sort. Like sorting playing cards in your hand: take the next card and slide it left until it sits in the right place. The left part is always sorted; it starts with one item. Take the next item and compare it with its left neighbour; swap while the neighbour is bigger. Already sorted list: only n minus one comparisons and zero moves — the best case. Reversed list: n times the quantity n minus one, over two comparisons — the worst case, O of n squared.

cs/cs-coding.c37d73ef3685: Don’t mix up: The famous nineteen forty-seven “bug” was a real moth stuck in a relay of the Harvard Mark two — but programmers had already used the word “bug” for faults before that.
cs/cs-coding.7dcd76466625: Condition, if or else. A condition lets the program decide: IF something is true, do this; ELSE do that. Sensors give the program something to decide about. If it’s raining, take an umbrella; else wear sunglasses.
cs/cs-coding.f700357d6472: Loop. A loop repeats commands. “repeat four” repeats a fixed number of times; “while” repeats as long as a condition is true. Don’t copy-paste — loop it!
cs/cs-coding.6ff8ead459df: Don’t mix up: Swapping two lines can change everything — right ninety then forward is not the same as forward then right ninety.

cs/cs-computers.46c51686807b: Arithmetic logic unit, ALU. The calculator of the CPU: adds, subtracts and compares, using circuits built from logic gates like your adder. An eight-bit adder is just eight adder circuits chained together, passing carries along. The ALU also checks things like “is the result zero?” — that powers JUMP IF ZERO.
cs/cs-computers.0b19f5989362: Program counter, PC. Holds the address of the NEXT instruction. After every fetch it adds one — unless a JUMP changes it. A JUMP instruction simply writes a new address into the PC. That is how loops work! Starting a program equals setting the PC to its first address.
cs/cs-computers.9a7c902678ff: Clock. A crystal that ticks billions of times per second. Every tick moves the CPU one step forward. Three gigahertz equals three billion ticks every second. Our CPU uses three ticks per instruction, fetch, decode, execute. Real CPUs overlap the steps, pipelining, and run several cores at once.
cs/cs-computers.44623f09a885: Inside the CPU. A CPU follows a list of instructions stored in memory — one tiny step at a time, billions of times a second. Instructions and data are both just numbers in memory. One zero five means “ADD the number in cell zero five”. The three-step loop — fetch, decode, execute — is called the instruction cycle. Click a part, PC, IR, ALU, ACC, memory, screen, to learn its job, then press Step.
cs/cs-computers.5efa424b7e66: Don’t mix up: Real CPUs use binary codes, like one zero one one zero zero zero zero, not decimal — we use decimal so you can read them.
cs/cs-computers.1d57f60f148e: Don’t mix up: “My phone has eight gigabytes of RAM and two hundred fifty-six gigabytes of storage” — two different things!
cs/cs-computers.6309400378dd: Instruction register, IR. Holds the instruction being worked on right now, so the control unit can decode it. In this CPU the first digit is the operation, one equals ADD, two equals SUB, three equals STORE, five equals LOAD, six equals JUMP, seven equals JUMP IF ZERO, nine zero zero equals OUT, zero zero zero equals HALT. The last two digits are an address in memory.
cs/cs-computers.7b3fb40bcc1b: Accumulator, ACC. A register that holds the number the ALU is working on. LOAD puts a number in, ADD changes it, STORE copies it out. Registers are the fastest memory of all — right inside the CPU. A modern CPU has dozens of registers, each sixty-four bits wide.

cs/cs-data-crypto.407eb9915692: Modern encryption. Today computers scramble data with secret keys that are long numbers — often one hundred twenty-eight or two hundred fifty-six bits. Two to the power of one hundred twenty-eight possible keys is so many that trying them all would take longer than the age of the universe. The padlock and “HTTPS colon slash slash” mean your connection to a website is encrypted.
cs/cs-data-crypto.e0f0cb438101: Frequency analysis. In English, E, about thirteen percent, T and A are the most common letters. Count the letters in a cipher text: its most common letter probably stands for E. The Arab scholar al-Kindi described this method in the eight hundreds.
cs/cs-data-crypto.232775cd0bd8: Caesar cipher. Shift every letter the same number of places: with key three, A to D, B to E… X to A. Julius Caesar reportedly used a shift of three for military messages. There are only twenty-five useful keys — a patient person can just try them all.
cs/cs-data-crypto.7001cc49a954: Bits and bytes. A bit is one zero or one — like a light switch, off or on. Eight bits equals one byte: two to the eighth equals two hundred fifty-six different patterns, enough for zero to two hundred fifty-five. One kilobyte about a thousand bytes, one megabyte about a million, one gigabyte about a billion.
cs/cs-data-crypto.495524fe8219: Pixels and RGB. A screen picture is a grid of tiny dots called pixels. Each pixel mixes red, green and blue light, each from zero to two hundred fifty-five — about sixteen point seven million colours. Two hundred fifty-five, two hundred fifty-five, two hundred fifty-five is white, zero, zero, zero is black, two hundred fifty-five, two hundred fifty-five, zero is yellow.
cs/cs-data-crypto.bec12bb6f907: Don’t mix up: Internet speeds use bits, megabits per second; file sizes use bytes, megabytes. Eight bits equals one byte!
cs/cs-data-crypto.5882e3d14228: Vigenère cipher. A key word gives a different shift for each letter: C equals two, O equals fourteen, D equals three, E equals four…. The same letter can turn into different letters, which hides the letter pattern. It was called “the indecipherable cipher” for about three hundred years — until people found ways to break it in the eighteen hundreds.
cs/cs-data-crypto.040859fe6ae7: Don’t mix up: Mixing light is not mixing paint: red plus green light makes yellow!

cs/cs-internet.7856ba64bb21: Undersea fiber-optic cable. Almost all data between continents travels through cables on the sea floor — not satellites. In deep water a cable is only about as thick as a garden hose. Ships lay it from giant spools. Repeaters every fifty to one hundred kilometers or so boost the light so it can cross a whole ocean.
cs/cs-internet.fa4b08b501bf: Fiber-optic cable. Glass threads thinner than a hair carry bits as flashes of light. Light in glass travels about two hundred thousand kilometers per second — Atlanta to Chicago in about five milliseconds. One fiber can carry many colours of light at once, each with its own stream of data.
cs/cs-internet.b48c5d1f1043: The two ends. The sender’s computer uses TCP, a protocol, 协议, to cut data into packets and number them. The receiver puts packets back in order by number and asks again for any that are missing. Each computer on the internet has an IP address such as two zero three dot zero dot one one three dot seven.
cs/cs-internet.72fe72d988cd: Wi-Fi radio link. Bits ride on radio waves between your laptop and the router. Walls and distance weaken the signal — that is why Wi-Fi gets slow far from the router. Radio waves move at almost the speed of light: three hundred thousand kilometers per second.
cs/cs-internet.f0922a915e67: Don’t mix up: Wi-Fi and mobile data, four G or five G, are different radio systems.
cs/cs-internet.e5e298ea6ad5: Your home Wi-Fi router. Wi-Fi sends bits as radio waves, usually two point four or five gigahertz — only across a few rooms. It gives each device at home a local address and shares one internet connection. From here, a cable, copper or fiber, runs to your internet service provider, ISP.

earth/atmosphere.5ff8112541e6: Ozone layer. Earth’s sunscreen, about fifteen to thirty-five kilometers. A zone inside the stratosphere where ozone gas, O three, is most concentrated. Ozone absorbs most of the Sun’s harmful ultraviolet, UV, rays, protecting living things from sunburn, skin cancer and eye damage. Chemicals called CFCs, once used in spray cans and refrigerators, thinned it, causing the “ozone hole” over Antarctica. A nineteen eighty-seven treaty, the Montreal Protocol, began phasing them out; they are now banned almost everywhere, and the layer is slowly healing.
earth/atmosphere.7782d1c65755: Troposphere. Zero to twelve kilometers, where weather happens. The lowest layer: about eight kilometers thick over the poles and sixteen to eighteen kilometers thick over the equator. It holds about seventy-five to eighty percent of all the air and almost all the water vapor, so nearly all clouds, rain and storms form here. Temperature drops about six point five degrees Celsius for every kilometer you climb, because this layer is heated from the ground below. Air here keeps mixing by convection: warm air rises and cool air sinks.
earth/atmosphere.d1a5672cda6a: Mesosphere. Fifty to eighty-five kilometers, meteors burn up here. The coldest layer: about minus ninety degrees Celsius near its top. Most meteors, “shooting stars”, burn up here as they rub against air molecules at high speed. Too high for planes and balloons, too low for satellites, so it is the least explored layer.
earth/atmosphere.eabcd2d3f7a7: Global winds. Uneven heating and Earth’s spin. The Sun heats the equator more than the poles. Warm air rises at the equator and cooler air flows in to replace it, forming giant convection loops. Earth’s rotation bends moving air, the Coriolis effect, so winds blow at an angle instead of straight north-south. Trade winds, zero to thirty degrees, blow from the east toward the equator; prevailing westerlies, thirty to sixty degrees, blow from the west; polar easterlies, sixty to ninety degrees, blow from the east. The westerlies carry most weather across the United States from west to east.
earth/atmosphere.812344453b7d: Stratosphere. Twelve to fifty kilometers, calm layered air. Air moves mostly sideways in calm layers with little up-and-down mixing, so the ride is smooth. Temperature RISES with height here, because ozone absorbs ultraviolet, UV, energy from the Sun. Weather balloons rise to about thirty to thirty-five kilometers before they burst. Big jets cruise near the bottom of this layer. It contains the ozone layer.
earth/atmosphere.97615617c0a4: Thermosphere. Eighty-five to six hundred kilometers, auroras and the ISS. The air is extremely thin. Its few particles absorb X-rays and UV light and can reach five hundred to two thousand degrees Celsius. It would not feel hot to you: there are so few particles that very little heat would reach your skin. Auroras, the northern and southern lights, glow here when charged particles from the Sun hit gas atoms. The International Space Station orbits in the thermosphere, about four hundred kilometers up. Its lower part, the ionosphere, bounces radio waves around Earth.
earth/atmosphere.3eabe6e94501: Common mix-up: The ozone hole is not what causes global warming. Losing ozone lets in more UV; global warming is caused mainly by extra greenhouse gases such as C O two.
earth/atmosphere.b2e15c5cd4f0: Exosphere. Above about six hundred kilometers, fades into space. The outermost layer, made mostly of very thin hydrogen and helium. Particles are so far apart they rarely collide, and some escape into space. Many satellites orbit here. The layer slowly fades into outer space about ten thousand kilometers up.

earth/climate.c7fe8c097574: High altitude. Higher equals colder. Air temperature drops about six point five degrees Celsius for every one thousand meters you climb. That is why mountaintops can have snow even near the equator, Mount Kilimanjaro, the Andes. Quito, Ecuador sits right on the equator, but at two thousand eight hundred fifty meters high it feels like spring all year.
earth/climate.de7eec63cdaf: Direct versus slanted sunlight. Latitude is the number one climate control. Near the equator the noon Sun is high, so rays hit nearly straight on and their energy is packed into a small area. Toward the poles the same beam hits at a low angle and spreads over a bigger area, so each square meter gets less energy. Slanted rays also pass through more atmosphere, which absorbs and scatters some of their energy. Move the beam-latitude slider and watch the bright spot stretch!
earth/climate.5610deb67685: Polar zones. Above sixty-six point five degrees, Arctic and Antarctic Circles. Sunlight always arrives at a low angle, spread thin over a large area. Winters have weeks of darkness, polar night; summers can have twenty-four-hour daylight, but it stays cold. Ice and snow reflect most sunlight back to space, keeping these regions even colder.
earth/climate.ca8f7f43aa8a: Earth’s twenty-three point five degree tilt. The cause of the seasons. Earth’s axis is tilted about twenty-three point five degrees, and it keeps pointing the same way in space as Earth orbits the Sun. In June the Northern Hemisphere tilts toward the Sun: more direct rays and longer days equals summer. In December it tilts away equals winter. The hemispheres have opposite seasons. Use the December, March and September, or June buttons!
earth/climate.5c2ea73ac728: Tropical zone. Between twenty-three point five degrees north and twenty-three point five degrees south. The noon Sun is high all year, and it is directly overhead at least once a year. Warm all year. Many places have a wet season and a dry season instead of summer and winter. Includes rainforests, Amazon, Congo, Singapore, and also deserts where air sinks.
earth/climate.b65462f40e9a: Temperate zones. Twenty-three point five degrees to sixty-six point five degrees, north and south. The Sun is never directly overhead, and its angle changes a lot through the year. That gives four distinct seasons: warm summers and cool to cold winters. Georgia, about thirty-one to thirty-five degrees north, and most of China lie in the northern temperate zone.

earth/earth-layers.fb7843b694e0: Asthenosphere. Soft, slowly flowing part of the upper mantle. Roughly one hundred to three hundred fifty kilometers below the surface, in the upper mantle. The rock is solid but hot enough to flow very slowly, like thick putty or warm candle wax. The rigid plates of the lithosphere glide on top of it. A tiny fraction, about one percent, may be melted, which helps it flow.
earth/earth-layers.dc317d069e3c: Continental crust. Thick, light rock that makes the continents. About thirty to seventy kilometers thick, thickest under high mountains. Made mostly of granite-like rock, rich in silicon, oxygen, aluminum and potassium. Low density, about two point seven grams per cubic centimeter, so it rides high and does not sink easily. Some continental rocks are about four billion years old.
earth/earth-layers.f8ff47dd5570: Outer core. The only liquid layer: molten iron and nickel. From about two thousand nine hundred kilometers to five thousand one hundred fifty kilometers deep, about two thousand two hundred fifty kilometers thick. Liquid iron and nickel at about four thousand to five thousand degrees Celsius. Swirling liquid metal makes Earth’s magnetic field, which guides compasses and shields us from the solar wind. S waves cannot travel through it. That is how scientists know it is liquid.
earth/earth-layers.2b1a83a545f4: Lithosphere. Rigid outer shell: crust and top of the mantle. Made of the crust plus the cool, rigid uppermost mantle. About one hundred kilometers thick on average, thinner under oceans, thicker under continents. It is broken into about fifteen major tectonic plates that move two to ten centimeters per year. The boundary between crust and mantle is called the Moho.
earth/earth-layers.b735a09cbac0: Inner core. A solid ball of iron and nickel at the center. A solid ball about one thousand two hundred twenty kilometers in radius, about seventy percent the size of the Moon. About five thousand two hundred degrees Celsius, roughly as hot as the surface of the Sun. It stays solid because the pressure is about three point six million times the air pressure at sea level. The densest layer: about thirteen grams per cubic centimeter, more than four times as dense as crust rock.
earth/earth-layers.6dcc53db99a4: Oceanic crust. Thin, dense rock under the oceans. Only about five to ten kilometers thick. Made of dark basalt, which has more iron and magnesium. Denser, about three point zero grams per cubic centimeter, than continental crust, so it sinks beneath it when the two collide. Young: almost none is older than about two hundred million years, because old ocean floor sinks back into the mantle.
earth/earth-layers.bea3bfbf5b52: Mantle. The thickest layer: hot, solid, slowly moving rock. The whole mantle is about two thousand nine hundred kilometers thick and makes up about eighty-four percent of Earth’s volume. Solid rock rich in iron and magnesium, peridotite in the upper part. Temperature rises from about one thousand degrees Celsius near the top to about three thousand seven hundred degrees Celsius at the bottom. Hot rock slowly rises and cooler rock sinks. These convection currents help move the plates. The mantle-core boundary at two thousand nine hundred kilometers is called the Gutenberg discontinuity.

earth/fossils-time.fe8211aa5e5a: Layer seven, Cenozoic sandstone. Petrified wood and insect in amber. The YOUNGEST layer: it is on top. Petrified wood: minerals replaced the wood cell by cell, keeping even the tree rings. Amber is hardened tree resin. An insect trapped in sticky resin can be preserved whole: a preserved-remains fossil. Other ways to keep original remains: freezing in ice, woolly mammoths, or sinking into tar pits.
earth/fossils-time.010efa465a85: Layer one, Cambrian shale. Trilobites, molds and casts. The OLDEST layer here: it is at the bottom, law of superposition. Trilobites were sea animals with hard, jointed shells, distant relatives of insects and crabs. They are extinct. Many are preserved as molds, the hollow print left when the shell dissolved, and casts, the mold later filled with minerals. Shale forms from fine mud settling in calm water, so this place was once a sea floor.
earth/fossils-time.c61c8aabc5e1: Layer six, Cretaceous chalk. Ammonites, index fossils. Chalk is made of the shells of microscopic sea plankton. Ammonites were squid-like animals with coiled shells. Each species lived for a short time but spread widely, so they make excellent index fossils. The sea returned! High sea levels flooded much of North America at this time. The Cretaceous ended sixty-six million years ago with a mass extinction that wiped out the dinosaurs, except birds, and the ammonites.
earth/fossils-time.952a5e014e79: Layer two, Ordovician limestone. Brachiopod shells and crinoid stems. Limestone forms in warm, shallow seas from the shells and skeletons of sea creatures. Brachiopods look like clams but are a different group of shelled animals. Crinoids, “sea lilies”, are animals related to starfish. Their stems break into little disc-shaped pieces. Climate clue: warm-sea fossils on dry land show that the surface and climate here have changed.
earth/fossils-time.3ab5d99440ed: Layer three, Devonian sandstone. Fish bones, petrified. The Devonian is called the “Age of Fishes”. The fish was buried quickly in sand. Minerals in groundwater filled the tiny spaces in its bones and turned them to stone, petrification. Sandstone forms from sand on beaches, in rivers or in deserts.
earth/fossils-time.59c8204c606f: Layer four, Carboniferous coal and shale. Fern leaves, carbon films. Coal formed from huge swamp forests of giant ferns and tree-sized club mosses. Pressed leaves left a thin black film of carbon: a carbon-film fossil. Climate clue: coal has even been found in Antarctica, so that land was once warm and swampy, and in a different place.
earth/fossils-time.c802fbe8f4c1: Layer five, Jurassic red sandstone. Dinosaur footprints, trace fossils. Dig away the layers above to see three-toed dinosaur tracks on the top of this layer. Footprints are trace fossils: evidence of what an animal did, not of its body. Burrows, nests and fossil dung, coprolites, are trace fossils too. Tracks show how an animal walked, how fast it moved and whether it travelled in groups. The red color comes from iron oxide, often a clue to a hot climate with dry seasons.
earth/fossils-time.356fba4ca225: Common mix-up: Trilobites are not insects or dinosaurs. They died out about two hundred fifty million years ago, before the first dinosaurs.
earth/fossils-time.99603d41c43d: Igneous dike, intrusion. No fossils: it was molten rock. Magma squeezed up through a crack and cooled into a wall of igneous rock. It cuts through layers one to six, so it is YOUNGER than all of them, cross-cutting relationships. Layer seven lies on top of it, so layer seven is younger still. Igneous rock can be dated in years using radioactive elements that decay at a steady rate, half-life. This is absolute dating. The dike is fifty million years old, so layer six must be older than fifty million years and layer seven younger.

earth/natural-resources.2fab49b12163: Wind power. Moving air spins turbines. Wind spins the giant blades, which turn a generator inside the nacelle at the top of the tower. Wind exists because the Sun heats Earth unevenly, so wind energy is really solar energy too. Power rises quickly with wind speed. Below about three meters per second the blades barely turn. Try the Wind slider!
earth/natural-resources.0f8d0feca74f: Biomass. Energy stored in living things. Wood, crop waste, manure and fuels made from corn or sugarcane, ethanol, can be burned for heat or electricity. Plants store the Sun’s energy through photosynthesis, so biomass is stored solar energy. It is renewable only if we replant as fast as we use it. Burning it still releases C O two and smoke.
earth/natural-resources.8b84729fd855: Natural gas. Gaseous fossil fuel, often found with oil. Natural gas, mostly methane, forms the same way as oil and collects above it in the trap, because gas is lighter. It heats homes, fuels stoves and runs power plants. Pipelines carry it across the country. It releases about half the C O two of coal when burned, but methane that leaks is a powerful greenhouse gas.
earth/natural-resources.d4d24b6a5564: Coal. Fossil fuel from ancient swamp plants. Coal formed from plants in swamps about three hundred million years ago that were buried, squeezed and heated over millions of years. Power plants burn coal to boil water; the steam spins turbines. See the black coal seam in the rock layers. Burning coal releases the most C O two of any fuel, plus pollution that causes smog and acid rain. Mining scars the land.
earth/natural-resources.58ba799a770a: Your town: saving energy. The cheapest energy is the energy you don’t use. Conservation means using less: turn off lights, unplug chargers, walk, bike or share rides. Efficiency means getting the same job done with less energy: LED bulbs use about seventy-five percent less electricity than old bulbs. Reduce, reuse, recycle: making new things from recycled aluminum uses about ninety-five percent less energy than making them from raw ore.
earth/natural-resources.26d384692416: Nuclear power. Splitting uranium atoms. In the reactor, uranium atoms split, nuclear fission, and release huge amounts of heat, which boils water to spin turbines. It makes no C O two while running, and a small amount of fuel makes a lot of energy. It is nonrenewable because uranium is a mined metal that will run out. The used fuel stays radioactive for thousands of years and must be stored safely.

earth/oceans.d4b1bae4821c: Continental slope. The steep drop from the shelf to the deep sea. It marks the true edge of the continent. The depth drops from about two hundred meters to three thousand to four thousand meters. Underwater avalanches of sediment carve deep submarine canyons into it.
earth/oceans.69ddd079d3a5: Mid-ocean ridge. An underwater mountain chain where new sea floor forms. The longest mountain range on Earth, about sixty-five thousand kilometers long, winding through every ocean. Plates pull apart here, a divergent boundary. Magma rises into the central rift valley and cools into new ocean crust: sea-floor spreading. Rock gets older the farther it is from the ridge. Iceland is a piece of the Mid-Atlantic Ridge that rises above sea level.
earth/oceans.3f59511099c9: Continental shelf. The shallow, gently sloping edge of a continent. The flooded edge of a continent, usually less than about two hundred meters deep. Sunlight reaches much of it, so it is rich in sea life and holds most of the world’s fishing grounds. Oil and natural gas are often drilled here. During ice ages, sea level was lower and much of the shelf was dry land.
earth/oceans.01379c3f5aaa: Seamount. An underwater volcanic mountain. A volcano that rises at least one thousand meters above the sea floor but does not reach the surface. A seamount whose top was flattened by waves when it was near the surface is called a guyot. Seamounts are hot spots for fish, corals and other life.
earth/oceans.03c9772a26ac: Ocean trench. The deepest part of the ocean. A long, narrow, very deep valley where one plate sinks beneath another, subduction. The Mariana Trench in the Pacific is about eleven thousand meters deep. Mount Everest would fit inside with room to spare. Strong earthquakes and tsunamis often start near trenches.
earth/oceans.a612d969caf2: Abyssal plain. The flat, deep ocean floor. One of the flattest places on Earth, about four thousand to six thousand meters deep. Covered by a thick blanket of fine mud and the tiny shells of plankton that sank from above. Totally dark and near freezing, yet strange animals still live here.

earth/plate-tectonics.9538894ae913: Transform fault. A crack where plates grind sideways past each other. The plates slide horizontally in opposite directions. Crust is neither created nor destroyed here. California’s San Andreas Fault is a transform boundary: the Pacific plate moves northwest about three to five centimeters per year relative to North America. Most transform faults are short offsets connecting pieces of mid-ocean ridges.
earth/plate-tectonics.4e0327ed4de4: Ring of Fire. Belt of volcanoes and earthquakes around the Pacific. A horseshoe-shaped belt about forty thousand kilometers long around the Pacific Ocean. About seventy-five percent of Earth’s active volcanoes and about ninety percent of its earthquakes happen here. It follows subduction zones where Pacific Ocean plates sink under the plates around them.
earth/plate-tectonics.2f8493fee564: Mid-ocean ridge. Underwater mountain range where plates pull apart. The longest mountain range on Earth: about sixty-five thousand kilometers long, almost all underwater. Magma rises into the crack, cools and becomes new basalt seafloor. A rift valley runs along the crest of the ridge. Iceland is a piece of the Mid-Atlantic Ridge that rises above sea level.
earth/plate-tectonics.d7b78c3461f0: Earthquakes. Sudden shaking when rocks slip. Rocks along a boundary lock together. Stress builds until they slip suddenly, releasing energy as seismic waves. The point underground where slipping starts is the focus; the spot on the surface right above it is the epicenter. Earthquakes happen at all three kinds of boundaries; the deepest, down to about seven hundred kilometers, happen along sinking plates.
earth/plate-tectonics.198c00a35d88: Seafloor spreading. The ocean floor grows outward from the ridge. New crust forms at the ridge and moves away on both sides like two conveyor belts. Rock is youngest at the ridge and gets older farther away. Earth’s magnetic field flips every so often. Cooling lava records it, leaving matching magnetic stripes on both sides of the ridge. Harry Hess proposed seafloor spreading in the early nineteen sixties, and the stripes proved it.
earth/plate-tectonics.2c11b13e4165: Ocean trench. Deepest valleys in the ocean, where a plate dives down. Forms where an oceanic plate bends and sinks beneath another plate. The Mariana Trench is the deepest place on Earth, about eleven thousand meters deep. Trenches form long curved lines around the Pacific Ocean.
earth/plate-tectonics.ab0411bee4ab: Oceanic plate. Thin, dense plate under the ocean. Its crust is dark basalt, only about five to ten kilometers thick. Denser than a continental plate, so it sinks, subducts, when the two collide. Because old ocean floor keeps sinking, none is older than about two hundred million years.
earth/plate-tectonics.5cbc9e52041f: Continental plate. Thick, light plate that carries land. Its crust is granite-like rock, thirty to seventy kilometers thick. Too light, buoyant, to sink far into the mantle. When two continental plates collide, the crust crumples upward into huge mountains.
earth/plate-tectonics.02da289508c0: Folded mountains. The tallest mountains, built by colliding continents. Neither continental plate sinks, so the crust crumples, folds and stacks up, growing thick and tall. India has been pushing into Asia for about fifty million years, building the Himalayas and Mount Everest, eight thousand eight hundred forty-nine meters. The Himalayas are still rising by a few millimeters each year. The Appalachian Mountains, including north Georgia’s Blue Ridge, formed in an ancient continental collision about three hundred million years ago.

earth/rocks-minerals.13ca553a7e9b: Magma and melting. Rock melts deep underground. Deep underground it is hot enough, about seven hundred to one thousand three hundred degrees Celsius, for rock to melt into magma. Magma is less dense than the solid rock around it, so it slowly rises. Any rock type, igneous, sedimentary or metamorphic, can melt and start the cycle again.

earth/soil.6bbcad376bd6: Air and water in pores. About half of soil is open space! A healthy soil is about forty-five percent minerals, five percent organic matter, twenty-five percent water and twenty-five percent air. Water and air fill the spaces, pores, between grains. Roots and soil animals need both. Permeability is how easily water flows through soil: fast through sand, slow through clay. Watch the rain: water slows down in the clay-rich B horizon and collects above the bedrock as groundwater.
earth/soil.986de40252c7: A horizon, topsoil. The richest, most alive layer. A mix of humus and small mineral grains, sand, silt and clay. Humus makes it dark. Most plant roots, earthworms and microorganisms live here. Farmers grow crops in topsoil. Forming just two point five centimeters of it can take hundreds of years. Some soils have a pale E layer under A, where water has washed minerals out.

earth/water-cycle.daa27778143c: Transpiration. Plants give off water vapor from their leaves. Roots take up water from the soil. It travels up the stem and escapes through tiny leaf pores called stomata. A large oak tree can transpire about one hundred fifty thousand liters, forty thousand gallons, of water in a year. About ten percent of the water vapor in the air comes from plants.
earth/water-cycle.39ba82e4c45b: Snow and glaciers. Water stored as ice. When it is cold, precipitation falls as snow and can pile up for years as glaciers and ice caps. Ice caps and glaciers hold about sixty-nine percent of Earth’s fresh water. In spring, snowmelt feeds rivers. Ice can also turn straight into vapor, sublimation. Lower the temperature and watch the snowcap grow!
earth/water-cycle.af86c8dc5e0b: Groundwater. Water stored in soil and rock underground. Water that sinks deep fills the pores and cracks in rock. The top of this soaked, saturated, zone is the water table. A rock layer that holds water and lets it flow is an aquifer. Wells pump water from aquifers. Groundwater moves very slowly, often centimeters to meters a day, and eventually seeps into rivers, lakes and the ocean. Groundwater is about thirty percent of Earth’s fresh water.
earth/water-cycle.991cfbf3ff20: Evaporation. Liquid water, water vapor, a gas. Heat from the Sun turns liquid water into invisible water vapor. About eighty-six percent of all evaporation comes from the oceans. When seawater evaporates, the salt stays behind, so the water vapor is fresh. Warmer temperatures mean faster evaporation: try the temperature slider.

earth/weather.9406df0af175: Spiral rain bands. Arms of storms. Long curved bands of clouds and thunderstorms that spiral in toward the center. They bring bursts of heavy rain and gusty winds, and can spin up small tornadoes. A whole hurricane can be five hundred kilometers or more across.
earth/weather.9815a8df398d: Warm ocean water. The hurricane’s fuel. Hurricanes need ocean water of at least about twenty-six point five degrees Celsius. Warm water evaporates, loading the air with water vapor. When that vapor condenses into clouds, it releases huge amounts of heat energy. Over land or cold water the fuel is cut off and the storm weakens. Try the ocean-temperature slider!
earth/weather.770d75a928f8: Cumulonimbus. Thunderstorm cloud. A giant tower cloud that can reach twelve kilometers or higher, with a flat anvil top where it hits the stratosphere. Strong updrafts of warm, moist air feed it. It brings lightning, thunder, downpours, hail and sometimes tornadoes. “Cumulus” means heap, and “nimbus” means rain cloud.
earth/weather.ac860a701ed8: Eyewall. Strongest winds and heaviest rain. A ring of towering thunderstorms around the eye. Here, warm moist air rises fastest. As its water vapor condenses, it releases heat that powers the whole storm. The eyewall has the fastest winds: over two hundred fifty kilometers per hour in a Category five hurricane.
earth/weather.34690ae696e7: The eye. Calm, clear center. The center of the hurricane, usually twenty to sixty kilometers across. Air sinks gently in the eye, so it is surprisingly calm, with light winds and sometimes blue sky. Danger: after the eye passes, the other side of the eyewall hits with winds from the opposite direction.
earth/weather.c4797773b72b: Cirrus. High, wispy ice clouds. Thin, feathery clouds high in the troposphere, above about six kilometers, made of ice crystals. Often the first sign of an approaching warm front: rain may arrive within a day or two. Nicknamed “mares’ tails” for their curly shapes.

earth/weathering-erosion.ec5cb5636ab6: V-shaped valley and canyon. Carved by a river cutting downward. As a river cuts down, weathering and gravity wear back the walls, giving a V shape. The Colorado River carved the Grand Canyon over about five to six million years; it is about one point eight kilometers deep, and its walls show layers of rock. Georgia’s Providence Canyon, “Little Grand Canyon”, formed in only about two hundred years, after poor farming in the eighteen hundreds let rain wash gullies into the soft soil — a human impact.
earth/weathering-erosion.6d387b670195: Glacier. A slow river of ice. Glaciers form where more snow falls each winter than melts each summer; the snow packs into ice. The ice slowly flows downhill, often a few centimeters to a meter per day. Rocks frozen into the bottom scrape and grind the bedrock, leaving scratches called striations. About twenty thousand years ago, ice sheets covered much of northern North America, but not Georgia.
earth/weathering-erosion.4f3c6d8986ed: Wind transport. Wind carries sand and dust. Sand moves by bouncing along the ground, saltation; fine dust can be carried thousands of kilometers. Dust from the Sahara regularly crosses the Atlantic Ocean to the Americas. In the nineteen thirties Dust Bowl, plowing and drought let wind blow away huge amounts of farm soil — a human impact.

economics/econ-growth.52029b24d7ef: What was happening: nineteen seventy-eight: China begins reform and opening up, Third Plenum of the eleventh Central Committee.
economics/econ-growth.25efaa49ee82: Hyperinflation: When a government prints money recklessly, prices can explode. Germany printed ten-billion-mark notes in nineteen twenty-three; in two thousand nine Zimbabwe issued a one-hundred-trillion-dollar note, see the photos below.
economics/econ-growth.f998226551cf: Entrepreneurship. Combining the other factors and taking the risk of a new business. Entrepreneurs spot a need, organize resources and risk their own money. The profit motive rewards them if customers want what they make. Georgia examples: Coca-Cola began in an Atlanta pharmacy in eighteen eighty-six; Chick-fil-A grew from a Hapeville diner.

economics/econ-personal-finance.f79abcb28f9c: Scams and fraud. Tricks that try to get your money or your passwords. Scammers pretend to be someone you trust, invent a problem or prize, rush you, and demand an odd payment method. Real companies never ask you to pay with gift cards or to share a login code. Report US scams at Report Fraud dot F T C dot gov; in China, the National Anti-Fraud Center, 国家反诈中心, runs an app and the nine six one one zero warning line.
economics/econ-personal-finance.0f02283c4e5c: Saving. Setting money aside for goals, emergencies and the future. Reasons to save: a goal, bike, college, emergencies, and the future. An emergency fund turns a surprise bill into a small problem instead of a debt. US bank deposits are insured by the FDIC up to two hundred fifty thousand dollars per depositor, per bank, per ownership category.
economics/econ-personal-finance.23b33e508aa3: Budget. A plan for spending and saving before the money is gone. List income, then needs, savings and wants. Fifty thirty twenty is a common rule of thumb: fifty percent needs, thirty percent wants, twenty percent savings — not a law. “Pay yourself first”: move savings out as soon as money arrives.
economics/econ-personal-finance.0f252161037c: Income. Money coming in — where every money plan starts. Income from work is limited: there are only so many hours to babysit, mow or work a shift. Teens earn from allowances, gifts, like red-envelope money, 压岁钱, and small jobs. On a paycheck, taxes come out first: gross pay is before taxes, net pay is what you keep.
economics/econ-personal-finance.adbb5da8b80e: Compound interest. Interest that earns interest — growth that speeds up over time. Simple interest is paid only on what you put in; compound interest is also paid on earlier interest. Rule of seventy-two: years to double, about seventy-two divided by interest rate, percent. Time matters most: starting ten years earlier can beat saving more later.

economics/econ-scarcity.392afc0c8941: Many people, little farmland: China’s farmland per person is less than half the world average. That is why “treasure and use every piece of land wisely and strictly protect farmland” is one of China’s basic national policies, in China’s eighth-grade geography textbook.
economics/econ-scarcity.2d1890914683: Scarcity. Limited resources, unlimited wants. Scarcity is always there — even rich people and rich countries have only twenty-four hours a day and limited land. Productive resources, factors of production: land or natural resources, labor, capital goods and entrepreneurship. Because of scarcity every society must answer three questions: what to produce, how to produce, and for whom.

economics/econ-systems.e6243d5c3c41: Command, planned, economy. The central government decides. What to produce? Whatever the government plan sets. How to produce? Planners assign factories, workers and quotas. For whom? The government decides who gets what, often rations. The government owns or controls most land, factories and resources. Strength: it can move huge resources fast toward a goal, heavy industry, dams, railways. Weakness: planners can’t know what millions of people want — shortages and waste are common, and there is little incentive to innovate. Examples: the Soviet Union, nineteen twenty-eight to nineteen ninety-one; North Korea and Cuba today come closest.
economics/econ-systems.e0fbb5cf4f4d: Changchun. In nineteen fifty-six the First Automobile Works in Changchun built New China’s first trucks, the “Jiefang”, Liberation.
economics/econ-systems.dd295a2f93ca: Tianjin. Tianjin is Beijing’s gateway to the sea, on the Bohai. Since two thousand eight high-speed trains link the two cities in about thirty minutes.
