economics/econ-systems.4332f74a0417: Mixed economy. Every real country mixes market and government decisions. What to produce? Mostly markets, plus some government choices. How to produce? Private firms and state firms, with rules. For whom? By prices, plus taxes and public services. The US is mostly market, yet the government builds highways, runs public schools and pays Social Security. China calls its system a socialist market economy: public ownership as the mainstay, many forms of ownership developing together, the market playing the decisive role in allocating resources and the government playing its role better. Countries move along the line over time — China after nineteen seventy-eight, Russia after nineteen ninety-one, India after nineteen ninety-one.

economics/econ-trade.c8add6431ad1: Absolute advantage. Making MORE of something with the same resources. Peach Isle catches six fish an hour; Bamboo Isle catches one. Peach Isle has the absolute advantage in fish. Peach Isle also gathers more coconuts per hour, three versus two — it has the absolute advantage in BOTH goods. Surprise: trade can still help both islands. Absolute advantage is not what decides who should make what.
economics/econ-trade.c34e543cac8e: Comparative advantage. Making something at a LOWER opportunity cost than others. On Peach Isle, one coconut costs two fish, the hour could have caught six fish instead of three coconuts. On Bamboo Isle, one coconut costs only one half fish. Bamboo Isle has the comparative advantage in coconuts. Peach Isle has the comparative advantage in fish, one fish costs one half coconut there, but two coconuts on Bamboo Isle. When each specializes in its comparative advantage and trades, total output rises.
economics/econ-trade.28ebc5f36e48: Amsterdam. Capital of the Netherlands, a city of canals. In the sixteen hundreds and seventeen hundreds Dutch ships brought Chinese porcelain, tea and silk here.
economics/econ-trade.a44953fabc3a: Economic globalization: After the two thousand eight to two thousand nine world financial crisis, trade’s share falls back, partly as China’s home market grows. The US stays lower because its huge home market buys most of what it makes.
economics/econ-trade.1f2202b872f8: Exchange rate. The price of one currency in terms of another. In twenty twenty-four, one dollar bought about seven yuan and twenty fen on average, World Bank. Most currencies move with supply and demand; China manages the yuan within a range. A stronger yuan makes Chinese exports pricier abroad and foreign trips cheaper for Chinese families.

ela/argument-writing.250716a6fed9: Claim. What you want the reader to believe or do. A claim is arguable: a reasonable person could disagree. “School starts at seven forty-five” is a fact, not a claim. Make it specific: who should do what? “Our school should add a twenty-minute recess” beats “Recess is good.” Strong claims often include a reason: “…because students focus better after a break.” Starters: “Our school should…”, “It is time to…”, “The best solution is…”. Claim equals what I think and why, in one sentence. A topic, “phones in school”, is not a claim. A claim takes a side.
ela/argument-writing.4556eed6d41d: Evidence. Facts, data, examples or expert words that support the claim. Strong evidence is specific, numbers, names, dates, reliable, an expert or careful study, and relevant, it really is about your claim. Weak evidence: one person’s story, an unnamed website, or data that is too old for the question. Introduce it: “According to the CDC, …”, “A twenty eighteen study found that…”. Two pieces of strong evidence beat five weak ones. Specific, Reliable, Relevant: S R R. A strong feeling is not evidence. “I really, really believe it” proves nothing.
ela/argument-writing.13f23a3694cc: Rebuttal. Why your claim still wins. A rebuttal answers the counterclaim with evidence or logic: “However, …”. You may admit part of it, a concession, then show why your side still matters more. Insults, “people who think that are clueless”, are not rebuttals; they are ad hominem attacks. Georgia’s grade eight standard adds the rebuttal to the claim, evidence and counterclaim you already know. “Yes, but…” with proof. “That might be a problem.” is only a concession. A rebuttal must push back.

ela/central-idea.e1cd73fd2cfa: Honeybees do one of the most important jobs on Earth: they help grow our food. As a bee drinks nectar, pollen sticks to its fuzzy body and rubs off on the next flower. That moved pollen lets plants make fruit and seeds. Apples, almonds, blueberries and many other crops depend on bee visits. Inside the hive, a single queen can lay more than one thousand five hundred eggs a day. Young workers clean cells and feed larvae, older ones build wax and guard the door, and the oldest fly out to gather food. A honeybee colony works like a well-organized city, with every bee doing a job. Honeybees also share information in an amazing way. A forager that finds flowers does a “waggle dance” that shows other bees the direction and distance to the food. Scientist Karl von Frisch decoded the dance and won a Nobel Prize in nineteen seventy-three. A bee’s wings beat more than two hundred times a second. Beekeepers have noticed something worrying. Honeybee colonies today face serious threats. Tiny parasites called varroa mites, pesticides, diseases and a shortage of wildflowers all weaken colonies. In some recent years, US beekeepers have reported losing a third or more of their hives. Farmers are planting strips of wildflowers, and scientists are breeding bees that resist mites. Protecting honeybees means protecting the food on our tables.

ela/character-pov.9d713dc3d4f7: Stave one, Christmas Eve. “Bah!” said Scrooge, “Humbug!” He snaps at his cheerful nephew Fred and refuses to give a penny to men collecting for the poor.
ela/character-pov.49a6f262c006: Stave two, Christmas Past. “The happiness he gives, is quite as great as if it cost a fortune.” Watching his kind old boss Fezziwig’s party, Scrooge praises generosity — and thinks of his own clerk.
ela/character-pov.fbe1205678ff: Stave four, Christmas Yet to Come. “I am not the man I was.” Shown a lonely, unmourned death, Scrooge begs for a chance to change.
ela/character-pov.94040a501777: Stave one, The miser. “Oh! But he was a tight-fisted hand at the grindstone, Scrooge! a squeezing, wrenching, grasping, scraping, clutching, covetous, old sinner!” The narrator tells us directly what Scrooge is like — a pile-up of greedy verbs.
ela/character-pov.0fd97163cd46: Stave three, Christmas Present. “Spirit,” said Scrooge, with an interest he had never felt before, “tell me if Tiny Tim will live.” He sees his clerk Bob Cratchit’s poor family and their sick boy — and begins to care.
ela/character-pov.fc11272130dd: Stave five, Christmas morning. “I am as light as a feather, I am as happy as an angel, I am as merry as a school-boy.” He sends the Cratchits a prize turkey, raises Bob’s salary and becomes “as good a man as the good old city knew”.
ela/character-pov.a08e963ed9a1: Stave one, Marley’s ghost. “I wear the chain I forged in life.” His dead partner warns him: a greedy life becomes a heavy chain. Scrooge is frightened, but not yet changed.

ela/grammar-sentences.4fd4f993dca5: Fragments and run-ons. The two most common sentence errors. Fragment: missing a subject or verb, or just a dependent clause. Fix: attach it to a sentence. Run-on, fused: “The bus was late we missed the bell.” Comma splice: “The bus was late, we missed the bell.” Fix a run-on four ways: period, semicolon, comma and FANBOYS, or make one clause dependent. Fragment equals too little. Run-on equals too much, no glue. Long is not equal to run-on. A long sentence that’s properly joined is fine.
ela/grammar-sentences.62cee90d520e: Compound-complex. Two or more independent clauses and at least one dependent. “When the lights flickered, Dad searched for the flashlight, and my little brother cheered.” Great for showing how events connect, but don’t chain too many: readers get lost. Dickens’s first sentence in A Tale of Two Cities is a famous giant. Compound and complex equals both rules at once. Count clauses, not words.
ela/grammar-sentences.79f2eb7f3e96: Phrase versus clause. A clause has a subject AND a verb; a phrase doesn’t. Phrase: “after the game”, “my little brother”: no subject and verb pair. Clause: “my brother cheered”: subject, brother, and verb, cheered. Independent clause: makes sense alone. Dependent clause: starts with a word like because, when, although, if, until and needs an independent clause. Clause equals who and does what. “Because I was tired.” has a subject and verb but is still a fragment: “because” makes it dependent.
ela/grammar-sentences.864b271dd2ec: Compound sentence. Two or more independent clauses joined. Join with a comma and FANBOYS: for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so. Or join with a semicolon: “The lights went out; we lit candles.” 人教版英语 calls this 并列句. FANBOYS equals For And Nor But Or Yet So. A comma alone can’t join two sentences: that’s a comma splice.
ela/grammar-sentences.4e228bf11f65: Simple sentence. One independent clause. “The storm knocked out the power.” Simple doesn’t mean short: “My little brother and I searched the dark kitchen for candles and matches.” is still simple. It can have two subjects or two verbs and still be one clause. One independent, zero dependent. Two verbs is not equal to two clauses. “I ran and jumped” is simple.
ela/grammar-sentences.d60b77b3fca1: Complex sentence. One independent and at least one dependent clause. Dependent first, comma: “When the lights flickered, Dad grabbed a flashlight.” Dependent last, usually no comma: “Dad grabbed a flashlight when the lights flickered.” Subordinating words: because, when, although, if, since, until, while, after, before. AAAWWUBBIS: as, although, after, while, when, unless, because, before, if, since. In English “complex” means it has a dependent clause, not that it is hard to read.

ela/narrative-techniques.7dd891102f45: Mix-up: A flashback often works as 插叙 when it interrupts the main story. 倒叙 starts with a later event, then goes back to tell the earlier events in order.
ela/narrative-techniques.36eb21a3f767: 倒叙 puts the ending first, then goes back to the start. Now readers ask “why?” instead of “what happens?”
ela/narrative-techniques.06c618a673c1: Chronological order, 顺叙 in Chinese, tells A, B, C, D in the order they happened. Clear and easy to follow.
ela/narrative-techniques.80c6fd7e4717: Connotation. The ideas or feelings a word suggests beyond its literal meaning, denotation. Thrifty, plus, economical, neutral, stingy, minus: the same habit, three different feelings. Effect: Word choice shapes mood and tone, and tells you how the author wants you to feel.
ela/narrative-techniques.e40d3b4aaa79: Foreshadowing, 伏笔, plants a small clue early. When it pays off later, 照应, the twist feels surprising but fair.
ela/narrative-techniques.e26cb3abe82c: A flashback interrupts the present to show an earlier moment, then returns. It often explains why a character acts. In Chinese this is close to 插叙.
ela/narrative-techniques.5592a57c6615: Mix-up: In medias res describes the opening. If the story then goes back to the beginning and tells earlier events in order, the structure can also be 倒叙.
ela/narrative-techniques.d0e06653ab06: Suspense, 悬念, is the tension of waiting. Authors build it by slowing the pace and holding back the answer.
ela/narrative-techniques.147149f3dd3a: Mix-up: 语文 adds 神态, facial expression, as its own method; in STEAL it falls under Looks or Actions.

ela/narrative-writing.ec0245ed27e8: Conflict. Someone wants something, and something stands in the way. No conflict, no story: “I went to the store and bought milk” is a list, not a story. Types: character versus character, versus nature, versus society, versus self, inner conflict. Raise the stakes: what happens if the character fails? Want and obstacle equals story. Conflict doesn’t have to be a fight. Being scared to sing at the talent show is conflict.

ela/research-media.6457ba41176b: Images can lie too. Edited, staged or out-of-context pictures. Check shadows, reflections, repeated patterns and edges that look cut out. Most misleading photos are real but used with a false caption. A reverse image search shows where a picture first appeared. Ask: what is outside the frame? Photo editing is older than computers: Soviet officials erased people from photos in the nineteen thirties.

ela/theme-plot.572ed802e999: Falling action. Loose ends get tied up. Tension drops. We learn the results of the climax. Jim reveals he sold his watch to buy the combs. Chinese classes often fold this into the ending, 结局.
ela/theme-plot.1ef01c08e72b: Rising action, one. Complications pile up. Tension climbs. Usually the longest part of a story. Each event makes the problem harder or the stakes higher. Della sells her hair: now there’s no going back.
ela/theme-plot.a3e6c7a6a237: Rising action, two. Even more pressure, right before the peak. Writers often slow down here to build suspense. Della waits by the door, whispering a prayer. Ask: what could go wrong now?
ela/theme-plot.fad881b774c9: Exposition. Meet the characters, the setting and the problem. Answers: who? where? when? what’s wrong? In “The Gift of the Magi”: a small New York flat, Christmas Eve, only one dollar and eighty-seven cents. Often ends with the inciting incident — the spark that starts the trouble.

ela/vocabulary-roots.67865813c81b: Latin roots. Everyday school and law words. dict equals say, spect or vis equals see, aud equals hear, port equals carry, rupt equals break, struct equals build, ject equals throw, tract equals pull. Romans spoke Latin; Spanish, French and Italian grew from it, so these roots help with those languages too. About three in ten dictionary words come straight from Latin. Interrupt equals break between. Eject equals throw out. vis and spect both mean “see”: one Latin root can have several forms.

geography/africa-asia.a1a99baba754: Ganges River. A sacred river for Hindus, about two thousand five hundred kilometers long. The Buddha taught, and great Indian empires grew, in the Ganges plain.
geography/africa-asia.dadc9462df8c: Euphrates River. It flows about two thousand eight hundred kilometers from the mountains of Türkiye through Syria and Iraq to the Persian Gulf. Ur, Uruk and Babylon stood beside it.
geography/africa-asia.2578809088de: Indus River. Pakistan’s lifeline. About three thousand two hundred kilometers from Tibet through northern India into Pakistan and the Arabian Sea. The ancient Indus Valley civilization, Harappa, Mohenjo-daro, grew up along it. Most of Pakistan’s farms depend on its irrigation canals; floods in twenty twenty-two covered a third of the country.
geography/africa-asia.f7d0ed8f1adb: Egypt. The gift of the Nile. North-east corner of Africa; the Sinai Peninsula reaches into Asia, and the Suez Canal crosses it. About ninety-five percent of its one hundred ten million people live in the narrow Nile valley and delta; the rest is desert. Farming with Nile water, natural gas, tourism, pyramids, and Suez Canal fees.
geography/africa-asia.f1c0e6887ce0: Lake Chad. A shallow lake on the edge of the Sahel that has shrunk by about ninety percent since the nineteen sixties, because of drought and water taken for farming.
geography/africa-asia.6352442e7fa1: Sahara. The largest hot desert on Earth. About nine million square kilometers across North Africa — roughly the size of the USA or China. Only about a quarter is sand dunes; most is rocky plateau and gravel plain. Daytime heat can pass forty-five degrees Celsius, but nights can be near freezing; people live at oases and along the Nile. It splits Africa into North Africa and Sub-Saharan Africa; camel caravans once carried gold and salt across it.
geography/africa-asia.ce4a88abb155: Great Green Wall, Sahel. A project started in two thousand seven by African countries to plant a belt of trees and grassland about eight thousand kilometers long across the Sahel, from Senegal to Djibouti, to hold back the desert.
geography/africa-asia.2548a817ec90: Congo River. Africa’s river with the most water — and the deepest river in the world, over two hundred twenty meters. It crosses the equator twice as it arcs through the rainforest.
geography/africa-asia.f93b733fca56: Kuwait. A small, oil-rich country at the top of the Persian Gulf. Iraq invaded it in nineteen ninety; when a US-led coalition drove Iraq’s army out in nineteen ninety-one, the retreating troops set more than six hundred oil wells on fire.
geography/africa-asia.04a5ab17f8a6: Iraq. A country along the Tigris and Euphrates rivers — the land of ancient Mesopotamia. In August nineteen ninety Iraq’s army invaded Kuwait, and in nineteen ninety-one a US-led coalition drove it out in the Persian Gulf War.
geography/africa-asia.ebed60551d66: New Delhi. Capital of India. Greater Delhi has over thirty million people and is one of the world’s largest city areas.
geography/africa-asia.4778c2f1839b: China. East Asia’s giant. Third- or fourth-largest country by area; it stretches from the Himalayas and deserts in the west to the Pacific coast. About one point four billion people, mostly in the wetter east along the Yangtze, Huang He and the coast. Coal, rare earths and hydropower; the world’s largest manufacturer and exporter. Faces air pollution, river pollution and floods; leads the world in solar and wind power.

geography/americas.a7e7d72da40f: São Paulo. Brazil’s biggest city and the largest city in the Southern Hemisphere, with about twenty-two million people in its metro area.
geography/americas.4824536098ee: Cuba. Cuba won independence from Spain after the Spanish-American War of eighteen ninety-eight. In October nineteen sixty-two American spy planes found Soviet missile sites here, only ninety miles from Florida, and for thirteen days the world feared a nuclear war.
geography/americas.531e54409778: Canada. The world’s second-largest country by area. Borders the USA to the south; coasts on the Pacific, Arctic and Atlantic oceans. About ninety percent of Canadians live within about one hundred sixty kilometers, one hundred miles, of the US border, where it is warmer and the land is better for farming and trade. Mostly cold with long winters; the far north is tundra and permafrost. Oil, Alberta, timber, fish, wheat, nickel, iron, uranium, fresh water and hydroelectricity. Issues: acid rain, Great Lakes pollution and damage from mining on the Canadian Shield.
geography/americas.45cc39cbf0fe: Amazon River. The river with the most water on Earth, flowing about six thousand four hundred kilometers east to the Atlantic. Its basin holds the world’s largest rainforest.
geography/americas.f608a8d6cac1: Mexico City. Capital of Mexico, built on the old Aztec capital Tenochtitlan, two thousand two hundred forty meters up in a mountain valley. About twenty-two million people live in its metro area.
geography/americas.f3f8cadd58d3: Quebec. Samuel de Champlain founded it in sixteen oh eight on cliffs above the Saint Lawrence River, and it became the capital of New France. It is the only city north of Mexico that still has its old city walls, and most people there speak French.

geography/climate-regions.b10f56eec9cc: Dry. Very little rain all year. Can be hot or cold; big day-night swings. Less than about two hundred fifty to five hundred millimeters a year. Dry climates get less rain than the water that evaporates. Deserts are the driest; steppes, semi-arid grasslands, get a little more rain. Many deserts sit near thirty degrees latitude, where sinking air stops clouds from forming, the Sahara, Arabia, Australia. Others are dry because mountains block rain, the rain shadow, or because they are far from any ocean, the Gobi. Cacti and camels store water. People live near oases and rivers like the Nile, herd animals, and use irrigation.
geography/climate-regions.f2c09d7c3f2f: Polar. Freezing cold almost all year. Warmest month below ten degrees Celsius. Very little, mostly snow. Near the poles sunlight hits at a low, slanted angle and spreads out, so it is cold even in summer. Tundra: the ground stays frozen, permafrost; only mosses, lichens and small shrubs grow in the short summer. Ice cap: Antarctica and Greenland are buried under ice sheets up to four kilometers thick. Polar bears, seals and penguins, Antarctica only. Very few people; the Inuit traditionally hunted and fished.
geography/climate-regions.12eeb70c4a48: Highland. Climate changes with altitude. Cooler the higher you go, minus six point five degrees Celsius per one thousand meters. Varies; windward slopes are wetter. Air gets thinner and colder as you climb, so mountains are cooler than the lowlands around them. On one tall mountain you can pass through several climates, from tropical forest at the bottom to snow at the top. Mount Kilimanjaro is just south of the equator, yet it has snow and glaciers on its peak. Llamas, yaks and snow leopards. People farm on terraces and grow potatoes and barley.
geography/climate-regions.7d1f7b027754: Tropical. Hot all year, near the equator. Every month above eighteen degrees Celsius. Very wet, or a wet and dry season. Near the equator the noon sun is high in the sky all year, so it is always hot. There is no real winter. Tropical wet, rainforest: heavy rain almost every day, like the Amazon and Congo basins. Tropical wet and dry, savanna: a long rainy season and a dry season, with grasslands and scattered trees. Rainforests hold over half of all plant and animal species. People grow bananas, cocoa, rice and rubber.
geography/climate-regions.8af338e15cb7: Continental. Cold, snowy winters and warm summers. Coldest month below minus three degrees Celsius; huge yearly range. Moderate, much of it in summer. Far from the ocean’s moderating effect, land heats up fast in summer and cools down fast in winter. Winters are long, snowy and freezing. Summers can be warm or even hot. The subarctic part has huge evergreen forests called taiga. It is found almost only in the Northern Hemisphere. Wheat and corn belts, dairy farms and forestry. Houses need strong heating for winter.
geography/climate-regions.199e201f5f46: Temperate, mild. Mild winters, warm or hot summers. Coldest month about minus three to eighteen degrees Celsius. Moderate; rain in all or some seasons. Temperate climates have four seasons, but winters are mild, with only a little snow. Humid subtropical: hot, humid summers and mild winters. This is the climate of Atlanta and most of Georgia! Mediterranean: hot, dry summers and mild, rainy winters. Marine west coast, London: cool and rainy all year. Rich farmland for wheat, fruit, cotton and olives. Many of the world’s big cities are here.

geography/europe-oceania.7b0c7d3387b0: Ural Mountains. The boundary between Europe and Asia. Run about two thousand five hundred kilometers north to south through western Russia, from the Arctic toward Kazakhstan. The traditional dividing line between Europe, west, and Asia, east. Very old and worn down by erosion; the highest peak is only one thousand eight hundred ninety-five meters. Rich in iron, copper, coal and gemstones; industrial cities such as Yekaterinburg grew here.
geography/europe-oceania.8e4a4c6f382e: Russia. The largest country on Earth. About seventeen million square kilometers, spanning Europe and Asia and eleven time zones; the Ural Mountains divide the two parts. Most people live in the European part, west of the Urals, where the climate is milder. Long, very cold winters; much of Siberia is frozen permafrost. Huge reserves of oil, natural gas, timber and minerals — energy is its main export.
geography/europe-oceania.508a39370f21: Air pollution in the UK. From coal smog to traffic fumes. Britain was the first country to industrialize, burning coal in factories and homes. The Great Smog of London, December nineteen fifty-two, lasted five days and killed thousands of people. The Clean Air Act of nineteen fifty-six banned smoky fuels in cities. Today traffic exhaust is the main problem; London’s Ultra Low Emission Zone charges polluting cars.
geography/europe-oceania.80e6b4ac98b2: Black Forest. Wooded mountains in south-west Germany. In the nineteen eighties acid rain killed many of its trees, which led to cleaner power plants and cars.
geography/europe-oceania.18a5e32079c4: United Kingdom. An island nation off north-west Europe. England, Scotland and Wales, on Great Britain, plus Northern Ireland; the English Channel separates it from France. Mild and rainy all year thanks to the North Atlantic Drift and westerly winds. Birthplace of the Industrial Revolution, coal and iron; North Sea oil and gas; London is a world financial centre. Issue: air pollution — from the deadly coal smog of nineteen fifty-two to today’s traffic fumes.
geography/europe-oceania.1e599ef41213: Chernobyl. In nineteen eighty-six a reactor at the nuclear power plant here exploded, spreading radioactive dust over much of Europe. A thirty-kilometer zone around it is still closed.

geography/landforms.e95191d468a1: Memory hint: Mountains equals high, steep and peaks. On a contour map, their lines are packed tightly together.
geography/landforms.08f483fffe6c: Lake. Water surrounded by land. A lake is a body of water surrounded by land. Most lakes are fresh water. Lakes fill low places: hollows dug by glaciers, cracks in the crust, old volcano craters, or dams. A reservoir is a human-made lake behind a dam, like Lake Lanier in Georgia. Great Lakes, USA and Canada. Lake Baikal, deepest. Lake Victoria, Africa. Caspian Sea, largest, salty.
geography/landforms.503d489ee2fb: Mountains. High land with steep sides and peaks. Mountains rise steeply far above the land around them. A long chain of mountains is a mountain range. Most big ranges form where tectonic plates collide and push rock upward, the Himalayas, or where volcanoes erupt. It gets colder as you climb, so high peaks can stay snow-covered all year. Himalayas, Mount Everest, eight thousand eight hundred forty-nine meters. Andes, Rocky Mountains, Alps, Blue Ridge Mountains in north Georgia.
geography/landforms.48a25d4a3be5: Memory hint: Elevation is measured from sea level, zero meters.
geography/landforms.f7b065e160a2: Plateau. High land that is flat on top. A plateau is a large area of high, fairly flat land with at least one steep side, like a giant table, it is also called a tableland. The Tibetan Plateau averages about four thousand five hundred meters high and is nicknamed the “Roof of the World”. Rivers often cut deep canyons into plateaus, like the Colorado River in the Colorado Plateau. Tibetan Plateau, Colorado Plateau, Deccan Plateau, India, Mexican Plateau, Brazilian Highlands.
geography/landforms.78360101f043: Memory hint: delta delta equals a triangle of mud at the river’s mouth.
geography/landforms.5b4665b0a741: Canyon. A deep, narrow valley with cliff walls. A canyon, or gorge, is a very deep, narrow valley with steep, cliff-like sides. Most canyons are carved by a river cutting down through rock over millions of years, erosion. The walls show layers of rock. The deeper the layer, the older it usually is. Grand Canyon, about one point eight kilometers deep, carved by the Colorado River. Yarlung Tsangpo Grand Canyon, Tibet. Tallulah Gorge, Georgia.
geography/landforms.e2960d6f9bae: Greenland. The world’s largest island, about two point two million square kilometers, mostly buried under an ice sheet up to three kilometers thick. Only about fifty-seven thousand people live there, on the coast.
geography/landforms.f70303c70b74: Ocean and coast. The huge salty water around the continents. Oceans are the largest bodies of salt water. They cover about seventy-one percent of Earth’s surface. There are five oceans: Pacific, largest, Atlantic, Indian, Southern and Arctic. The coast is where land meets the sea. Move the sea-level slider to see how coastlines change. Pacific Ocean, Atlantic Ocean, Georgia’s coast, Indian Ocean, Mediterranean Sea, Caribbean Sea.
geography/landforms.ec02a9049560: Delta. New land built at a river’s mouth. When a river reaches the sea it slows down and drops its sediment. Over time this builds a fan- or triangle-shaped delta. The name comes from the Greek letter delta, capital delta, a triangle. Delta soil is very fertile, so deltas are crowded with farms and people, but they flood easily. Nile Delta, Ganges-Brahmaputra Delta, largest, Mississippi Delta, Yangtze River Delta, Pearl River Delta.
