geography/world-religions.316383a266f1: Judaism: by tradition, Abraham traveled from Ur to Canaan about eighteen hundred B C E. Judaism teaches belief in one God. The Torah is its holiest text.
geography/world-religions.34f2b99cc6b9: Three world religions in the textbook. Grade nine World History covers Buddhism, ancient India, Siddhartha Gautama, Christianity, first century C E, Roman-ruled Palestine, Jesus, and Islam, early seventh century C E, Arabian Peninsula, Muhammad. The textbook traditionally places the founding of Buddhism in the sixth century B C E.
geography/world-religions.28da2b476cc3: Jerusalem. Around thirty C E, Jesus was crucified in Jerusalem. Christians believe he rose from the dead there. Jerusalem was an early center of Christianity and is sacred in both Judaism and Christianity.
geography/world-religions.791d02cbbe9e: Muslims date Muhammad’s first revelation near Mecca to six hundred ten C E. The Quran and the Five Pillars guide Muslim life.
geography/world-religions.af590d133847: In twenty twenty, about three out of four people identified with a religion. This lesson explores seven traditions from Asia.
geography/world-religions.3688005cc728: Five hundred B C E. Five hundred fifty-one to four hundred seventy-nine B C E, Confucius teaches in Qufu, China.
geography/world-religions.87934e840b8d: Mecca, Islam. According to Islamic tradition, Muhammad received his first revelation near Mecca in six hundred ten C E. Mecca, with the Kaaba, is Islam’s holiest city; Muslims around the world face it to pray.
geography/world-religions.49f267af1aba: Thirty C E. Circa thirty C E, Jesus teaches in Judea: Christianity begins in Jerusalem.
geography/world-religions.6910ad3060c2: Eighteen hundred B C E. Circa eighteen hundred B C E, Abraham, by tradition, travels from Ur to Canaan: the roots of Judaism.
geography/world-religions.53cb83cc819a: Today. Colors highlight the largest religious group or a mix of local traditions in selected places, using estimates around twenty twenty. Tap a highlighted place to learn more.
geography/world-religions.1aff5c2ec946: Fifteen seventeen C E. Martin Luther’s protest in fifteen seventeen helps spark the Protestant Reformation.
geography/world-religions.c1e5026995f7: Judaism. Abraham, father of the Jewish people, by tradition; the Torah tells how Moses received God’s law. Ancient Israel and Judah, Southwest Asia. Jewish tradition traces its roots to Abraham in Canaan, circa eighteen hundred B C E, traditional date. Key texts: The Torah, first five books of the Hebrew Bible, Tanakh; the Talmud records rabbinic discussions of Jewish law and tradition. One God, who made a covenant, a special agreement, with Abraham and his descendants. Follow God’s laws, including the Ten Commandments. Keep the Sabbath: a weekly day of rest from Friday evening until Saturday nightfall
geography/world-religions.3a884cdad00c: Qufu, Confucianism. Confucius, five hundred fifty-one to four hundred seventy-nine B C E, lived and taught in Qufu, in the state of Lu, today Shandong. His followers and later generations collected his sayings in the Analects.
geography/world-religions.0d5767c0f46e: Today. Pew estimates that about three in four people identified with a religion in twenty twenty. Switch to “Today” to explore the map.
geography/world-religions.c9c8c94266f6: Seven hundred twelve C E. The Kojiki records myths connected with Shinto. The tradition is older than this text.
geography/world-religions.5f684e418e3d: One hundred C E. Over the following centuries, Hindu and Buddhist traditions spread in Southeast Asia.
geography/world-religions.4497b23a3e8b: Vedic South Asia, Hinduism. Hinduism grew from ancient traditions of the Indian subcontinent. The Vedas, its oldest sacred texts, began to take shape around fifteen hundred B C E in the northwest of the Indian subcontinent.
geography/world-religions.b33c2166a4db: Five hundred twenty-eight B C E. Traditional date for Siddhartha Gautama’s enlightenment at Bodh Gaya.
geography/world-religions.848d2b297118: One hundred B C E. Second century B C E, Han China makes Confucian learning official.
geography/world-religions.956bc943b14f: Buddhism in Han China: White Horse Temple. Buddhism reached China from the Indian subcontinent through Central Asia around the transition from the Western Han to the Eastern Han. Tradition dates the founding of Luoyang’s White Horse Temple to sixty-eight C E and tells of monks bringing sutras on a white horse.
geography/world-religions.b2a8ad499ac9: Han Chinese. Language: Chinese, Sino-Tibetan family. Where: All of China: about ninety-one percent of China’s one point four billion people, twenty twenty census. Religion: Many follow no organized religion; Buddhism, Daoism and folk traditions; Confucian family values
geography/world-religions.a7222442e0be: Hinduism has no single founder. Its oldest texts, the Vedas, began to take shape in South Asia around fifteen hundred B C E. Hindus believe in karma and samsara: the soul is reborn again and again.
geography/world-religions.92f6a97aed44: Bodh Gaya, Buddhism. Here, by tradition, Siddhartha Gautama sat under a tree until he reached enlightenment and became the Buddha, sixth or fifth century B C E. He went on to teach in the Ganges plain.
geography/world-religions.d74641dccdcf: Six hundred ten C E. Islamic tradition dates Muhammad’s first revelation near Mecca to this year.
geography/world-religions.0ea293f8ee94: On a timeline, B C E years count down toward year one, and C E years count up. There is no year zero.
geography/world-religions.f63f79fd154f: Two thousand B C E. The story begins in Mesopotamia and Canaan…
geography/world-religions.0eadf0ed13ff: Ise, Shinto. Shinto grew out of ancient Japanese practices. The map uses seven hundred twelve C E because the Kojiki, an early written source for its myths, dates to that year. Ise Grand Shrine honors the sun goddess Amaterasu.
geography/world-religions.53c2c2fa89c6: Three hundred seventy-two C E. Three hundred seventy-two, Goguryeo establishes an academy. Three hundred eighty, The Roman Empire makes Nicene Christianity its official faith.
geography/world-religions.56eb63a274a0: One thousand B C E. According to biblical tradition, King David makes Jerusalem his capital around this time. The First Temple follows.
geography/world-religions.0b36fec7592f: Christianity grew out of the teachings of Jesus in the first century C E. Christians believe he is the Son of God. His followers spread those teachings as far as Rome.
geography/world-religions.b28add70315b: Fifteen hundred B C E. Circa fifteen hundred B C E, The earliest Vedic texts begin taking shape in the northwestern Indian subcontinent.
geography/world-religions.cbb79d86c3f2: Xuanzang travels west. The Tang monk Xuanzang traveled to India and studied at Nalanda. He returned to Chang’an in six hundred forty-five with hundreds of Buddhist texts. The Great Tang Records on the Western Regions, compiled from his account, describes the places he visited or learned about. Xi’an’s Big Wild Goose Pagoda was built to house Buddhist texts and other items from his journey.
geography/world-religions.f89d0064acd5: Two hundred fifty B C E. Around this time, Buddhist teachings reach Sri Lanka, according to local tradition.
geography/world-religions.f6359339b6bd: One thousand C E. One thousand to ten ninety-nine, Theravada Buddhism spreads in Myanmar, Thailand and Cambodia.
geography/world-religions.f9a0f1f62374: Christianity. Jesus of Nazareth, circa four B C E to circa thirty C E, a Jewish teacher; his followers, apostles such as Peter and Paul, spread his message. Circa thirty C E, The movement began among Jesus’s followers in Roman-ruled Southwest Asia, especially in Jerusalem. Key texts: The Bible: the Old Testament shares books with the Hebrew Bible. The New Testament includes accounts of Jesus’s life and teachings and other early Christian writings. Christians believe in one God. Most understand God as the Trinity: Father, Son and Holy Spirit. Jesus is the Son of God and the savior; he died on a cross and rose from the dead. Love God, and love your neighbor as yourself

georgia/ga-20th.d6c6922ec6ce: Bell Bomber plant, Marietta. Built B twenty-nine Superfortress bombers. Bell Aircraft built B twenty-nine bombers here. At its peak about twenty-eight thousand Georgians worked at the plant — many of them women. Marietta grew from eight thousand six hundred sixty-seven people in nineteen forty to twenty thousand six hundred eighty-seven by the end of the decade. Lockheed builds planes on the site today.
georgia/ga-20th.ab7ba678d143: Brunswick shipyard. J. A. Jones: ninety-nine ships in about two years. The J. A. Jones shipyard in Brunswick built ninety-nine Liberty ships in about two years. Workers poured in from farms, and the town boomed.
georgia/ga-20th.82c50718363e: Camp Gordon, Chamblee. Training ground of the eighty-second “All-American” Division. Opened in July nineteen seventeen northeast of Atlanta. It trained the eighty-second “All-American” Division — almost half of it Georgians. Today the site is an airport, DeKalb-Peachtree.
georgia/ga-20th.540e0c037f0e: Souther Field, Americus. Almost two thousand military pilots trained here. A World War One flight school northeast of Americus. It trained almost two thousand military pilots.
georgia/ga-20th.d33cc2d8a3ff: Thomasville. Where the boll weevil was first found in Georgia. The boll weevil crossed from Mexico into Texas in the eighteen nineties and spread east. It was first found in Georgia at Thomasville in nineteen fifteen. Georgia’s crop fell from about two point eight million bales, nineteen fourteen, to about six hundred thousand, nineteen twenty-three.
georgia/ga-20th.de53a7982af2: Camp Wheeler, Macon. Home of the thirty-first “Dixie” Division. The thirty-first “Dixie” Division trained here; more than twelve thousand Georgians served in it. The camp reopened for training in World War Two.
georgia/ga-20th.ba84bdff6d57: Techwood Homes, Atlanta. The first federal public housing project in the US. Built with New Deal money near Georgia Tech; FDR dedicated it in nineteen thirty-five and families moved in in nineteen thirty-six. It replaced crowded slums with brick apartments — but was for white families only; University Homes nearby was built for Black families.
georgia/ga-20th.3789ce2e524f: Warm Springs. Where FDR swam, planned and died. FDR first came in nineteen twenty-four, hoping the eighty-eight degrees Fahrenheit spring water would help his polio. He built the Little White House in nineteen thirty-two. He died here on April twelfth, nineteen forty-five, while an artist was painting the “Unfinished Portrait.”
georgia/ga-20th.c74b6810b405: Savannah shipyard. Southeastern Shipbuilding: eighty-eight ships. Southeastern Shipbuilding near Savannah built eighty-eight ships. It employed more than fifteen thousand people. Liberty ships carried food, fuel and weapons across the oceans to the Allies.
georgia/ga-20th.303d14460a0d: Don't mix up: In nineteen eighteen disease was as big a danger as the enemy: the flu swept through crowded training camps.
georgia/ga-20th.7999225e9ac1: Athens, UGA. About two thousand Navy combat pilots trained here. The US Navy trained about two thousand combat pilots at the University of Georgia. Colleges across the state helped train soldiers and sailors.
georgia/ga-20th.4eb4fb1da534: Camp Hancock, Augusta. Infantry camp and one of the Army’s first airfields. Home of the twenty-eighth “Keystone” Division. It was the Army’s second military airfield. In October nineteen eighteen the flu hit hard: about three thousand cases and the camp was quarantined.
georgia/ga-20th.1768089222fb: Fort Benning, Columbus. The world’s largest infantry school in World War Two. Founded as Camp Benning in nineteen eighteen. In World War Two it was the largest infantry training school in the world; paratroopers trained here too. Renamed Fort Moore in twenty twenty-three, it became Fort Benning again in twenty twenty-five — base names can change!

georgia/ga-civilrights.a472c31a5e5a: Athens. Hunter and Holmes open UGA, January nineteen sixty-one. In January nineteen sixty-one a federal judge ordered the University of Georgia to admit Charlayne Hunter and Hamilton Holmes, its first Black students. Governor Ernest Vandiver ordered the university closed, but a federal judge reversed that the next day. On January eighteenth, nineteen sixty-one, Vandiver gave up “massive resistance” and backed the Sibley Commission’s plan; the legislature passed it on January thirty-first. Hunter became a famous journalist; Holmes became a doctor.
georgia/ga-civilrights.a8030345f19d: Don't mix up: UGA was desegregated in January nineteen sixty-one; Atlanta’s public schools followed in August nineteen sixty-one.
georgia/ga-civilrights.fe62adf71c01: Savannah. Desegregation before the federal law. NAACP leader W. W. Law led protests and boycotts in Savannah. City leaders agreed to desegregate public and private facilities from October first, nineteen sixty-three. That was about eight months before the federal Civil Rights Act of nineteen sixty-four.
georgia/ga-civilrights.2e79c12e12ce: Don't mix up: Savannah’s agreement was local; the Civil Rights Act of nineteen sixty-four made desegregation national law.
georgia/ga-civilrights.c41688e98432: Atlanta. Auburn Avenue, SCLC, SNCC — and “too busy to hate”. Martin Luther King Jr. was born at five oh one Auburn Avenue in nineteen twenty-nine and preached at Ebenezer Baptist Church with his father. The SCLC was founded here in nineteen fifty-seven; SNCC made Atlanta its headquarters in October nineteen sixty. College students began the Atlanta Student Movement in nineteen sixty with “An Appeal for Human Rights” and lunch-counter sit-ins. Atlanta’s public schools began to desegregate peacefully on August thirtieth, nineteen sixty-one. Mayor Ivan Allen Jr. testified for the civil rights bill in Congress in nineteen sixty-three — rare for a white Southern mayor.
georgia/ga-civilrights.a8233cc7f1d2: Columbus. One voter’s lawsuit opens the ballot box. Dr. Thomas Brewer recruited Primus King to try to vote in the July fourth, nineteen forty-four, Democratic primary. King was turned away. His lawsuit, King versus Chapman, struck down Georgia’s whites-only primary in nineteen forty-five; the ruling was upheld in nineteen forty-six. In one-party Georgia the Democratic primary decided who won, so this opened real voting power. Black voter registration jumped to about one hundred twenty-five thousand within months.
georgia/ga-civilrights.ed6198e7f04a: Albany. A whole community against segregation. SNCC field secretaries Charles Sherrod and Cordell Reagon came to register voters in nineteen sixty-one. In mid-November nineteen sixty-one local groups united as the Albany Movement, with Dr. William G. Anderson as president. More than one thousand people were jailed; Martin Luther King Jr. was arrested here in December nineteen sixty-one and jailed again in nineteen sixty-two. Bernice Johnson Reagon and the SNCC Freedom Singers carried Albany’s freedom songs across the country.
georgia/ga-civilrights.27e3a6c41ef0: Americus. Young protesters face harsh charges. In nineteen sixty-three student leaders in Americus were charged with “insurrection,” a crime that could carry the death penalty. They were later released — the case showed how far some officials would go to stop protests.
georgia/ga-civilrights.02113b476db8: Don’t mix up: The white primary ended in nineteen forty-six, but the county unit system still kept city voters weak until nineteen sixty-two.

georgia/ga-civilwar.782b29b8c57f: Milledgeville. Secession — and a mock repeal. The secession convention met here in January eighteen sixty-one and voted two hundred eight to eighty-nine to leave the Union. On November twenty-third, eighteen sixty-four, Sherman’s left wing took the capital; Union officers held a mock session in the statehouse and “repealed” secession.
georgia/ga-civilwar.dcda68146128: Fort Pulaski. The blockade tightens. A brick fort guarding the mouth of the Savannah River, with brick walls about seven and a half feet thick. Union rifled cannon on Tybee Island, one to two miles away, broke through the walls in about thirty hours. After it fell, Savannah was almost closed to blockade runners for the rest of the war.
georgia/ga-civilwar.483f43cfaa53: Fort McAllister. The door to the sea opens. An earthwork fort guarding the Ogeechee River south of Savannah. Union troops stormed it in about fifteen minutes, opening contact with the Union navy and its supplies.
georgia/ga-civilwar.2f435feea003: Dalton and Resaca. The Atlanta Campaign begins. Sherman’s roughly one hundred thousand men faced Joseph E. Johnston’s roughly sixty thousand near Dalton. Instead of attacking head-on, Sherman kept swinging around Johnston’s flank, forcing him to retreat south. Both armies followed the Western and Atlantic Railroad — the lifeline to Atlanta.
georgia/ga-civilwar.39a00b63a2e8: Savannah. A “Christmas gift” for Lincoln. Confederate troops left Savannah, and Sherman’s army marched in without a battle. Thousands of freedom seekers had followed the army across Georgia. In January eighteen sixty-five Sherman issued Field Order Number fifteen, setting aside coastal land for freed families.
georgia/ga-civilwar.a25148228b67: Atlanta. Its fall helped re-elect Lincoln. In July eighteen sixty-four John Bell Hood replaced Johnston and attacked at Peachtree Creek, July twentieth, and the Battle of Atlanta, July twenty-second. After Sherman cut the last railroad at Jonesboro, Hood left the city; Union troops entered on September second, eighteen sixty-four. Sherman wired Washington: “Atlanta is ours, and fairly won.” The good news helped Lincoln win the November election. In November Sherman’s troops burned the city’s railroads, depots and factories before marching east.
georgia/ga-civilwar.31faae48679c: Andersonville. The deadliest prison camp of the war. Built in Sumter County, far from the fighting, to hold Union prisoners. About forty-five thousand men were held here; nearly thirteen thousand died, mostly of disease, poor food, bad water and exposure. The camp commander, Henry Wirz, was tried and executed after the war. Today it is home to the National Prisoner of War Museum, honoring all American POWs.
georgia/ga-civilwar.e674c68835d9: Harpers Ferry. Today: Harpers Ferry, West Virginia. In October eighteen fifty-nine John Brown and twenty-one men seized the US arsenal here, hoping to arm enslaved people for an uprising. Marines captured him in the small brick fire-engine house now called “John Brown’s Fort”, which still stands where the Potomac and Shenandoah rivers meet.
georgia/ga-civilwar.e8b286b9263d: Chickamauga. The largest battle in Georgia. Confederate General Braxton Bragg attacked Union General William Rosecrans along Chickamauga Creek. A gap in the Union line let Confederates break through on September twentieth; General George Thomas held firm and became the “Rock of Chickamauga.” About thirty-four thousand six hundred total casualties — second only to Gettysburg. A Confederate victory, but the Union kept Chattanooga, the gateway to Georgia.
georgia/ga-civilwar.12f1e7c96a35: Memory hint: eighteen sixty-three Chickamauga, C-side wins, eighteen sixty-four Atlanta falls, September, March to the Sea, November to December, Savannah, a Christmas gift.
georgia/ga-civilwar.e795f2d9a58c: Kennesaw Mountain. Sherman’s one big frontal attack. Confederates dug in on the mountain. Sherman attacked head-on and lost about three thousand men to about one thousand Confederates. He went back to flanking moves, and Johnston retreated again. Nearby Big Shanty, today’s Kennesaw, is where Union raiders stole the locomotive “General” in the Great Locomotive Chase, April eighteen sixty-two.

georgia/ga-colony.d3341d06275c: Upriver at the Fall Line. High, healthy ground — but more than one hundred miles upriver. Big ships can’t get there, so every supply would take weeks.
georgia/ga-colony.83c5e56b7ef2: Yamacraw Bluff. A bluff about forty feet high on the Savannah River, about eighteen miles from the ocean: ships can sail up, the high ground is dry and easy to defend, and Tomochichi’s Yamacraw and Mary Musgrove’s trading post are next door.

georgia/ga-geography.4ad467ffcbaa: Brasstown Bald. Four thousand seven hundred eighty-four feet, one thousand four hundred fifty-eight meters — the roof of Georgia. On a clear day you can see four states from the tower on top: Georgia, Tennessee, North Carolina and South Carolina.
georgia/ga-geography.bf5c448140b6: Don’t mix up: Atlanta is in the Piedmont, not in the mountains — it is about one thousand fifty feet high, but on rolling hills.
georgia/ga-geography.6043985121e4: Blue Ridge. Georgia’s tallest mountains. Location: the northeast corner. Brasstown Bald, four thousand seven hundred eighty-four feet or one thousand four hundred fifty-eight meters, is the highest point in Georgia; the Appalachian Trail starts at Springer Mountain. Climate: the coolest region, with some snow in winter and the most rain in the state — up to about seventy to eighty inches a year. Agriculture: apples, Ellijay. Cattle, poultry and hardwood forests on steep slopes. Economy: tourism, hiking, rafting, Tallulah Gorge. Timber — and the eighteen twenty-nine gold rush at Dahlonega.
georgia/ga-geography.d3ffe896aa78: Chattahoochee River. Atlanta’s water supply and part of the Alabama border. About four hundred thirty miles from the Blue Ridge to the Florida line. Lake Lanier stores its water for metro Atlanta; Columbus grew at its Fall Line falls; it forms much of the Georgia-Alabama border.
georgia/ga-geography.7026479d7d66: Savannah River. The border with South Carolina. About three hundred miles long, it forms the Georgia-South Carolina border. Augusta grew at its Fall Line; Savannah, near its mouth, became Georgia’s first city and today a giant port.
georgia/ga-geography.7bfdfb8a6f54: Piedmont. Rolling hills and red clay. Location: from the mountains down to the Fall Line — about a third of Georgia. “Piedmont” means “foot of the mountains.” Climate: hot summers, mild winters, about fifty inches of rain. Rolling hills of red clay, colored by iron, and granite such as Stone Mountain. Agriculture: poultry, Gainesville calls itself the “Poultry Capital of the World”, cattle, dairy, timber; it was cotton country in the eighteen hundreds. Economy: the most people and jobs — Atlanta, Athens and the busy Hartsfield-Jackson airport; business, transportation, government and universities.
georgia/ga-geography.9340b8623abf: Tallulah Gorge. A gorge almost one thousand feet deep. The Tallulah River cut this gorge about two miles long. In nineteen seventy Karl Wallenda walked across it on a tightrope.
georgia/ga-geography.a3fc81d1674b: Valley and Ridge. Ridges and fertile valleys side by side. Location: the northwest, between the Appalachian Plateau and the Blue Ridge. Long ridges such as Taylor Ridge run southwest to northeast with valleys between. Climate: mild — cooler than the south, with about fifty to fifty-five inches of rain. Agriculture: grain, hay, cattle, poultry and dairy in the limestone valleys. Economy: manufacturing — Dalton is called the “Carpet Capital of the World”; Rome grew where two rivers meet to form the Coosa.
georgia/ga-geography.682c0701484e: Appalachian Mountains, Springer Mountain. The southern end of a one thousand five hundred-mile mountain chain. The Appalachians cover the Blue Ridge, Valley and Ridge and Appalachian Plateau. Mountains block easy travel, so north Georgia was settled later — and its rain feeds rivers for the whole state.
georgia/ga-geography.a7879c0d8634: Stone Mountain. A huge granite dome. This granite dome rises about eight hundred twenty-five feet above the land around it, summit one thousand six hundred eighty-six feet. Granite is a big Piedmont resource — Elberton calls itself the “Granite Capital of the World.”

georgia/ga-government.b9e5c71e3f30: The Governor. Carries out and enforces the laws. Governor: at least thirty, a US citizen for fifteen years and a Georgia resident for six years. A four-year term, at most two terms in a row. The lieutenant governor has the same qualifications, presides over the Senate and becomes governor if the office is empty. The governor writes the budget proposal, sets the revenue estimate, signs or vetoes bills and can veto single spending items. Other statewide elected officers include the secretary of state, attorney general, state school superintendent and agriculture commissioner. State agencies do the daily work: Department of Education, Department of Transportation, GDOT, Department of Driver Services, your license, Department of Natural Resources, state parks, Department of Juvenile Justice.
georgia/ga-government.22c69b29c466: General Assembly. Makes the laws and passes the budget. Two chambers: the Senate, fifty-six senators, and the House of Representatives, one hundred eighty representatives. All serve two-year terms. Qualifications: senators at least twenty-five, representatives at least twenty-one; US citizens; Georgia residents for two years and district residents for one year. Meets every year from the second Monday in January for forty legislative days — usually into late March or early April. Leaders: the lieutenant governor presides over the Senate; the House elects its own Speaker. Committees, Education, Appropriations, Judiciary…, study every bill first — most bills never leave committee. Spending and tax bills must start in the House.
georgia/ga-government.6d819ca357a1: The Courts. Interprets the laws and administers justice. Supreme Court: nine justices — the highest court; it decides questions about the constitution and reviews the most serious cases. Court of Appeals: fifteen judges who check trial courts for legal mistakes. Trial courts: superior, felonies, divorce, land. State. Juvenile. Probate, wills, marriage licenses. And magistrate, warrants, small claims. Judges are chosen in nonpartisan elections — no party label on the ballot. When a seat opens early, the governor appoints a judge. Dual purpose: interpret what the laws mean, and administer justice by deciding cases fairly.

georgia/ga-modern.8ac36d54264b: Film studios, Fayetteville. Sound stages south of Atlanta. In two thousand eight Georgia began offering film and TV companies a tax credit of up to thirty percent of what they spend in the state. Big studio campuses grew up around Atlanta, such as Trilith Studios in Fayetteville and Tyler Perry Studios on the old Fort McPherson army base. Direct spending hit a record of about four point four billion dollars in fiscal twenty twenty-two, then fell to two point six billion dollars in fiscal twenty twenty-four after Hollywood strikes.
georgia/ga-modern.f0f191b5e812: Port of Brunswick. America’s busiest port for autos and heavy machinery. Ships here are “roll-on and roll-off”: cars, tractors and bulldozers drive on and off. In twenty twenty-four and again in twenty twenty-five the Georgia Ports Authority reported Brunswick as the nation’s busiest port for autos and heavy equipment. Twenty twenty-five: about seven hundred seventy-nine thousand autos plus more than fifty-three thousand units of heavy machinery.
georgia/ga-modern.42924533ff56: Downtown Atlanta. Where the nineteen ninety-six Games and two mayors reshaped a city. Maynard Jackson, mayor from nineteen seventy-four, and Andrew Young, nineteen eighty-two to nineteen ninety, helped turn Atlanta into an international city. Centennial Olympic Park, built for nineteen ninety-six on run-down land, is now ringed by attractions such as the Georgia Aquarium, the World of Coca-Cola and the National Center for Civil and Human Rights — tourism in action. The Carter Center, founded by Jimmy and Rosalynn Carter in nineteen eighty-two, is a few miles east.
georgia/ga-modern.90888e896095: Plains. A town of only a few hundred people that produced a president. Carter was born here on October first, nineteen twenty-four, and farmed peanuts after leaving the Navy. He died at home in Plains on December twenty-ninth, twenty twenty-four, aged one hundred — the longest-lived US president. Jimmy Carter National Historical Park preserves his boyhood farm, school and campaign depot.
georgia/ga-modern.d00f1f31c7e3: Don’t mix up: Carter served one term as president, nineteen seventy-seven to nineteen eighty-one, but more than forty years as a past president.
georgia/ga-modern.306654ee7a35: Don’t mix up: Jackson’s name was added in two thousand three, after he died — not when the airport opened.
georgia/ga-modern.0aefd921dd50: Hartsfield-Jackson Airport. A gateway that puts most Americans within a short flight. William Hartsfield started the airport on an old racetrack in nineteen twenty-five. It has been the world’s busiest passenger airport since nineteen ninety-eight, seventy-three point five million travelers that year — except in twenty twenty, when a Chinese airport passed it during COVID nineteen. Record: about one hundred ten point five million passengers in twenty nineteen; one hundred eight point one million in twenty twenty-four. Five runways; a four hundred-foot control tower, two thousand six.
georgia/ga-modern.02aa89c93731: Don’t mix up: TEU counts twenty-foot box units, not ships or tons.
georgia/ga-modern.731d3e4a8fe9: West Point. Kia’s first US assembly plant. Kia’s plant on the Alabama line started building cars in two thousand nine. Factories like this bring suppliers too — parts makers set up nearby in Georgia and Alabama. Cars made here can leave by rail and truck, and some are shipped from Georgia’s ports.
georgia/ga-modern.91c09361478f: Port of Savannah. Georgia’s doorway to world trade. Garden City Terminal handles containers — standard steel boxes measured in TEU, one twenty-foot box equals one TEU. The channel was deepened from forty-two to forty-seven feet, twenty fifteen to twenty twenty-two, so bigger ships can come in more fully loaded. Fiscal twenty twenty-one: five point three million TEU — the first Southeast or Gulf port over five million. Record: five point seven six million in fiscal twenty twenty-two.
georgia/ga-modern.28ee4043ee62: Ellabell, Bryan County. Hyundai Motor Group Metaplant America. Hyundai began full production of electric cars here in October twenty twenty-four; the grand opening was in March twenty twenty-five. The company aims for about eight thousand five hundred jobs at the plant by twenty thirty-one, plus thousands more at suppliers. It sits close to the Port of Savannah — handy for parts coming in and cars going out.

georgia/ga-native.287fdc2db913: Sapelo Island shell rings. Huge rings of oyster and clam shells, some about three hundred feet across, built roughly four thousand years ago. Archaeologists think people gathered here for feasts — and maybe lived around the rings.
georgia/ga-native.4d67616d69e8: Stallings Island, near Augusta. A small island in the Savannah River covered with shells left by Archaic people. Pottery made here about four thousand five hundred years ago, tempered with Spanish moss or palmetto fibers, is among the oldest in North America.
georgia/ga-native.8741ec7063ee: Etowah Mounds, Cartersville. A fifty-four-acre town with six mounds, a plaza and a defensive ditch and palisade; several thousand people lived here. The sixty-three-foot mound probably held the chief’s or priest’s house. Famous finds include a pair of painted marble statues and copper plates showing bird-like dancers. Many historians think this was Itaba, a town de Soto passed in August fifteen forty.
georgia/ga-native.4f79774289d1: Yamacraw, Savannah. A small Creek band led by Tomochichi lived on Yamacraw Bluff. In seventeen thirty-three Tomochichi agreed to let Oglethorpe’s colonists settle here — the founding of Savannah.
georgia/ga-native.bf2cfe91aad9: Santa Catalina de Guale, Saint Catherines Island. The chief Spanish mission among the Guale people on the Georgia coast. Burned in the Guale revolt of fifteen ninety-seven, rebuilt by Franciscans in sixteen oh five, abandoned after raids in sixteen eighty. Archaeologists rediscovered the lost mission in the nineteen eighties.
georgia/ga-native.200c8e9cec92: Ichisi, near Macon. De Soto’s army reached the chiefdom of Ichisi in late March fifteen forty; its center is thought to be the Lamar mound site at Macon. From here he pushed northeast to Ocute on the Oconee River.
georgia/ga-native.3c89d378d78b: Kolomoki Mounds. Georgia State Parks calls it the oldest and largest Woodland site in the southeastern US. Mound A is fifty-seven feet high — the largest Woodland platform mound in eastern North America. Smaller burial mounds held people buried with pottery and other offerings.
georgia/ga-native.8b397bb63c28: Rock Eagle effigy mound. A giant bird shape made of white quartz rocks: about one hundred two feet from head to tail and one hundred twenty feet from wingtip to wingtip. No one knows exactly when or why it was built — it is best seen from the tower beside it.
georgia/ga-native.33cbb6b18aa7: Coosa, Little Egypt site. The main town of Coosa, a chiefdom whose power stretched hundreds of miles into Tennessee and Alabama. De Soto arrived on July sixteenth, fifteen forty, and took the chief hostage to force help. The site now lies under Carters Lake.
georgia/ga-native.4394eda199fc: Ocmulgee Mounds, Macon. A Clovis point found here shows Paleo hunters passed through more than twelve thousand years ago. About A D nine hundred Mississippian farmers built a town here; the Great Temple Mound stands fifty-five feet tall. The Earth Lodge, a round council chamber, has an original floor radiocarbon-dated to about A D ten fifteen — with seats for about fifty people.

georgia/ga-reconstruction.51e7e7bea994: Milledgeville. Where Georgia undid secession. October eighteen sixty-five: a convention here repealed secession, abolished slavery and refused to pay the Confederate debt — Johnson’s conditions. December eighteen sixty-five: the legislature ratified the thirteenth Amendment. The state prison here held Leo Frank in nineteen fifteen before a mob took him away.
georgia/ga-reconstruction.d592f0127922: Atlanta. Railroad hub, “capital of the New South”. The eighteen sixty-seven to eighteen sixty-eight convention met here and moved the capital from Milledgeville to Atlanta. Home of the International Cotton Exposition, eighteen eighty-one, and the Cotton States Exposition, eighteen ninety-five. Black colleges grew here: Atlanta University, Morehouse, Spelman, Clark. W. E. B. Du Bois taught at Atlanta University, eighteen ninety-seven to nineteen ten. Site of the nineteen oh six race massacre and the nineteen thirteen Leo Frank trial.
georgia/ga-reconstruction.2045bf292e21: Macon. A minister turned lawmaker. Henry McNeal Turner, an AME church minister and former Union Army chaplain, organized Black voters across Georgia and was elected to the legislature from Bibb County, Macon, in eighteen sixty-eight. When Black members were expelled in September eighteen sixty-eight, Turner gave a fiery speech defending their right to serve. He later became a bishop and argued that Black Americans might find freedom only by leaving the US.
georgia/ga-reconstruction.0a9fd557e81d: Memory hint: nineteen thirteen trial, nineteen fifteen commutation, nineteen fifteen lynching, nineteen eighty-six pardon.
georgia/ga-reconstruction.e3ce91ee4484: Memory hint: Atlanta rose from the ashes: rails. Capital, eighteen sixty-eight. Expositions, eighteen eighty-one, eighteen ninety-five.
georgia/ga-reconstruction.6c802ccffe2e: Don’t mix up: The eighteen eighty-one exposition was the International Cotton Exposition; Booker T. Washington spoke at the eighteen ninety-five Cotton States Exposition.
georgia/ga-reconstruction.559f2c57cd37: Camilla. The eighteen sixty-eight Camilla massacre. September eighteen sixty-eight: Black and white Republicans marched to a political rally in Camilla. Armed white men fired on the marchers; about a dozen Black people were killed. Violence like this — and Klan threats — kept many Black voters away from the polls that November.
georgia/ga-reconstruction.00ec72141133: Don’t mix up: The nineteen eighty-six pardon did not rule on guilt; it said Georgia failed to protect Frank and give him justice.
georgia/ga-reconstruction.bbad1042c951: Savannah. “Forty acres” — promised, then taken back. January eighteen sixty-five: after meeting Black ministers in Savannah, General Sherman issued Field Order Number fifteen, setting aside coastal land in plots of up to forty acres for freed families. About forty thousand people settled on that land — but President Johnson returned most of it to the former owners later in eighteen sixty-five. Savannah stayed Georgia’s main cotton port in the New South years.
georgia/ga-reconstruction.e7d2dbdbd7bb: Marietta. Antisemitism and mob violence. Mary Phagan, the thirteen-year-old murder victim, was from Marietta. In August nineteen fifteen a mob took Leo Frank from the Milledgeville prison and lynched him near Marietta. Months later the Ku Klux Klan was refounded on nearby Stone Mountain; Jewish Georgians felt the danger for years.
georgia/ga-reconstruction.76286e4e0739: Darien, McIntosh County. Black political power on the coast. Tunis Campbell, a Freedmen’s Bureau agent from New Jersey, organized freedpeople on the coast and was elected state senator in eighteen sixty-eight. He was one of the Black legislators expelled in eighteen sixty-eight and reseated in eighteen seventy. Opponents later had him jailed and sentenced to hard labor — a sign of how hard Black leaders were pushed out.
georgia/ga-reconstruction.7840e15beab9: Thomson. Voice of the Populists. Tom Watson, a lawyer from Thomson, led Georgia’s Populist Party in the eighteen nineties for struggling farmers. In Congress he pushed for Rural Free Delivery: mail carried to farm families’ doors for free. After his political defeats he turned against Black and Jewish Americans, and his newspapers stirred hatred during the Leo Frank case.

georgia/ga-removal.2e1edfb834ac: June to September eighteen thirty-eight. Camps near Fort Cass, Charleston, Tennessee. Families wait through a hot, dry summer in crowded camps, and disease spreads. John Ross wins permission for the Cherokee to manage their own removal, so most groups wait until fall to leave. A few groups go by river in June, blue dashed line.
georgia/ga-removal.25962b73fcc5: Indian Springs, eighteen twenty-five. Washington, eighteen twenty-six to eighteen twenty-seven. In eighteen twenty-five William McIntosh signed away the last Creek land in Georgia; Creek law enforcers executed him. The eighteen twenty-six Treaty of Washington replaced his treaty, and a final eighteen twenty-seven agreement took the last strip. Given out in the eighteen twenty-seven lottery. No Creek land was left in Georgia.
georgia/ga-removal.6ccc0243523e: October eighteen thirty-eight. Nashville, Tennessee. About a dozen groups of roughly one thousand people each set out on the northern route, with wagons, on horseback and on foot.
georgia/ga-removal.1962f603b59f: Treaty of the Creek Agency, eighteen eighteen. The Creek ceded land near the heads of the Ocmulgee and Apalachee rivers. It became Gwinnett and Walton counties. Given out in the eighteen twenty lottery.
georgia/ga-removal.ed6193ae1bc9: Cherokee treaties of eighteen seventeen and eighteen nineteen. The Cherokee ceded land in the northeast mountains. It became Habersham, Hall and Rabun counties. Given out in the eighteen twenty lottery.
georgia/ga-removal.c52b89dc2c2b: January to March eighteen thirty-nine. Indian Territory, Tahlequah, Oklahoma. The last groups arrive in March eighteen thirty-nine. The Cherokee begin rebuilding their nation, with Tahlequah as its capital.
georgia/ga-removal.3fa92aed3590: First Treaty of Indian Springs, eighteen twenty-one. The Creek ceded land between the Ocmulgee and Flint rivers. It included the place where Atlanta would later grow. Given out in the eighteen twenty-one lottery.
georgia/ga-removal.ceb7341bccbc: January to February eighteen thirty-nine. Springfield, Missouri. The groups push west across the Missouri Ozarks in the middle of winter.
georgia/ga-removal.73c69d69a5b2: December eighteen thirty-eight to January eighteen thirty-nine. The Mississippi River crossing. Ice on the Mississippi stops the crossing. Thousands wait for weeks in freezing weather in southern Illinois, and many die.
georgia/ga-removal.2fb3a235c393: May eighteen thirty-eight. New Echota, Georgia, Fort Wool. Soldiers go from farm to farm gathering Cherokee families, often with no time to pack. Families are held in stockades such as Fort Wool, here at the former Cherokee capital.
georgia/ga-removal.313ebc0f5692: Treaties of Augusta, seventeen eighty-three. New York, seventeen ninety. In seventeen eighty-three a few Creek leaders signed away land up to the Oconee River; most Creek rejected it and years of fighting followed. In seventeen ninety Creek leader Alexander McGillivray accepted the Oconee line in the Treaty of New York. The Cherokee also gave up land in the northeast in seventeen eighty-three, Franklin County. Georgia gave this land out as headrights.
georgia/ga-removal.19b528aaddd9: Treaty of Fort Jackson, eighteen fourteen. After the Creek War, eighteen thirteen to eighteen fourteen, General Andrew Jackson forced the Creek Nation to give up about twenty-three million acres in Alabama and south Georgia. Even Creek who had fought on the US side lost land. Georgia gave the land out in the eighteen twenty lottery.
georgia/ga-removal.d6b75cfc1326: November eighteen thirty-eight. Hopkinsville, Kentucky. Cherokee leaders White Path and Fly Smith died near here. A park marks their graves today.
georgia/ga-removal.03fdea10df1f: Late eighteen thirty-eight. Golconda, Illinois — the Ohio River. The groups cross the Ohio River by ferry.
georgia/ga-removal.4c6f4923b271: Treaties of Fort Wilkinson, eighteen oh two, and Washington, eighteen oh five. The Creek ceded land between the Oconee and Ocmulgee rivers. Georgia gave it out in its first land lottery, eighteen oh five. Milledgeville, the next capital, was laid out here in eighteen oh three.
georgia/ga-removal.3b2049571118: Treaty of Augusta, seventeen sixty-three. After the French and Indian War, Creek and Cherokee leaders met British officials at Augusta. They ceded land between the Savannah and Ogeechee rivers and a coastal strip south to the Saint Marys River. Settlers poured into the new backcountry.
georgia/ga-removal.604ac8f124fc: Treaty of Augusta, seventeen seventy-three, “New Purchase”. Cherokee and Creek leaders gave up about two million acres north of the Little River. The land paid off debts that Native hunters owed to British traders. It became Wilkes County — the Kettle Creek country of the Revolution.
georgia/ga-removal.cda2604b8c09: Treaty of New Echota, eighteen thirty-five. Georgia surveyed the Cherokee Nation and gave it away in the eighteen thirty-two land and gold lotteries — while Cherokee families still lived there. In eighteen thirty-five a small “Treaty Party” signed it away without the consent of the elected Cherokee government. In eighteen thirty-eight the US Army forced the Cherokee out: the Trail of Tears.
georgia/ga-removal.2f4be526347c: Agreement with Tomochichi and the Lower Creek, seventeen thirty-three. Tomochichi, leader of the Yamacraw, welcomed James Oglethorpe at Yamacraw Bluff. Lower Creek leaders agreed to English settlement on the coast between the Savannah and Altamaha rivers. The Trustees, and later the King, granted this land to colonists.

georgia/ga-revolution.57d9256d7683: Athens. The first state-chartered public university. The legislature chartered the University of Georgia on January twenty-seventh, seventeen eighty-five. Abraham Baldwin, who wrote the charter, was its first president. Classes began in eighteen oh one at Franklin College on six hundred thirty-three acres given by John Milledge. The town was named Athens after the ancient Greek center of learning.
georgia/ga-revolution.7f561de4c06a: Brier Creek. A Patriot defeat after Kettle Creek. Just weeks after Kettle Creek, British troops surprised a Patriot army camped at Brier Creek. Hundreds of Patriots were killed, captured or drowned trying to escape across the creek and swamps. The defeat let the British keep their hold on most of Georgia through seventeen seventy-nine.
georgia/ga-revolution.7ea727d69214: Kettle Creek. Georgia’s great Patriot victory. About seven hundred Loyalists under Colonel John Boyd were marching to join the British at Augusta. About four hundred Patriot militia under Andrew Pickens, John Dooly and Elijah Clarke surprised their camp in Wilkes County. Boyd was mortally wounded; casualties were about twenty-one Patriots and one hundred fifteen Loyalists, estimates. Austin Dabney, a free Black artilleryman, was badly wounded here and later honored by the state.
georgia/ga-revolution.e4d469654a7d: Don’t mix up: UGA was chartered in seventeen eighty-five but didn’t hold classes until eighteen oh one.
georgia/ga-revolution.ee11a0d3d19d: Savannah. Liberty Boys, a British capture and a failed siege. Liberty Boys met at Tondee’s Tavern in seventeen seventy-four to seventeen seventy-five to protest British laws. The Declaration of Independence was read aloud here on August tenth, seventeen seventy-six. British troops captured Savannah on December twenty-ninth, seventeen seventy-eight, and held it until July seventeen eighty-two. On October ninth, seventeen seventy-nine, a French-American attack on the British lines failed; Casimir Pulaski was mortally wounded.
georgia/ga-revolution.cee6067e6d0f: Augusta. Changed hands again and again. The British occupied Augusta in early seventeen seventy-nine, left, and returned in seventeen eighty. Elijah Clarke attacked it in September seventeen eighty but had to retreat. On June fifth, seventeen eighty-one, Patriots under Pickens, Clarke and Henry Lee forced the British to surrender Augusta. Georgia’s government met here from seventeen eighty-six until the capital moved to Louisville in seventeen ninety-six.
georgia/ga-revolution.5b4fd3c4455b: Midway and Sunbury. Georgia’s most eager Patriots. Saint John’s Parish sent Dr. Lyman Hall to the Continental Congress in seventeen seventy-five, before the rest of Georgia joined. Lyman Hall and Button Gwinnett both had ties to this parish. At Fort Morris in Sunbury, November seventeen seventy-eight, Colonel John McIntosh answered a British demand to surrender: “Come and take it!” Liberty County, created in seventeen seventy-seven, got its name from the parish’s Patriot spirit.
georgia/ga-revolution.1aa2a2bd0586: Milledgeville. The capital keeps moving west. Laid out as the new capital in eighteen oh three on land recently ceded by the Creek. Named for Governor John Milledge. The legislature first met here in eighteen oh seven; it stayed the capital until eighteen sixty-eight, when Atlanta took over.
georgia/ga-revolution.f4f06b32e2e2: Louisville. A town built to be the capital. Planned as a new capital closer to the center of the settled land. Named for King Louis the Sixteenth of France, who had helped the Americans win the war. In seventeen ninety-six the papers of the Yazoo land sale were burned here in public.

math/angles.f603a0b4da57: Do the same inside a right angle. Now the two parts always add to ninety degrees. Two angles that add to ninety degrees are called complementary.
math/angles.db5517fb7189: One angle is enough! Here one angle is one hundred fifteen degrees. Its vertical angle is also one hundred fifteen degrees. Its neighbours on the line are — one hundred eighty degrees minus one hundred fifteen degrees equals sixty-five degrees — and the bottom crossing copies the top. All eight angles from one.
math/angles.35b315ba8d56: Split a straight angle with a ray. However the ray turns, the two angles always fill the half turn, so they add to one hundred eighty degrees. Two angles that add to one hundred eighty degrees are called supplementary.
math/angles.28ce977f3677: Common mix-up: Complementary angles add to ninety degrees, supplementary to one hundred eighty degrees, C comes before S, just as ninety comes before one hundred eighty. And corresponding or alternate interior angles are equal only when the two lines are parallel.
math/angles.0cce647d8a7e: Two lines cross and make four angles. Turn one line: the angles change, but opposite angles always match. Why? a plus b equals one hundred eighty degrees and b plus c equals one hundred eighty degrees, so a equals c. Opposite angles like these are vertical angles, and they are always equal.
math/angles.e453f235ccaa: Now a triangle. Its angles measure about sixty-three degrees, fifty-one degrees and sixty-six degrees. Tear off the three corners and put them side by side: together they make a straight line, one hundred eighty degrees.
math/angles.9afe5917b5c8: An angle measures how far something turns. Spin the yellow ray: a quarter turn is ninety degrees, a right angle, a half turn is one hundred eighty degrees, a straight angle, and a full turn is three hundred sixty degrees.
math/angles.b10b37c71f16: Use it: a triangle has angles of forty-seven degrees and sixty-eight degrees. The third angle is — x equals one hundred eighty degrees minus forty-seven degrees minus sixty-eight degrees equals sixty-five degrees.
math/angles.8605c4f108a4: Why always? Draw a line through the top corner, parallel to the bottom side. The Z shapes are alternate interior angles, so copies of the two bottom angles fit along that line beside the top angle. A straight line is one hundred eighty degrees, so a plus b plus c equals one hundred eighty degrees in every triangle.
math/angles.1ace70b6077f: So all eight angles come in just two sizes. Matching corners are corresponding angles; the Z-shaped pair are alternate interior angles; both pairs are equal. Same-side interior angles add to one hundred eighty degrees. Tilt the transversal: it all stays true.

math/area.c65037c561bb: A triangle seems harder. The trick: take a second copy, turn it halfway around and attach it. Two identical triangles make a parallelogram with area b h, so one triangle has half: A equals one half times b h equals one half times five times three equals seven point five.
math/area.b462c12828a2: Now push the top sideways to make a parallelogram. Unit squares no longer fit neatly. The base is still five, and the height, measured straight up from the base, is still three, even though the slanted side got longer.
math/area.8f02397d4568: Cut off the triangle on the left along the height line and slide it to the right. It fits exactly! The parallelogram becomes a five times three rectangle, so its area is also — A equals b h equals fifteen.
math/area.de63688b9a55: Worked example: a house-shaped pentagon. Split it into a six times three rectangle and a triangle with base six and height two. Area equals eighteen plus one half times six times two equals eighteen plus six equals twenty-four square units.
math/area.3f325f1033d5: A trapezoid has two parallel bases, b one and b two. Same trick: a turned copy makes a parallelogram whose base is b one plus b two. So the trapezoid is half of it: A equals one half times the quantity b one plus b two, times h, equals one half times the quantity two plus five, times three, equals ten point five.
math/area.e59db2295e79: Every formula came from the same idea: rearrange the shape into one you already know. Rectangles and parallelograms: b h. Triangles: half a parallelogram. Trapezoids: half a parallelogram with base b one plus b two.
math/area.e8ee03485ea3: Common mix-up: The height is measured straight up, perpendicular to the base, not along the slanted side! And the triangle and trapezoid formulas both have a one half because each is half of a parallelogram.
math/area.91586d957797: Now slide the top corner left and right, parallel to the base. The triangle changes shape, even leaning outside its base, but the base and height stay the same, so the area never changes: still seven point five.
math/area.05d1e20bbaad: Area counts how many unit squares it takes to cover a shape. This rectangle has three rows of five squares, so its area is — five times three equals fifteen square units.

math/circle-theorems.b38e92859937: Two radii and the arc between them bound a sector. Let n degrees be the turn at the center along that arc and r be the radius. Divide n degrees by three hundred sixty degrees to find the fraction of a full turn. Multiply the circumference by that fraction for arc length, or multiply the full area by it for sector area.
math/circle-theorems.ba8c73f35c3d: A cyclic quadrilateral has all four vertices on one circle. Drag A or C and watch angle B and angle D change while their sum stays at one hundred eighty degrees.

math/circles.d7a8d3db9744: Now the area: how much space is inside? Slice the circle into eight equal pieces, like a pizza. All the yellow crust together is the circumference, two pi r.
math/circles.724254bff310: This number, the same for every circle, is called pi: pi equals C over d equals three point one four one five nine and so on, a decimal that never ends or repeats. So C equals pi d, and because d equals two r, also C equals two pi r.
math/circles.51a27f3cfc02: Common mix-up: Circumference, C equals two pi r, is a length, centimeters; area, A equals pi r squared, is an area, square centimeters. Area uses the radius: a circle with diameter ten centimeters has area pi times five squared, about seventy-eight point five square centimeters, not pi times ten squared.
math/circles.8f7e66b70ee5: Measure it with diameters: one, two, three, and a little bit more, about zero point one four of a diameter. So the circumference is a bit more than three diameters: C is about three point one four times d.
math/circles.db2d8e275126: Is that just this wheel? Unroll circles with diameters two centimeters, three point five centimeters and five centimeters. Bigger circles have longer circumferences, but C divided by d is always about three point one four, because every circle is a scale copy of every other circle.
math/circles.4311e4345d9c: Here is a wheel whose diameter, the blue line straight across the middle, is one unit. Mark the spot touching the ground. If the wheel rolls exactly one full turn, how far does it travel?
math/circles.0b9420656e8b: Try it with a thirty-centimeter pizza. The crust is — C equals pi times thirty, is about ninety-four point two centimeters. For area use the radius, fifteen centimeters: A equals pi times fifteen squared, is about seven hundred six point nine square centimeters.

yuwen/yw-classics.dcff64a1131c: Summer Palace. Today: Haidian, Beijing. A huge royal garden with Longevity Hill and Kunming Lake. Its Long Corridor is painted with more than fourteen thousand pictures.

yuwen/yw-expository.3463ece4ca12: Lugou, Marco Polo, Bridge. Today: southwest of Beijing. A stone bridge from eleven ninety-two with nearly five hundred carved lions. Japanese troops attacked here in nineteen thirty-seven, and all of China rose to resist.

yuwen/yw-hanzi.12b70dfaef28: Yin Ruins, Yinxu. Today: Anyang, Henan. Over one hundred fifty thousand oracle bones with the earliest Chinese writing were dug up here, and the eight hundred thirty-two kilogram Houmuwu Ding.

yuwen/yw-song-ci.9f04fec67217: Luoyang. Thirteen dynasties made Luoyang their capital. Near the city, the Longmen Grottoes hold about one hundred thousand Buddhist statues carved into the cliffs.
